title: Targets
text:
This project uses the targets package for pipeline management in R. The targets package helps to automate the workflow by defining a series of steps (targets) that depend on each other. Each target represents a piece of data or a computation, and targets ensures that only the necessary parts of the pipeline are re-executed when changes occur.
Here is a visual network showing the relationships between the targets in this project:

title: Lake Rotorua — GLM Configuration
text:
This page documents the General Lake Model (GLM v4) configuration used for simulating the lake’s thermal dynamics, water balance, and nutrient cycling. The model is coupled to the Aquatic EcoDynamics (AED) library for biogeochemical processes.
The AEME package was used to retrieve and format lake characteristics, boundary conditions, and monitoring data for model configuration and validation. The glm4.nml and aed.nml files define the physical and biogeochemical model parameters, respectively, while CSV files provide time series of inflows, meteorological forcing, and phytoplankton parameters.






Note



All simulation configuration files, scripts, and outputs documented here correspond to the baseline run (run_id: aeme_base).

title: Lake Rotorua — GLM Configuration
text:
Model schematic
The schematic below shows the overall GLM–AED model configuration for Lake Rotorua, including the principal inflows, outflow, atmospheric forcing, and the biogeochemical modules activated in this simulation.





  
    Show parameter labels
    
  
  
  


  
    
      Hypsograph & sediment zones
      
    
    
  
  
    
      AED biogeochemical modules
      
    
    
  











TipSchematic notes






Inflows: Four principal inflows are configured (Hamurana, Ohau, Waiowhiro, Waiteti streams). Loads are derived from monitored flow and water quality data (BoPRC).
Outflow: The Ohau Channel is the sole surface outflow; weir crest elevation set at 279.38 m a.s.l.
Meteorology: Half-hourly data from the Rotorua Airport NIWA station (agent 89894), gap-filled using ERA5 reanalysis where needed.
WWTP: Treated effluent from Rotorua WWTP is included as a point-source inflow.
AED modules active: NIT (nitrogen), PHO (phosphorus), OGM (organic matter), PHY (phytoplankton).
Sediment: 5-zone benthic configuration (benthic_mode = 2); zone-specific oxygen/N/P fluxes and sediment heat-model parameters from measured internal loading data — see the “Sediment zones” tab below.

title: Lake Rotorua GLM-AED calibration report
text:
This page documents the calibration work done on the Lake Rotorua GLM-AED model after the first biogeochemistry (step 2b) and alum (step 3) fits. Everything below was run on the project machine with the scripts in calibration/ (see Section 6); the figures come from website/images/. The page does not execute any code, so it renders without the model outputs.
What was done, in order

Reviewed why total N and total P and the nutrient species were still poorly fitted after step 2b, built budget tools (R/nutrient_budget_helpers.R), and tried three variants of the nutrient calibration (2c, 2d, 2e).
Read the AED source (libaed-water) and found structural reasons for the misfit: no sediment nitrate sink, inert P sorption, inert particulate organic matter, and sediment fluxes that are applied with an oxygen and temperature factor.
Found that the model was light-limited because its suspended solids were about 7 times too high (34 g/m³ against a few g/m³), with attenuation of 2.3 m⁻¹ against 0.8 observed. The biology had been tuned to a dark lake.
Calibrated the light and solids parameters (stage l), then recalibrated the phytoplankton and nutrients under the corrected light (f), then added diatoms with a silica supply and seasonal-cycle terms (g).
Switched the alum module on and calibrated the alum parameters to FRP and total P (alum), then tuned bottom-water oxygen and anoxia with alum on (o). Two further rounds (p, l2, o2) tested a joint FRP stage and a second light and oxygen fit.

Main limitations: surface FRP is about 45% low (high-FRP episodes are missed), the 2021-22 total P rebound is not reproduced, and there is no month-to-month skill for chlorophyll, total P or FRP (Section 5).

title: Lake Rotorua GLM-AED calibration report
text:
2 Set-up common to the stages

2.1 Model and data

Model: GLM v4 with AED. AED modules in the build: sedflux (constant 2D, four sediment zones), noncohesive solids, oxygen, silica, nitrogen, phosphorus, organic matter (with refractory pools), phytoplankton (cyanobacteria, greens, diatoms), totals and alum.
Forcing: hourly bias-corrected ERA5 (wind unscaled), 14 inflows including rainfall, geothermal and the wastewater plant, and the Ōhau weir outflow file.
Spin-up: 540 days in every run.
Two bases. The pre-alum base calibration/step2/aeme_base_1990_v2.rds has no alum dose in its inflows; the alum base calibration/step3/aeme_base_2005_alum.rds does (Utuhina from 2006-06, Puarenga from 2010 with a gap in 2019). Any alum calibration has to use the alum base. A first attempt on the pre-alum base gave 80 identical members because no alum entered the lake.
Observations: lake chemistry at two sites since 1990 (about 25 samples a year), buoy and sensor oxygen and temperature (dense from 2007), Secchi depth, the visible-light extinction coefficient (VLEC, 1996-2017), PAR profiles and turbidity.



2.2 Calibration method

Ensemble smoother with multiple data assimilation (ES-MDA) in calibration/step2/step2_ies.R: an ensemble of 60 to 120 parameter sets, 5 or 6 assimilation steps, parameters on a [0,1] scale (log where the range spans orders of magnitude), run in parallel. The final best member is the lowest-phi member of the last ensemble.
Residuals are in units of a stated tolerance, so each counts equally. The score phi is the mean squared residual. The standard nutrient score has bias and RMSE of log ratios for chlorophyll, total P, FRP, total N, nitrate and ammonium in the surface 0-5 m, five chlorophyll signature terms, and a temperature and oxygen guard. Later stages added terms (Table 1).
Stage switches are in calibration/step2/step2_common.R and chosen with the environment variable S2_STAGE. Each stage starts from the previous best member and fixes everything it does not free.
Unattended chains: calibration/step2/pipeline*.sh run a stage, then a 20- or 17-year forward run and the diagnostics, writing progress to calibration/logs/pipeline.status.



2.3 Diagnostic tools written







Tool
Purpose




R/nutrient_budget_helpers.R
nutrient_budget(), budget_table(), plot_nutrient_budget(): N and P budgets (t/yr) from the GLM mass-balance csv (inflow, outflow, stock change) and output.nc (denitrification, uptake, sediment fluxes)


R/phyto_limitation_helpers.R
phyto_limitation(), plot_phyto_limitation(): share of growth limited by light, N, P or silica, by month or hour


calibration/step2/run_forward.R
one forward run of a stage’s best member, with the mass balance written


calibration/anoxia/01_bottom_anoxia.R
observed against simulated bottom DO and anoxic days per water year


calibration/alum/01_alum_fit.R
FRP, total P and chlorophyll by year for an alum-on run


calibration/light/*.R
light data audit, model light check, resuspension sensitivity

3.1 Why the nutrient fit stalled (2c-2d)
Step 2b left total N and P well fitted but the species poorly fitted (FRP and ammonium too low, nitrate too high). Variant 2c anchored the sediment FRP and ammonium release to zone values that had been derived from zone-median summer concentrations. These are not measured fluxes, which I should have flagged. The result was worse: the release was recycled by the phytoplankton and settled out again (Table 2).



Table 2: Surface means from 20-year forward runs, 1990-2009.

The budgets showed why (Figure 1). In 2b the lake lost 355 t N/yr internally (71% of 502 t/yr inflow), of which 192 t/yr was water-column denitrification, and 11.6 t P/yr of a 29.4 t/yr input. In 2c the sediment ammonium release was 1,732 t N/yr and the FRP release 57 t P/yr (twice the external P load), yet the internal loss barely changed: the extra nutrient was taken up and lost again.






Figure 1: N and P budgets for the forward runs (2b, 2c, 2d, 2e members).





3.2 What the AED source showed
Reading libaed-water (and the alum module in AED_Tools_Private/libaed-dev) gave structural explanations, each confirmed against the model output:

No sediment nitrate sink. fsed_nit = 0 in all four sediment zones, and the linked SDF_Fsed_nit overrides aed_nitrogen’s own value. The only large N sink was water-column denitrification NIT_nit × Rdenit × Kdenit/(Kdenit+O2) × fT × NO3/(5+NO3), which the calibration pushed high even in oxic water.
Sediment fluxes are not the parameter value. The realised ammonium flux is Fsed_amm × Ksed_amm/(Ksed_amm+O2) × fT; with oxic bottom water this is about 12-14% of the parameter in summer.
P sorption was inert. ads_use_external_tss = .true. makes the module read an empty global tss instead of the simulated solids, so adsorbed P was about 2% of FRP and the sorption parameters kpo4p and w_po4ads had no effect. A test with the switch off (Table 3) showed that real sorption removes more P and worsens FRP, so it was left off.
Particulate organic matter was nearly inert. w_pom ended at -0.006 m/d, PON and POP hydrolysis rates imply timescales of years, resuspension is off and the sediment organic pools do not evolve; settled material is simply lost.
Alum pH efficiency is off. ads_use_pH = .false., so the alum factor fpH is 1; there is also no carbon module to supply pH.

3.3 Variant 2e: structural fixes
2e added a per-zone sediment nitrate flux (with Fsed_nit_model = 2), made Ksed_amm and Ksed_nit free, capped rdenit at 5, and widened the settling and hydrolysis ranges for POM. The calibration score fell to 0.59 (2b: 0.70) but the held-out score rose to 2.06 (2b: 1.48), so it overfitted. Sediment nitrate uptake became a large sink (288 t N/yr), chlorophyll was 16.1 µg/L and nitrate 2.4 times observed. The next diagnostic explained why.


3.4 Light limitation was the real problem
In AED the growth rate is R_growth × fT × min(fI, fNit, fPho, fSil). The growth-limitation function showed the light factor was the smallest for 80-90% of the biomass in every season (Figure 2), even with the daily output sampled at midday. Hourly output (nsave = 1, one year) confirmed this: the model output is in UTC, so the daily samples at 00:00 UTC were midday in New Zealand, and in daylight (PAR > 1) cyano was 70% light-limited and 30% P-limited, green 79% light, 15% N and 6% P.






Figure 2: Share of growth limited by each factor, by month, 2e member.



The light data audit (calibration/light/01_light_data.R) gave priors for the attenuation:

3.5 The light stage and the biology refit

l (10 parameters): epsilon, tau_0 and w_ss for both solids classes, Ke_ss, Kw and KePHY against Kd (VLEC or 1.85 / Secchi), TSS against 1.5 × turbidity, and a temperature guard. Score 0.51 → 0.34: mean TSS 4.8 g/m³ and Kd 0.62-0.72 m⁻¹ against 0.79 observed. Timing of resuspension was not captured (r about 0.1). Chlorophyll then rose to about 50 µg/L with P as the limiting factor, as expected.
f: biology and nutrients recalibrated with the light fixed. It tied 2b (score 0.70) and chlorophyll returned to 14.7 µg/L, but the seasonal cycle was wrong: model chlorophyll peaked in January-March (24-31 µg/L against 10-13 observed) and was about half the observed in July-October, so nitrate piled up in winter (0.07-0.11 against 0.02-0.035).
Silica. Silica was 1 mmol/m³ everywhere, so diatoms were always limited. With 150-300 mmol/m³, a September-October diatom bloom appeared (chlorophyll 10-14 µg/L against 5 µg/L) and October nitrate fell from 0.095 to 0.012-0.044 g/m³ (Table 6). AEME multiplies large SIL_rsi inputs by 16.64 (a g/m³ to mmol/m³ conversion applied above an unknown threshold), so the concentration is written directly into the built inflow files.
g: freed seven diatom parameters, set silica to 200 mmol/m³ (an assumption; no stream silica measurement was available) and added monthly-climatology terms for chlorophyll, nitrate, ammonium, FRP and total P to the score. This is the best biology so far: on the shared metrics the calibration score is 0.61 and held-out 1.32 (2b: 1.48).

3.6 Alum calibration
With alum on (step 3 alum base, 2005-2022, pools accumulating), the 2g member with the old step 3 alum values removed too much P (total P and FRP biased low). Eight alum parameters (w_ala, k_w, K_P, k_s, k_age_w, k_age_s, k_bur, k_res) were calibrated to FRP, total P, chlorophyll, nitrogen and aluminium, with tighter FRP scales than step 3.

The held-out years showed the weakness: observed total P rose from 0.014 g/m³ (2018) to 0.030 (2021) and 0.040 (2022), while the simulation stayed at 0.014-0.018. The dose record itself reproduces the Puarenga gap in 2019 (dose 0), so the model sees the dosing change. Round 2 widened the ranges and moved the calibration window to 2020-06; the best score was unchanged (0.50) and the full-period fit was slightly worse, so round 1 was kept. A joint stage (p) freeing the alum parameters and the sediment P release also gave no gain (best score stayed 0.52). The missing piece is probably an event-driven external P load in 2021-22 (the inflow P concentrations are nearly constant in the file) or alum-bound P release; a pH-dependent alum efficiency (fpH) would need a pH series and the carbon module (lake pH median 6.85, 5-95% range 6.06-7.82).

3.7 Bottom anoxia
The 2g member (alum off) reproduced the daily bottom oxygen at 17 m and deeper (r = 0.90, bias +0.25 mg/L) but underestimated anoxia: 96 anoxic days against 240 observed on the observed days, and none at all in 2008, 2009, 2012 and 2020. The depletion rate of bottom DO in October-February was also about half the observed in several years.
Stage o (alum on) freed the sediment oxygen demand in four zones, Ksed_oxy, theta_sed_oxy, rdom_minerl, rpoc_hydrol and theta_minerl, with the score extended by bottom-DO bias and RMSE, anoxic days and annual minimum per water year, and the depletion rate. Results over 2005-2022 are in Table 8.

title: Lake Rotorua GLM-AED calibration report
section: 4 Bugs and quirks found in the toolchain
text:
4 Bugs and quirks found in the toolchain

AEME get_var() now returns the simulated column named value, not sim; csps_pair() was updated.
Weir fit: the newer AEME fits a GLM weir by default, which breaks the nml check; glm_weir = FALSE is needed in the build to keep the outflow file.
wq_init_vals are about 1000 times too low (oxygen 0.32 against oxy_initial 312.5); the effect fades within about 1.5 years (differences below 5% after 1990), so the 540-day spin-up covers it.
Silica: inputs above an unknown threshold are multiplied by 16.64 on build.
No inflow_param(), and LKE_photich and RAD_secchi are not available as model output for glm_aed (naming entries only). Simulated Secchi is not available, so the light stage compares the extinction coefficient to the observed Kd.
Configuration switches (structural nml settings) must be written with write_configuration(); run_aeme_param() only edits parameters in an existing nml. R scripts must not be edited while a run is reading them.
Disk: the alum-on runs write about 6 GB per worker; eight workers filled the drive once. Use six workers and delete */runs/work and forward build folders after use.

title: Lake Rotorua GLM-AED calibration report
text:
5 Known limitations and next steps

FRP: surface FRP is about 45% low in the 2007-2022 mean. The model matches most years (observed values are often near detection) but misses episodes such as 2009 and the 2021-22 rebound.
Total P rebound in 2021-22 is not reproduced; an event-driven external load or alum-bound P release is the likely cause.
Timing: month-to-month correlation is about zero for chlorophyll, total P and FRP, and the light and solids timing (Kd r about 0.1) is not captured.
Alum pH efficiency (fpH) is off. Calibrating pH_opt and sigma_pH needs a prescribed pH series (the ph_mode option in aed_carbon).
Silica (200 mmol/m³) is an assumption; a stream measurement would replace it.
Choose the final member (O for anoxia, O2 for chlorophyll and bottom FRP) and rerun the NZESM scenarios and the alum/no-alum comparison with it. The scenario and uncertainty runs in calibration/scenarios30 and calibration/uncertainty were made with the earlier 2b and step 3 members and have not been rerun.

title: Lake Rotorua GLM-AED calibration report
text:
6 Reproducing the work
All stage scripts are in calibration/step2/, calibration/light/, calibration/anoxia/ and calibration/alum/. The parameter tables of the final members are in calibration/final/ (params_step2o_best.csv, params_step2o2_best.csv, plus the light round 2 and 2g members) with a README.
# one stage (example: the alum stage), 80 members x 6 iterations, 6 workers
powershell -File calibration/step2/run_step2alum.ps1

# forward run of a stage's best member (20 years, alum on)
S2_BASE=calibration/step3/aeme_base_2005_alum.rds FWD_STAGE=o FWD_ALUM=1 \
  FWD_START=2005-01-01 FWD_STOP=2022-06-29 Rscript calibration/step2/run_forward.R

# diagnostics
ANOX_RUN=o Rscript calibration/anoxia/01_bottom_anoxia.R
ALUM_RUN=o Rscript calibration/alum/01_alum_fit.R
FWD_STAGES=o Rscript calibration/step2/run_limitation.R
None of the new calibration folders (calibration/, R/phyto_limitation_helpers.R, R/nutrient_budget_helpers.R) and none of the new figure folders under website/images/ has been committed to git yet.

Code
library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(ggplot2); library(patchwork)
library(knitr); library(scales)   # ncdf4 is only needed to rebuild the summaries (helpers use ncdf4::)
source("../R/alum_scenario_helpers.R")

theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
            theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.background = element_blank()))

# Analysis window: the first two years of each run are spin-up (alum pools
# start at zero, so they are *not* in equilibrium before dosing history builds up).
WIN_START <- as.Date("2013-07-01")
WIN_STOP  <- as.Date("2021-06-30")
N_YR      <- as.numeric(WIN_STOP - WIN_START + 1) / 365.25
K_BUR     <- 0.01      # d-1, aed_alum burial rate in these runs (aed.nml default)
rm30 <- \(x) as.numeric(stats::filter(x, rep(1/30, 30), sides = 2))   # 30-day running mean

tags_all <- c("S0", "S1", "W_0.3", "W_1.0", "W_1.5", "W_5",
              "R_1.4", "R_0.5", "R_0.3", "R_0.15",
              "RES_0.001", "RES_0.01", "RES_0.1", "SURF")
tags <- tags_all[file.exists(file.path(alum_run_dir(tags_all), "output", "output.nc"))]
labels <- c(S0 = "S0 no alum", S1 = "S1 historical dose",
            `W_0.3` = "w_ala 0.3", `W_1.0` = "w_ala 1", `W_1.5` = "w_ala 1.5",
            W_5 = "w_ala 5",
            `R_1.4` = "capacity x1.43 (Al:P 0.7:1)", `R_0.5` = "capacity x0.5",
            `R_0.3` = "capacity x0.3", `R_0.15` = "capacity x0.14 (Al:P 7:1)",
            `RES_0.001` = "resusp k_res 0.001", `RES_0.01` = "resusp k_res 0.01",
            `RES_0.1` = "resusp k_res 0.1", SURF = "surface dose 0.1 mmol/m2/d")

runs <- lapply(setNames(tags, tags), read_alum_run)
lake <- bind_rows(lapply(runs, `[[`, "lake")) |>
  mutate(scenario = factor(scenario, tags, labels[tags]))
zone <- bind_rows(lapply(runs, `[[`, "zone")) |>
  mutate(scenario = factor(scenario, tags, labels[tags]))
lw <- lake |> filter(Date >= WIN_START, Date <= WIN_STOP)   # analysis window

lab <- function(t) factor(labels[[t]], labels[tags])
S0 <- "S0 no alum"; S1 <- "S1 historical dose"
pal <- c("S0 no alum" = "grey35", "S1 historical dose" = "#d95f02")

title: Alum scenarios in the Lake Rotorua GLM-AED model
text:
Purpose and set-up
This page summarises the full GLM-AED output (output.nc) of the alum scenarios run by scripts/alum/01_run_scenarios.R with the calibrated stage 1–3 parameters (calibration/checkpoints/final/), the real inflow/meteorological forcing and the reconstructed alum dosing history (Puarenga and Utuhina dosing, converted to an inflow ALU_ala concentration by calc_alum_inflow()). It follows the diagnostics used in the aed_alum stress tests, but applied to the lake rather than to idealised boxes.







Scenario
What changes




S0
no alum (ALU_ala = 0 in all inflows)


S1
historical dosing, default alum parameters (w_ala = 0.5 m/d, 1 mol P capacity per mol Al)


w_ala 0.3, 1, 1.5, 5
floc settling velocity: thesis central value 0.5 m/d, plausible range 0.3–1.5, 5 as a weakly-mixed upper bound


capacity x1.43 … x0.14
P-binding capacity per Al scaled onto the dosed inflows: 1.43 = jar test (Al:P 0.7:1), 0.14 = operational field value (~7:1)


resuspension
simResuspension on (thesis recommendation) with k_res 0.001, 0.01, 0.1 d⁻¹


surface dose
no inflow dosing; whole-lake S_ala = 0.10 mmol P/m²/d (the thesis’ mean-rate equivalent)



The settling velocities of 20–100 m/d in the thesis are for individually tracked large flocs (1–3 mm) in still water. The thesis explicitly treats them as upper bounds, because wind mixing keeps flocs suspended longer, and recommends 0.5 m/d (0.3–1.5) for the model. An earlier version of this page swept w_ala up to 100 m/d, which is outside that recommendation; it has been replaced by the thesis-based set above.
: Scenarios {.striped}


Code
cat("Scenarios found:", paste(tags, collapse = ", "), "\n")








Note



Interpret differences, not absolute values. The staged calibration fits lake P poorly (stage 3 FRP KGE < 0, positive FRP/TP bias), and the TP series is still rising through the first years of each run. Everything below is therefore expressed as alum minus no-alum (S1 − S0) wherever possible.


Units: concentrations are mmol P/m³ (1 mmol P/m³ = 31 µg P/L); masses are kg P; benthic pools are summed over the four sediment zones.

title: Alum scenarios in the Lake Rotorua GLM-AED model
text:
1. Inflow loading

1.1 P and Al loads by stream


Code
il <- read_alum_inflow_loads("S1", start = WIN_START, stop = WIN_STOP) |>
  mutate(wy = as.integer(format(Date + 184, "%Y")))   # water year ending 30 June

load_tab <- il |>
  group_by(stream) |>
  summarise(`Flow (Mm3/yr)` = sum(flow_m3d) / 1e6 / N_YR,
            `FRP (t P/yr)`  = sum(frp_kgd) / 1e3 / N_YR,

      caption = "Mean annual external loads over the analysis window (S1 inflow files).")

ann <- il |> group_by(wy) |>

p1 / p2




1.2 How much P-binding capacity is added relative to the P load?


Code
cap <- il |> summarise(
  Al_t = sum(al_kgd) / 1e3, cap_tP = sum(ala_kgd) / 1e3,
  TP_t = sum(tp_kgd) / 1e3, FRP_t = sum(frp_kgd) / 1e3)
kable(tibble(
  Quantity = c("Al dosed (t, window)", "P-binding capacity dosed (t P, 1 Al : 1 P)",
               "External TP load, all streams (t P)", "External FRP load, all streams (t P)",
               "Capacity / TP load", "Capacity / FRP load"),
  Value = c(cap$Al_t, cap$cap_tP, cap$TP_t, cap$FRP_t,
            cap$cap_tP / cap$TP_t, cap$cap_tP / cap$FRP_t)), digits = 2)


The nominal capacity added is a large multiple of the FRP actually delivered. Alum is dosed in streams that carry only part of the P load, so most capacity is expected to remain unused or be aged away (§5).

2. In-lake concentrations

tab <- lw |> group_by(scenario) |>
  summarise(FRP = mean(frp_mean) * 31, `FRP bottom` = mean(frp_bot) * 31,
            TP = mean(tp_mean) * 31, `Chl-a` = mean(chl_mean), .groups = "drop")

  mutate(`dFRP %` = 100 * (FRP / b$FRP - 1), `dTP %` = 100 * (TP / b$TP - 1),

2.1 Comparison with observations
Observations are the buoy/CTD/survey data held in the Aeme object (observations()$lake), averaged by day over the epilimnion (0–5 m) or hypolimnion (15–21 m; the model lake is 21 m deep). The model is sampled over the same depth bands (volume-weighted). The real lake was dosed, so S1 is the scenario to compare with the data; S0 shows how far the no-alum counterfactual departs from what was measured.


Code
obs <- read_alum_obs() |> filter(Date >= WIN_START, Date <= WIN_STOP)
vmap <- tribble(
  ~var_aeme,   ~band, ~col,       ~scale, ~panel,
  "PHS_frp",   "epi", "frp_epi",  31,     "FRP, epilimnion (ug P/L)",
  "PHS_frp",   "hyp", "frp_hyp",  31,     "FRP, hypolimnion (ug P/L)",
  "PHS_tp",    "epi", "tp_epi",   31,     "TP, epilimnion (ug P/L)",
  "PHS_tp",    "hyp", "tp_hyp",   31,     "TP, hypolimnion (ug P/L)",
  "PHY_tchla", "epi", "chl_epi",  1,      "Chl-a, epilimnion (ug/L)",
  "CHM_oxy",   "hyp", "oxy_hyp",  1,      "Oxygen, hypolimnion (mg/L)")
mod_long <- lw |> filter(scenario %in% c(S0, S1)) |>
  select(Date, scenario, all_of(vmap$col)) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(Date, scenario), names_to = "col") |>
  left_join(vmap, by = "col") |> mutate(value = value * scale)
obs_long <- obs |> inner_join(vmap, by = c("var_aeme", "band"))
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = mod_long, aes(Date, value, colour = scenario), linewidth = .35) +
  geom_point(data = obs_long, aes(Date, obs), size = .8, alpha = .6, colour = "black") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal, name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)




Code
# Model sampled on the observation date; bias = model - obs
ev <- bind_rows(lapply(split(vmap, seq_len(nrow(vmap))), \(m) {
  o <- obs |> filter(var_aeme == m$var_aeme, band == m$band)
  lake |> filter(Date %in% o$Date) |>
    transmute(Date, scenario, model = .data[[m$col]] * m$scale) |>
    inner_join(select(o, Date, obs), by = "Date") |> mutate(panel = m$panel)
})) |> filter(!is.na(model), !is.na(obs))
met <- ev |> group_by(panel, scenario) |>
  summarise(n = n(), `obs mean` = mean(obs), `model mean` = mean(model),
            bias = mean(model - obs), RMSE = sqrt(mean((model - obs)^2)),
            r = suppressWarnings(cor(model, obs)), .groups = "drop")
kable(met |> filter(scenario %in% c(S0, S1)), digits = 2,
      caption = "Model vs observations (S0 and S1) on observation dates, analysis window.")




Code
tab_obs <- ev |>
  filter(panel %in% c("TP, epilimnion (ug P/L)", "FRP, epilimnion (ug P/L)", "Chl-a, epilimnion (ug/L)")) |>
  group_by(panel, scenario) |>
  summarise(bias = mean(model - obs), RMSE = sqrt(mean((model - obs)^2)), .groups = "drop") |>

3.3 Internal FRP release and bottom-water oxygen
The sediment FRP input flux (fsed_frp, 0.003–0.010 mmol P/m²/d by zone) is not applied as-is: AED scales it by an oxygen half-saturation term, so the realised exchange PHS_frp_dsf is only a fraction of the potential SDF_Fsed_frp whenever the bottom water is oxygenated. Internal loading therefore depends on whether the bottom water goes anoxic.

            `Min hypolimnion O2 (mg/L)` = min(oxy_hyp),

            `Max hypoxic volume (%)` = 100 * max(hypox_vol),
            `Potential FRP flux (t P)` = sum(fsed_frp_kgd) / 1e3,
            `Realised FRP release (t P)` = sum(dsf_frp_kgd) / 1e3, .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(`Realised / potential (%)` = 100 * `Realised FRP release (t P)` / `Potential FRP flux (t P)`)
kable(ox, digits = 2, caption = "S1: bottom-water oxygen and internal FRP release by water year (first and last years are partial).")

  summarise(rel_t = sum(dsf_frp_kgd) / 1e3 / N_YR, pot_t = sum(fsed_frp_kgd) / 1e3 / N_YR)
kable(tibble(
  Quantity = c("Potential sediment FRP flux (t P/yr)", "Realised internal FRP release (t P/yr)",
               "External FRP load (t P/yr)", "External TP load (t P/yr)",

Warning



If the model never reaches anoxia while the observations do (compare the counts above), the realised internal release is a lower bound: the oxygen limitation is under-applied in the model, and any alum effect on internal loading cannot be tested. Check the hypolimnetic oxygen demand (stage-3 fsed_oxy, stratification) before calibrating alum against bottom-water FRP.

title: Alum scenarios in the Lake Rotorua GLM-AED model
section: 5. How much P does alum remove?
text:
5. How much P does alum remove?
For each scenario we integrate, over the analysis window:

Capacity dosed – ALU_ala delivered by the dosed inflows (kg P-equivalent).
P bound – FRP taken up by suspended alum (ALU_uptake_w × layer volume) plus FRP taken up by settled alum (ALU_uptake_s × zone area). These are direct model fluxes.
Where the bound P goes – GLM does not output the floc settling or burial fluxes, so they are inferred by mass closure from the pools:

exported: outflow volume × surface-layer ALU_alp;
settled to bed = water-column uptake − exported − Δ(suspended ALU_alp);
buried = settled to bed + benthic uptake − Δ(ALU_ben_alp).

As an independent check the burial implied by k_bur × ALU_ben_alp is also integrated; the ratio to the closure-implied burial should be ≈ 1.



Code
cap_by <- function(tag) {
  il <- read_alum_inflow_loads(tag, start = WIN_START, stop = WIN_STOP)
  cap <- sum(il$ala_kgd)
  if (tag == "SURF") {                       # S_ala (mmol P/m2/d) x surface area x days
    d <- lake |> filter(scenario == labels[["SURF"]], Date >= WIN_START, Date <= WIN_STOP)
    cap <- sum(0.10 * d$surface_area_m2) * MMOL_TO_KG
  }
  cap
}
bud <- lw |> group_by(scenario) |>
  arrange(Date) |>
  summarise(
    uptake_w = sum(uptake_w_kgd), uptake_s = sum(uptake_s_kgd),
    d_alp_w = last(alp_kg) - first(alp_kg),
    d_alp_s = last(ben_alp_kg) - first(ben_alp_kg),
    burial_kbur = sum(K_BUR * ben_alp_kg),
    exported = sum(overflow_m3 * alp_top) * MMOL_TO_KG,
    ala_end = last(ala_kg) + last(ben_ala_kg),
    .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(tag = tags[match(as.character(scenario), labels[tags])]) |>
  rowwise() |> mutate(capacity = cap_by(tag)) |> ungroup() |>
  mutate(removed = uptake_w + uptake_s,
         settled = uptake_w - exported - d_alp_w,
         buried  = settled + uptake_s - d_alp_s,
         kbur_ratio = burial_kbur / buried,
         eff = removed / capacity)

bt <- bud |> filter(scenario != S0) |>
  transmute(Scenario = as.character(scenario),
            `Capacity dosed (t P)` = capacity / 1e3,
            `Uptake: water (t P)` = uptake_w / 1e3,
            `Uptake: benthic (t P)` = uptake_s / 1e3,
            `Total bound (t P)` = removed / 1e3,
            `Efficiency (bound / capacity)` = eff,
            `Exported (t P)` = exported / 1e3,
            `Settled to bed (t P)` = settled / 1e3,
            `Buried (t P)` = buried / 1e3,
            `Pool change: water (t P)` = d_alp_w / 1e3,
            `Pool change: bed (t P)` = d_alp_s / 1e3,
            `k_bur check (ratio)` = kbur_ratio)
kable(bt, digits = 2, caption = "Alum phosphorus budget over the analysis window.")








Tip



Bound P ends up almost entirely in the sediment; the closure-implied burial and the k_bur × stock estimate should agree. A ratio well above 1 would mean the benthic pool is being drained faster than the closure allows (i.e. the reported benthic mass is inconsistent with the settling that fed it) and points at the benthic bookkeeping rather than at the lake result.




Code
fb <- bud |> filter(scenario == S1) |>
  transmute(`Pool change: water` = d_alp_w, `Pool change: bed` = d_alp_s,
            Buried = buried, Exported = exported) |>
  pivot_longer(everything()) |> mutate(value = value / 1e3)
ggplot(fb, aes(reorder(name, -value), value, fill = name)) + geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") + labs(x = NULL, y = "t P")

  transmute(Date, `water column` = cumsum(uptake_w_kgd) / 1e3,
            `benthic` = cumsum(uptake_s_kgd) / 1e3) |>
  left_join(mutate(il1, `capacity dosed` = cumsum(cap) / 1e3) |> select(Date, `capacity dosed`),
            by = "Date") |>
  mutate(`total bound` = `water column` + benthic) |>
  pivot_longer(-Date)
ggplot(cum, aes(Date, value, colour = name)) + geom_line() +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2", name = NULL) + labs(y = "t P (cumulative)", x = NULL)

            `Realised internal FRP release (t P/yr)` = sum(dsf_frp_kgd) / 1e3 / N_YR,
            .groups = "drop")
i0 <- inv |> filter(scenario == S0)
kable(inv |> mutate(`dTP stock vs S0 (t P)` = `TP stock, mean (t P)` - i0$`TP stock, mean (t P)`,
                    `dExport vs S0 (t P/yr)` = `TP export (t P/yr)` - i0$`TP export (t P/yr)`),
      digits = 2, caption = "Lake P inventory, outflow export and sediment release by scenario (potential = input flux; realised = after oxygen limitation, see 3.3).")

  select(Date, scenario, tp_kg) |> mutate(tp_kg = tp_kg / 1e3)

  scale_colour_manual(values = pal, name = NULL) + labs(y = "TP stock (t P)", x = NULL)

        `FRP (ug/L)` = FRP, `dFRP %` = 100 * (FRP / s0$FRP - 1),

         ) |>

p



6.1 P-binding capacity per Al (jar test vs field)
The thesis gives Al:P = 0.7:1 in the jar test but ~7:1 in the field. This is the largest unknown in how much of the dosed Al is available to bind lake P, and it acts like a scale factor on the dosed capacity.


Code
rs <- c(S1, "capacity x1.43 (Al:P 0.7:1)", "capacity x0.5", "capacity x0.3",
        "capacity x0.14 (Al:P 7:1)")

dr <- lw |> filter(scenario %in% c(S0, rs)) |>
  select(Date, scenario, tp_mean) |> pivot_wider(names_from = scenario, values_from = tp_mean) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(Date, all_of(S0))) |>
  mutate(d = rm30(value - .data[[S0]]) * 31)

  geom_line(linewidth = .4) + scale_colour_viridis_d(name = NULL, option = "C", end = .85) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(y = "ΔTP vs S0 (ug P/L)", x = NULL)




Code
ratio_tab <- ev |>
  filter(panel %in% c("TP, epilimnion (ug P/L)", "FRP, epilimnion (ug P/L)", "Chl-a, epilimnion (ug/L)"),
         scenario %in% c(S0, rs)) |>
  group_by(panel, scenario) |> summarise(bias = mean(model - obs), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(scale = c(1.43, 0.5, 0.3, 0.143, 1, NA)[match(as.character(scenario),
           c("capacity x1.43 (Al:P 0.7:1)", "capacity x0.5", "capacity x0.3",
             "capacity x0.14 (Al:P 7:1)", S1, S0))]) |> filter(!is.na(scale))

  geom_line() + geom_point() + scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  labs(x = "P-binding capacity per Al (relative to 1:1)", y = "Model − observed")




6.2 Resuspension
The thesis recommends resuspension on (alum is concentrated near-shore, fragile flocs), but gives no value for k_res. The runs below bracket it. Resuspension returns settled alum to the bottom water, so it should raise bottom-water alum-bound P and lower net burial.


Code
rl <- c(S1, "resusp k_res 0.001", "resusp k_res 0.01", "resusp k_res 0.1")
rl <- rl[rl %in% levels(lw$scenario)]
rr <- lw |> filter(scenario %in% rl)
pr1 <- ggplot(rr, aes(Date, ben_alp_kg / 1e3, colour = scenario)) + geom_line(linewidth = .4) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(name = NULL, option = "C", end = .85) + labs(y = "Settled ALU_alp (t P)", x = NULL)
pr2 <- ggplot(rr, aes(Date, alp_bot, colour = scenario)) + geom_line(linewidth = .4) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(name = NULL, option = "C", end = .85) + labs(y = "Bottom ALU_alp (mmol/m3)", x = NULL)
pr1 + pr2 + plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom")




6.3 Surface dose vs inflow dose
Dosing in the stream puts alum into the lake where the stream enters, with the stream discharge and P load. The surface-dose scenario applies the equivalent mean rate evenly over the lake, with the stream P load not carrying any alum. Compare the budget rows for “surface dose” and S1 above.


Code
sf <- lw |> filter(scenario %in% c(S0, S1, "surface dose 0.1 mmol/m2/d")) |>
  select(Date, scenario, frp_mean, tp_mean) |> pivot_longer(c(frp_mean, tp_mean))
ggplot(sf, aes(Date, value * 31, colour = scenario)) + geom_line(linewidth = .35) +
  facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1,
             labeller = as_labeller(c(frp_mean = "FRP (ug P/L)", tp_mean = "TP (ug P/L)"))) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(name = NULL, option = "C", end = .8) + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)

title: Alum scenarios in the Lake Rotorua GLM-AED model
text:
7. What to check next

Burial check – the k_bur ratio in §5 should be ≈ 1; if not, inspect the benthic bookkeeping (settling flux is not exported by GLM-AED; add a diagnostic).
w_ala – the thesis supports 0.5 m/d (0.3–1.5); the larger floc speeds it measured are quiescent upper bounds. Calibrate within about 0.3–1.5 (log scale), and only against FRP/TP in dosed years once the baseline FRP/TP bias is understood.
Capacity per Al – the jar-test (0.7:1) and field (~7:1) Al:P ratios span a factor of 10 in effective dose; this is likely a more influential unknown than w_ala and should be a calibration parameter (it scales the dosed ALU_ala).
Resuspension – recommended on by the thesis, k_res unconstrained.
pH efficiency – the thesis suggests pH_opt = 7, sigma_pH = 1, but this needs aed_carbon (for CAR_pH), which the lake configuration does not include; not tested here.
Identifiability – only lake FRP/TP/chl-a constrain the alum parameters (no Al or floc observations), so calibrate at most 3–4 parameters.
Natural experiment – Puarenga was not dosed in WY2020. The S1 − S0 response that year is a useful independent check on the dose–response.

Click to expand: Summary

Key Findings - Lake Barleber (Germany), an artificial gravel pit lake successfully remediated with aluminium sulphate in 1986, remained mesotrophic for nearly 30 years before undergoing sudden re-eutrophication in 2016–2017, with TP increasing from ~40 µg L⁻¹ to ~270 µg L⁻¹ and massive cyanobacterial blooms developing. - Internal P loading from sediments was identified as the primary driver of re-eutrophication; estimated P release for 2017 was approximately 600 kg for the whole lake, consistent with sediment incubation experiments showing significant P release only under anoxic conditions. - The reducible (redox-dependent, Fe/Mn-bound) P fraction (BD-P) constituted 37–58% of total P in surface sediments, indicating high sensitivity to reductive release under anoxia. - Temperature and anoxia acted synergistically: anoxic high-temperature incubations produced SRP release rates approximately five times higher than anoxic low-temperature treatments (0.94 ± 0.23 vs ~0.17 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹), confirming temperature as a major amplifying factor. - Multiple P-retention indicators (NaOH-Al:NaOH-P, NaOH-Al:(NH₄Cl+BD)-P, and Sum-Al:Sum-Fe ratios) were all below recommended thresholds, demonstrating that the Al adsorption capacity of the sediment had been substantially exhausted after three decades. - Sediment focusing and low sedimentation rates (estimated at ~0.9 cm yr⁻¹) in this closed, autochthonous lake are proposed as factors that prolonged initial treatment effectiveness by keeping the Al-rich layer near the sediment surface.
Aluminium Sulphate Treatment: Results - The 1986 treatment applied 480 tonnes of aluminium sulphate (36 g Al m⁻², 5.7 mg Al L⁻¹ volumetric dosage), which successfully restored the lake to clear water within one year, with macrophytes re-establishing and TP remaining low (173–373 kg lake-wide) for nearly 30 years — well above the mean treatment longevity of ~11 years reported for Al-treated lakes globally. - P fractionation of the 40 cm sediment core identified a distinct NaOH-Al and NaOH-P peak at 28–34 cm depth, consistent with the depth expected for the 1986 Al application given the estimated sedimentation rate, confirming that the Al layer persisted in the sediment but had been progressively buried and diluted. - NaOH-Al:NaOH-P molar ratios across the sediment column (3–6) were uniformly below the recommended thresholds of 10 (Rydin and Welch 2000) and 12.6 (de Vicente et al. 2008), indicating that Al adsorption capacity had been exhausted relative to the P pool. - The Sum-Al:Sum-Fe ratio decreased approximately 5-fold from its value at the time of Al application, falling below the threshold of >3 proposed as necessary to prevent P release, and the NaOH-Al:(NH₄Cl+BD)-P ratio of ~3 in the upper sediment was far below the recommended threshold of >25. - High background sulphate concentrations (~500 mg L⁻¹ before treatment, rising after Al addition) promoted sulphide formation, which permanently immobilised Fe as iron sulphides and reduced the active iron pool competing with Al for P binding — a mechanism specific to aluminium sulphate treatment that would not apply to poly-aluminium chloride. - Al floc formed during treatment is susceptible to resuspension by wind and benthivorous fish activity (both documented at Lake Barleber), meaning the Al-rich layer was continuously mixed with new, lower-P-binding sediment rather than remaining as a discrete buried stratum, further eroding treatment effectiveness over time. - The tipping point towards re-eutrophication followed a three-stage mechanism: (1) gradual exhaustion of Al adsorption capacity causes non-bound P to accumulate in the BD-P pool; (2) the BD-P pool approaches saturation, making the system vulnerable to anoxic release; (3) wind mixing events rapidly transport released P from the hypolimnion to the photic zone, triggering bloom formation that then self-reinforces through elevated sediment oxygen demand and further SRP accumulation.
Implications & Recommendations - Al treatment of lakes is not a permanent solution; longevity depends on Al dose/area, hydraulic residence time, lake morphology (Osgood index), sedimentation rate, and background sulfate concentrations — the latter promoting sulphide formation that immobilises Fe and reduces the active iron pool available for P binding. - Re-eutrophication risk is likely to increase under climate warming, as longer and more intense stratification periods will extend anoxic conditions and raise hypolimnetic temperatures, accelerating organic matter mineralisation and internal P loading. - Regular post-treatment monitoring of sediment P fractionation and Al retention molar ratios in the upper 5 cm is essential to detect declining P adsorption capacity before re-eutrophication occurs. - Poly-aluminium chloride is recommended in preference to aluminium sulphate, given that the high background sulphate concentration in Lake Barleber contributed to sulphide formation and loss of the active iron P-binding pool. - Many treated lakes will require repeated aluminium application to sustain acceptable water quality; this should be planned as part of long-term lake management rather than treated as a one-off intervention.

2022

Hamill (2022)
Trend and State of Nutrients in Lake Rotorua Streams 2002–2022.
River Lake Ltd for Bay of Plenty Regional Council.
PDF


Click to expand: Summary

The report focuses on nine major streams contributing to Lake Rotorua’s water quality. - Nutrient trends were assessed using the seasonal Kendall test over three periods: 2002-2022, 2002-2010, and 2010-2019. - The analysis includes total nitrogen (TN), total phosphorus (TP), and dissolved reactive phosphorus (DRP) concentrations and loads.
Nutrient Concentrations and Stream Flows This section details the mean flow rates and nutrient concentrations in the streams entering Lake Rotorua.

The mean flow to Lake Rotorua from 2002-2022 was 11.8 m³/s, with Hamurana being the largest contributor at 2.63 m³/s.
The highest total nitrogen concentrations were found in Waiohewa (2839 mg/m³) and the highest total phosphorus concentrations in Waingaehe (123 mg/m³).
Streams like Hamurana, Awahou, and Waingaehe showed high concentrations of dissolved reactive phosphorus (DRP), with ratios of DRP to TP between 80-90%.

Trends in Nutrient Concentrations Over Time This section discusses the observed trends in nutrient concentrations across the monitored streams.

From 2002 to 2022, TN concentrations increased in Hamurana, Awahou, and Waiteti, particularly in Awahou and Waiteti since 2010.
TN concentrations decreased in Puarenga and possibly Ngongotaha, but this trend did not continue post-2010.
TP concentrations increased in Hamurana, Ngongotaha, Utuhina, Puarenga, Waingaehe, and Waiohewa, with trends continuing since 2010 in all but Waingaehe.

Nutrient Loads to Lake Rotorua

The nine main streams transported an average of 410 t/y of nitrogen and 28 t/y of phosphorus from 2002-2022.
The highest TN loads came from Awahou (71.1 t/y), Puarenga (67.4 t/y), and Hamurana (66.5 t/y).
TP loads were primarily contributed by Hamurana (7.5 t/y), Puarenga (5.1 t/y), and Awahou (3.9 t/y).




Mangeya (2022)
Groundwater Modelling Report.
Jacobs for Bay of Plenty Regional Council (Toi Moana).


Click to expand: Summary

Project Background and Objectives
The Bay of Plenty Regional Council engaged Jacobs to develop a groundwater flow model for the Rotorua Water Management Area to enhance water management practices. The Rotorua Water Management Area covers approximately 1,100 km². The model aims to improve understanding of groundwater systems and surface water interactions. It will inform groundwater allocation limits and assess various abstraction scenarios.
Scope of Work for Groundwater Modelling
The project involved several key tasks to develop and document the groundwater model.

Analyze available data and create a conceptual hydrogeological model.
Develop and calibrate a transient three-dimensional numerical groundwater flow model using MODFLOW.
Simulate predictive scenarios and document the model development and predictions.
Deliver the numerical model and associated files to the Bay of Plenty Regional Council.

Limitations of the Groundwater Modelling

The model does not account for certain factors that could affect groundwater and surface water quality.
Excludes the impact of groundwater extraction on water quality. Does not consider density effects from variable groundwater salinity or temperature. Ignores two-phase fluids in the active geothermal reservoir.

Estimated catchment loads of nitrogen and phosphorus to the Rotorua Te Arawa Lakes.
ERI report 143, University of Waikato.
PDF


Click to expand: Summary

Importance and Context

Rotorua Te Arawa Lakes are culturally, historically, and ecologically significant.
Water quality varies with catchment characteristics: undeveloped (e.g., Tikitapu, Okataina) vs. highly developed agricultural/forestry (e.g., Rotorua, Rerewhakaaitu, Okaro).
Lake water quality is strongly influenced by nutrient inputs from surface and groundwater flows.

Methodology for Nutrient Loads

Used updated export coefficient approach and Overseer® modelling for nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P).
Land use areas calculated for surface and groundwater catchments.
Nutrient loss rates estimated per land use, accounting for local factors (e.g., pest impacts, forest removal).
Additional sources included geothermal inputs, septic systems, municipal wastewater, atmospheric deposition, and hydrological connections among lakes.
Attenuation estimated from physiography to produce a consistent regional nutrient budget.

Key Findings and Implications

Agricultural land contributes disproportionately to N and P loads.
Geothermal, atmospheric, and connected-lake sources are significant in some catchments.
Many catchments exceed ‘reference’ nutrient loads by 2–3×, complicating restoration.
Provides basis for assessing internal lake loading and guiding catchment/lake management strategies.

Modeling the effects of climate change on water quality of Lake Rotorua, New Zealand.


Click to expand: Summary

Modelling Hydrology and Water Quality This study integrates a catchment model with a lake water quality model to assess the impacts of nutrient load reductions and climate change on a eutrophic lake.

The study combines SWAT and DYRESM–CAEDYM models to simulate nutrient dynamics and water quality.
The models performed satisfactorily in simulating observed data, indicating accurate representation of key processes.
Nutrient load reductions from agricultural practices had minor effects on lake nutrient concentrations.
Climate change projections for 2090 showed significant impacts on nutrient levels and water quality.

Nutrient Load Reductions and Their Effects The study evaluates how reducing nutrient loads affects the trophic state of Lake Rotorua.

Simulations indicated that reducing fertilizer and wastewater irrigation had limited impact on lake nutrient concentrations.
The projected climate change for 2090 is expected to increase internal nutrient loading significantly.
Polymictic lakes like Lake Rotorua are particularly vulnerable to eutrophication due to climate change.

Climate Change Impacts on Water Quality This section discusses the influence of climate change on hydrological cycles and nutrient dynamics.

Increased precipitation is predicted to raise total phosphorus loads by 3.3%–16.5% in Danish streams.
A study in Slovenia projected total nitrogen losses could increase by 5.3% to 80.2% due to climate change.
Climate change is expected to directly affect lake water temperature and stratification, altering nutrient dynamics.

title: Resources
text:
2016

Smith et al. (2016)
Phosphorus and nitrogen loading restraints are essential for successful eutrophication control of Lake Rotorua, New Zealand. PDF


Click to expand: Summary

Key Findings - Generalised additive models applied to a 14-year (2001–2015) dataset from Lake Rotorua found highly significant (p < 0.001) declines in total phosphorus (TP), total nitrogen (TN), and chlorophyll a (Chl-a) in surface waters, refuting claims that water quality had continued to decline despite mitigation. - Alum dosing in the Utuhina and Puarenga Stream inflows had a highly significant reducing effect on TP and Chl-a (p < 0.001), with near 4-fold reductions in Chl-a at maximum dosing rates, but no significant effect on TN. - Correlations of Chl-a with both TP and TN were highly significant, and the difference between the two correlation coefficients was not significant, indicating that algal productivity responds to both nutrients rather than either alone. - Bioassay studies in Lake Rotorua consistently demonstrated co-limitation of phytoplankton growth by both N and P, with spatial and temporal variation in which nutrient was more limiting. - Policies focused solely on reducing N loads risk stimulating dominance by heterocystous, N₂-fixing cyanobacteria (e.g. Dolichospermum, Aphanizomenon), whose bloom concentrations are strongly correlated with water column TP.
Implications & Recommendations - Both N and P loads to Lake Rotorua must be controlled simultaneously for effective eutrophication management; a single-nutrient strategy is insufficient and potentially counterproductive. - Alum dosing in tributary inflows is effective for short-term P reduction but is not recommended as a perpetual measure; its continuation should be contingent on progress in catchment-scale land-use change and nutrient runoff mitigation. - Achieving the target Trophic Level Index of 4.2 requires TN loads below 435 t y⁻¹ and TP loads below 37 t y⁻¹ — major reductions from current inputs dominated by agricultural land use (~75% of N load, ~45% of P load). - “Legacy P” stored in fertilised soils and streambed sediments, and long groundwater residence times (decades to over a century), mean that water quality responses to catchment management will be substantially lagged and require long-term commitment. - Continued monitoring of nutrients, Chl-a, and cyanobacterial biovolume should be maintained to track restoration trajectories and evaluate the relative contributions of alum dosing versus catchment management.

title: Resources
text:
2015

Abell et al. (2015)
Lake Rotorua Treated Wastewater Discharge: Environmental Effects Study ERI Report 80, University of Waikato. PDF


Click to expand: Summary

Key Findings

The treated wastewater discharge contributes a measurable nutrient load to Lake Rotorua, which may influence the lake’s trophic status, algal growth, and water-quality trends.
There is evidence of spatial variability in how the discharge impacts the lake — e.g., nearer to the discharge site showing different water quality versus more remote parts of the lake.
The effectiveness of the current wastewater treatment and discharge regime is assessed and found to have limitations: even treated wastewater can contribute significant nutrient inputs if volumes are large and/or treatment is not optimised.
The report discusses the lake’s capacity to assimilate or dilute the nutrient load, and whether it is being exceeded or approaching thresholds that may degrade ecological health.

Implications & Recommendations

Management of wastewater inputs to Lake Rotorua must account not just for concentration of nutrients in the effluent but for volume of discharge and how that interacts with lake hydrodynamics (mixing, stratification, residence time).
Upgrading treatment processes, reducing nutrient concentrations further, or reducing the volume of discharge may be necessary to protect lake health.
Monitoring of water quality and ecological responses (algal blooms, oxygen levels, benthic habitat) should continue and be linked explicitly to discharge data to evaluate trends.
Lake management strategies should take a holistic view: catchment land-use, inflows, internal nutrient cycling, and wastewater discharges all interact to determine lake condition.

Click to expand: Summary

Lake Rotorua’s Water Quality Challenges Lake Rotorua has faced significant water quality decline due to nutrient loads and land use changes, necessitating a comprehensive management strategy.

Lake area: 80 km², mean depth: 10 m.
Cultural significance to the Te Arawa people and vital for tourism and recreation.
Water quality deterioration began in the 1960s, linked to treated wastewater inputs and land use changes from forest to pasture.
Urban wastewater discharge ceased in 1991, but ongoing pastoral expansion, especially dairy farming, has continued to impact water quality.
Legacy effects from historical land use and nutrient pools in sediments complicate current management efforts.

Modelling Approach for Water Quality Management A modelling approach is essential for assessing the impacts of land use, climate change, and management actions on Lake Rotorua’s water quality.

Integrated multiple models: SimCLIM, ROTAN, CLUES, DYRESM-CAEDYM.
SimCLIM predicts climate data (temperature, rainfall) for the Rotorua catchment up to 2100.
ROTAN simulates streamflows and nitrate transport between surface water and groundwater.
CLUES estimates annual average phosphorus loads in streams.
DYRESM-CAEDYM models vertical distribution of water temperature and nutrient cycling relevant to trophic state.

Nutrient Load Reduction Requirements To improve water quality, significant reductions in nitrogen and phosphorus loads are necessary.

At least 350 tonnes of nitrogen and a similar amount of phosphorus must be removed annually.
Target Trophic Level Index (TLI) value set at 4.2 to restore water quality.
Climate change is expected to exacerbate challenges, increasing stratification and internal nutrient loading.
Internal nutrient release from sediments is comparable to external loads, complicating management.

Internal Nutrient Loading and Management Strategies Addressing internal nutrient loading is critical for achieving long-term water quality goals in Lake Rotorua.

Internal loading from sediments contributes significantly to nutrient levels, especially during stratification.
Chemical flocculants may reduce internal loading but have limited duration of effectiveness (approximately four years).
Effective sediment capping can offset water quality deterioration but requires prior reduction of catchment nutrient loads.

title: Lake Rotorua V4 - GLM-AED output plots
text:
0. Helpers
profile_vars/zone_vars are read straight off the NetCDF file’s dimensions (AEME has no catalogue of “every variable in this output” — it only knows the variables it has a name mapping for), so this is the one place raw ncdf4 is used outside the sediment-heat section. get_var() happily accepts either the AED name ("OXY_oxy") or AEME’s own name ("CHM_oxy") for everything found this way.


Code
nc <- nc_open(outfile)
var_dims <- sapply(names(nc$var), function(v) sapply(nc$var[[v]]$dim, `[[`, "name"))

profile_vars <- names(var_dims)[sapply(var_dims, function(d) "z" %in% d)]
zone_vars    <- names(var_dims)[sapply(var_dims, function(d) {
  "nzones" %in% d && !"z" %in% d && !"sed_layers" %in% d
})]

long_name <- function(var) {
  v <- nc$var[[var]]
  if (is.null(v)) return(var)
  sprintf("%s (%s)", if (nzchar(v$longname)) v$longname else var, v$units)
}

cat(sprintf("%d profile variables, %d zone variables\n", length(profile_vars), length(zone_vars)))


160 profile variables, 37 zone variables


Code
# A handful of AED variable names aren't recognised by AEME's fuzzy matcher even
# though they're just renamed internally (e.g. dissolved oxygen is `CHM_oxy`, not
# `OXY_oxy`) - resolve those explicitly rather than letting get_var() error.
var_alias <- c(OXY_oxy = "CHM_oxy")
resolve_var <- function(var) unname(ifelse(var %in% names(var_alias), var_alias[var], var))

#' GLM writes each layer against a moving Lagrangian grid, so `get_var()`'s depths
#' don't line up day to day - interpolate onto a common depth-below-surface grid
#' before tiling, or the heatmap comes out as sparse, misaligned slivers.
grid_profile <- function(df, nz = 150) {
  depths <- seq(0, max(df$depth, na.rm = TRUE), length.out = nz)
  df |>
    group_by(Date) |>
    group_modify(~ data.frame(depth = depths,
                               value = approx(.x$depth, .x$value, xout = depths, rule = 2)$y)) |>
    ungroup()
}

#' Depth-time heatmap for a (lon, lat, z, time) variable, via AEME::get_var()
plot_profile <- function(var, cmap = "viridis") {
  df <- get_var(aeme, model = "glm_aed", var_sim = resolve_var(var), remove_spin_up = FALSE) |>
    grid_profile()
  ggplot(df, aes(x = Date, y = depth, fill = value)) +
    geom_raster() +
    scale_y_reverse() +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = cmap, na.value = NA) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "depth (m)", fill = NULL, title = var,
         subtitle = long_name(var)) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 10), plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 8))
}

#' One line per sediment zone for a (lon, lat, nzones, time) variable
plot_zone <- function(var) {
  df <- get_var(aeme, model = "glm_aed", var_sim = resolve_var(var), remove_spin_up = FALSE)
  ggplot(df, aes(x = Date, y = value, colour = factor(nzones))) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = "zone", title = var, subtitle = long_name(var)) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 9), plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 7),
          legend.position = "bottom")
}

title: Lake Rotorua V4 - GLM-AED output plots
text:
1. Lake-level summary
plot_wlev() and plot_wbal() are AEME’s built-ins for the two standard GLM diagnostics; the temperature and heat-balance panels are assembled from get_var() since AEME has no single “lake summary” plot for them.


Code
temp_panel <- bind_rows(
  get_var(aeme, model = "glm_aed", var_sim = "surface_temp") |> mutate(series = "Surface Temp"),
  get_var(aeme, model = "glm_aed", var_sim = "max_temp")     |> mutate(series = "Max Temp"),
  get_var(aeme, model = "glm_aed", var_sim = "min_temp")     |> mutate(series = "Min Temp")
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Date, y = value, colour = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Surface Temp" = "firebrick", "Max Temp" = "darkorange",
                                  "Min Temp" = "steelblue")) +
  labs(title = "Surface / max / min temperature (degC)", x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")


✔ Variable 'surface_temp' matched to 'HYD_surft'.


Code
heat_panel <- bind_rows(
  get_var(aeme, model = "glm_aed", var_sim = "LKE_Qsw") |> mutate(series = "Qsw"),
  get_var(aeme, model = "glm_aed", var_sim = "LKE_Qe")  |> mutate(series = "Qe"),
  get_var(aeme, model = "glm_aed", var_sim = "LKE_Qh")  |> mutate(series = "Qh"),
  get_var(aeme, model = "glm_aed", var_sim = "LKE_Qlw") |> mutate(series = "Qlw")
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Date, y = value, colour = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "Heat balance components", x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

lake_summary <- (plot_wlev(aeme, model = "glm_aed") | plot_wbal(aeme, model = "glm_aed")) /
  (temp_panel | heat_panel)
lake_summary

title: Lake Rotorua V4 - GLM-AED output plots
text:
4. Dynamic sediment heat model
sed_heat_model = 2 gives every sediment zone a vertical soil-temperature profile, integrated by zZSoilTemp with the zone-average water temperature as its surface boundary condition. This is a (time, nzones, sed_layers) array with no AEME variable mapping, so it’s read directly from the NetCDF file.
What to look for: the seasonal signal should damp and lag with depth, and the deepest node should be flat.


Code
nc <- nc_open(outfile)  # reopen: the handle from the setup chunk is no longer valid after AEME reads the file
sed_temp  <- ncvar_get(nc, "sed_temp")        # (sed_layers, nzones, time)
sed_depth <- ncvar_get(nc, "sed_layer_depth") # (sed_layers)
zone_ztemp <- ncvar_get(nc, "zone_ztemp")     # (nzones, time)
sed_hf     <- ncvar_get(nc, "sed_heatflux")   # (nzones, time)
time_vals  <- as.Date(ncvar_get(nc, "time") / 24, origin = strsplit(ncatt_get(nc, "time", "units")$value, "since ")[[1]][2])
n_zone     <- dim(sed_temp)[2]

cat("sediment nodes (m below SWI):", round(sed_depth, 3), "\n")


sediment nodes (m below SWI): 0 0.02 0.05 0.1 0.2 0.4 0.8 1.5

sed_df <- expand.grid(layer = seq_len(dim(sed_temp)[1]), zone = seq_len(n_zone), t = seq_along(time_vals)) |>
  mutate(Date = time_vals[t], depth = sed_depth[layer], value = sed_temp[cbind(layer, zone, t)])
water_df <- expand.grid(zone = seq_len(n_zone), t = seq_along(time_vals)) |>
  mutate(Date = time_vals[t], value = zone_ztemp[cbind(zone, t)])

sed_temp_plot <- ggplot(sed_df, aes(x = Date, y = value, colour = sprintf("%.2f m", depth))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = water_df, aes(colour = "water"), linewidth = 0.9, colour = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~ sprintf("zone %d", zone - 1), ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "degC", colour = NULL, title = "Sediment temperature profile by zone") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Bay of Plenty Regional Council’s Ōhau Channel at SH33 (site FL230406) is the outlet of Lake Rotorua. The bulk export (ohau_wq_url, read by read_bop_lab_csv_url() into the ohau_wq_data target) has seven lab variables: NH4-N, nitrate plus nitrite N (NNN), total N (TN), dissolved reactive P (DRP), total P (TP), total suspended solids (TSS) and water temperature. section: 2 Open item: changes in laboratory and method
text:
2 Open item: changes in laboratory and method
To check (Tadhg). There may have been a change in sampling methodology or laboratory testing somewhere in the record. Nothing in the export documents it, so none of the trends, steps or period comparisons below should be read as real until it is resolved. Two boundaries are visible in the portal metadata:

2015-07-05: the record changes from “Labstar - Legacy Data” to “Routine”, for every variable at once (the last legacy sample is 2015-06-15).
2020-12 to 2021-01: the grade codes change from 200 (all data to 2020-12-06) to 400, 500 and 600 (all data from 2021-01-17).

The TP and DRP step in 2011 to 2012 and the 1993 to 1995 peak do not line up with either boundary, so they may be real, or they may come from a change that the metadata does not record (a laboratory, a method, a detection limit or a sampling depth). To find out: the BOPRC data owner for FL230406, the laboratory method history for TP, DRP and TN, any change in reporting limits (many DRP and nitrate values are at or near zero), and the sampling depth and position at SH33. Until then, treat the step as a result that needs this check, in particular where it is used as evidence for the model’s early-dosing response.

title: Ōhau Channel water quality
text:
3 Time series








Figure 1: Ōhau Channel lab results, 1985 to 2026. Grey: legacy data; blue: routine data. Black line: annual median. Dashed lines: the start of dosing on the Utuhina (2006-06-15) and Puarenga (2010-01-14).






Phosphorus fell, and not at the start of dosing. The annual median TP stayed near 0.04 g/m³ until 2010 (0.043, 0.041, 0.037, 0.037 and 0.033 g/m³ in 2006 to 2010) and dropped to 0.023 in 2011 and 0.014 in 2012. DRP shows the same step, from a median of 0.008 g/m³ before dosing to 0.003.
Nitrogen did not fall. TN has a median of 0.33 g/m³ from 2009. Nitrate plus nitrite is higher after 2010.
Early data are noisy. The 1993 to 1995 peak in TP, DRP and NH4-N is unexplained. It is worth checking before using the 1990s data as a baseline.

The model’s TP is too low once alum is applied, and the shortfall starts early. With alum the model TP median is 0.020 g/m³ against 0.038 observed in 2005 to 2010 (-42%), and 0.015 against 0.024 in 2011 to 2022 (-37%). The no-alum run matches the observed TP before 2010 (-4%) and is 98% too high afterwards. The observed outlet TP did not fall during the Utuhina-only years (median 0.038 against 0.041 before), but the model falls to 0.02 within about two years of the first dose.
This corrects an earlier statement. The TP low bias is not confined to 2011 onwards. It is already there in 2006 to 2010, and the lake TLp is 0.39 too low in that period (and 0.30 and 0.33 in 2011 to 2016 and 2017 to 2022). The model response to the first dosing is too fast or too strong, or the observed system had offsetting increases in load that the model lacks.
DRP is about right. With alum the model is +35% (2005 to 2010) and -37% (2011 to 2022) at values of a few mg/m³, whereas without alum the model’s median DRP is about 4 times (2005 to 2010) and 10 times (2011 to 2022) the observed value. The observed DRP is therefore a strong case that alum or an equivalent sink is operating.
TN is good. With alum the TN bias is +2% for 2011 to 2022 (0.337 against 0.322 g/m³) and the correlation is 0.31. The no-alum run is 49% too high.
NH4-N and nitrate are close in level but not in timing. The bias is -17% to -30% for NH4-N and about +7% to -27% for nitrate, with correlations of 0.5 for nitrate in 2011 to 2022 and near zero for NH4-N.
TSS is 25% to 45% low and uncorrelated (correlation 0.16 to 0.24). TSS was never a calibration target. Possible causes, not tested here, are missing wind resuspension and particles from storm inflows, which would also fit the model’s weak Secchi response in the TLI analysis.
Temperature is right. The correlation is 0.95, the bias in the mean is within 3% and the RMSE is 1.6 °C.
Year-to-year and monthly skill is low for the nutrients (correlations from -0.15 to 0.16 for TP, DRP and NH4-N), so the model reproduces levels and the alum response, but not individual months.

title: Ōhau Channel water quality
text:
10 What this suggests

The outlet TP is a stronger test of the alum response than the lake sites alone: it shows no change during the Utuhina-only years and a step to 0.02 g/m³ in 2011 to 2012. The model shows the opposite sequence. A reason to check is whether the Utuhina dosing in 2006 to 2010 is too effective in the model (the in-stream binding fraction, or the alum parameters), or whether other inputs rose then.
The outlet TN and DRP data constrain the model well enough to be used as extra calibration data, in particular TN, which the lake record has only occasionally.
The nitrate difference between the outlet and the lake sites needs an explanation before either is used as the target for nitrate.

text: Simulating pH

title: Lake Rotorua Modelling
text:
The Problem
pH ignores pH_initial because it’s diagnostic, not prognostic

aed_carbon tracks DIC as a conserved state variable; pH is recomputed every timestep from DIC + Total Alkalinity via CO2SYS — pH_initial is only the solver’s first guess
Default alk_mode = 1 hardcodes a salinity regression fit to Caboolture, QLD — no general-purpose option, no way to supply real TA data
id_talk (a TA state variable ID) is declared in aed_carbon.F90 but never registered — the intended dynamic TA path was never finished


alk_mode = 0 is also broken — CO2SYS calls are commented out and the solver never converges. Modes 1–5 are all site-specific Queensland regressions. Nothing in the shipped module supports user-supplied alkalinity.

title: Lake Rotorua Modelling
text:
The Fix: alk_mode = 6
New option on branch feature/fixed-alkalinity-mode — bypasses every regression:
&aed_carbon
   alk_mode   = 6
   talk_fixed = 2200.0   !# Total Alkalinity, umol/kg
/

talk_fixed defaults to NaN — mode 6 without it fails loudly at startup
Get talk_fixed from real TA measurements, or back-solve from (DIC, observed pH) via PyCO2SYS
Observed pH becomes a validation target, not a model input
Higher TA → higher pH; response is nonlinear, steepest near pKa values (~6.3, ~10.3)
Verified with clean compile and full library build — not yet run end-to-end through GLM
If a single constant isn’t sufficient, the next step is finishing id_talk as a real dynamic state variable with a depth-varying initial profile

title: Rotorua Light
text:
Lake Rotorua’s GLM-AED setup needs a light extinction (Kw) parameterisation. The options considered were:

A single static Kw (one value for the whole run).
A monthly Kw climatology (12 calendar-month values, time-varying).
A fully dated time-varying Kw built from the observed record.
A decomposed background Kw (observed Kw minus the fraction attributable to phytoplankton/turbidity), for use when AED’s own biology should generate the biotic part of light extinction dynamically.

This document works through the diagnostics behind that decision for the Rotorua PAR/Kd record, and lands on a recommendation for the climate scenario runs specifically (as opposed to a historical hindcast).
The helper functions used throughout live in R/recommend_light_parameterisation.R.

title: Rotorua Light
text:
Lake Rotorua’s GLM-AED setup needs a light extinction (Kw) parameterisation. The options considered were:

A single static Kw (one value for the whole run).
A monthly Kw climatology (12 calendar-month values, time-varying).
A fully dated time-varying Kw built from the observed record.
A decomposed background Kw (observed Kw minus the fraction attributable to phytoplankton/turbidity), for use when AED’s own biology should generate the biotic part of light extinction dynamically.

This document works through the diagnostics behind that decision for the Rotorua PAR/Kd record, and lands on a recommendation for the climate scenario runs specifically (as opposed to a historical hindcast).
The helper functions used throughout live in R/recommend_light_parameterisation.R.

title: Rotorua Light
section: Static vs. time-varying Kw: the trade-offs
text:
Static vs. time-varying Kw: the trade-offs
Time-varying Kw (monthly or dated) can capture real seasonal drivers of light attenuation — spring runoff/turbidity pulses, algal self-shading, CDOM inputs, ice-off resuspension — that a single Kw cannot. Where good profile data exist, throwing that signal away by collapsing to one number misrepresents both the clear and the turbid periods.
The trade-offs:

More data wrangling and another forcing file to QC.
Monthly resolution still misses short-lived bloom/storm spikes.
If Kw has been used as a tuning knob to compensate for other model deficiencies (mixing scheme, inflow temperatures), imposing an independently-derived time-varying Kw removes that degree of freedom and can expose calibration problems elsewhere.
A poorly-constrained time-varying curve (built on noisy or sparse data) is worse than a well-chosen static value.

Static Kw is defensible when extinction is dominated by relatively stable factors, when supporting data are too sparse/noisy to justify more resolution, or — as turns out to matter most here — when there is no calendar correspondence between the simulated period and the observed record, which is exactly the case for a forward climate scenario.

title: Rotorua Light
text:
GLM-AED’s own light feedback
When AED is coupled to GLM with bioshade_feedback = .true., light extinction is not just the prescribed Kw — GLM adds AED’s own simulated biotic/particulate extinction on top, additively (glm_aed.F90, update_light):
par(i) = par(i+1) * EXP( -(Kw + localext_up) * dz(i+1) )
IF (bioshade_feedback) extc(i) = Kw + localext
localext is the sum of whatever AED modules contribute a light-extinction diagnostic — in this setup that includes:

aed_phytoplankton — self-shading from simulated chlorophyll.
aed_noncohesive — extinction from simulated suspended sediment, Ke_ss(i) * SS_conc(i) summed across size classes. The active configuration:

&aed_noncohesive
   num_ss = 2
   ss_initial = 3, 1
   Ke_ss = 0.06, 0.06
   settling = 1
   w_ss = 0.5, 0.03
   rho_ss = 1800, 1200
   d_ss = 2e-05, 4e-06
   resuspension = 1
   epsilon = 0.02
   tau_0 = 0.04, 0.03
   tau_r = 1
   fs = 1, 1
   Fsed = 0, 0
   decay = 0, 0
   simSedimentMass = .false.
   sed_porosity = 0.3
   diag_level = 10
/
Practical consequence: the prescribed Kw/Kw_file should represent only the background (non-biotic, non-suspended-sediment) extinction — water + CDOM + anything not reproduced by AED’s own state. If a Kw derived from field-measured Kd (which already contains the biotic + SS signal at the time of sampling) is combined with bioshade_feedback and an active aed_noncohesive, the biotic/SS contribution is double-counted, over-attenuating light and biasing production, DO, and thermal structure.

title: Rotorua Light
section: Configuring GLM to use a time-varying Kw
text:
Configuring GLM to use a time-varying Kw
For reference, if a time-varying background is used, the &light namelist and Kw_file CSV are:
&light
   light_mode       = 0        ! single-Kw Beer-Lambert; required for Kw_file
   Kw               = 0.37     ! fallback/initial value
   Kw_file          = 'kw.csv' ! time-varying background Kw forcing
   n_bands          = 2
   light_extc       = 1.0, 0.5
   energy_frac      = 0.5, 0.5
   Benthic_Imin     = 10
   albedo_mode      = 1
   albedo_mean      = 0.08
   albedo_amplitude = 0.02
/
time,Kd
2015-01-01,0.62
2015-02-01,0.58
2015-03-01,0.51

The time column must use the same time_fmt/timezone as the &meteorology block.
GLM performs a daily lookup (holds the most recent row’s value), not sub-daily interpolation — the file needs one row per day you want a distinct value for.
Kw_file only drives the single scalar ExtcCoefSW, so it requires light_mode = 0; it has no effect on the per-band light_extc array used by light_mode = 1.

Light extinction parameterisation recommendation
--------------------------------------------------
Input:              kw (n = 147, 0 dropped for NA/ordering)
Date range:         2003-08-20 to 2025-08-20 (23 distinct year(s))
Median sample gap:  35 days (max 426 days)
Kw:                 mean 0.714, median 0.601, sd 0.373, CV 0.52 (m^-1)
Interannual R^2:    47% of variance explained by year
Seasonal ratio:     1.62x (max:min monthly mean, detrended by year)

Recommendation: DATED TIME-VARYING Kw (use observed time series directly)

Year explains 47% of total variance in Kw, more than the seasonal cycle does
(interannual regime shifts / trends dominate over any recurring monthly
pattern, detrended seasonal ratio = 1.62x). A generic monthly climatology
would blend these regimes together and misrepresent most individual years.
Recommend driving GLM with the actual dated observations (interpolated/held
constant between sampling dates) for the specific years being simulated,
rather than a synthetic 'typical year' climatology. If a single
representative value is still needed (e.g. for scenario runs outside the
observed period), use the static mean/median (0.714 / 0.601 m^-1) with the
caveat that it will still miss whichever regime the simulated period actually
falls into.




Code
plot(kd_recommendation)










Key finding: interannual variability dominates over seasonality

Kd mean 0.71 m⁻¹, CV 0.52, range 0.25–1.92 m⁻¹.
Year explains ~47% of total variance — more than the seasonal cycle does. Annual means step from ~0.35–0.43 m⁻¹ (2003–2008) to a noisy 0.32–1.4 m⁻¹ regime from 2009 onward.
After removing each year’s own mean, the detrended seasonal ratio is only ~1.6–1.85x, and mostly driven by a handful of bloom/turbidity events rather than a robust recurring monthly pattern.
A pooled multi-year monthly climatology would blend a real interannual regime shift with a weak seasonal signal, misrepresenting most individual years — hence the function’s recommendation of a dated time-varying series over a monthly climatology for a hindcast.

title: Rotorua Light
section: Decomposing observed Kd into background vs. biotic components
text:
Decomposing observed Kd into background vs. biotic components
Available overlapping chemistry: CHLA (mg/m^3) and Turbidity (NTU) are the two usable predictors of the biotic/particulate extinction component (Secchi is itself just another optical measurement of the same quantity, so it is not used as a predictor).


Code
# `chem` should be one row per Kd date (aggregate multiple depths/stations to
# a single near-surface value per date *before* this step — the first attempt
# at this joined on Date without deduplicating, inflating n from 147 to 841
# rows and producing an unreliable, pseudo-replicated fit).
kw_decomp <- decompose_kw_biotic(
  date      = light_data$Date,
  kw        = light_data$Kd,
  chla      = light_data$chla,
  turbidity = light_data$turbidity
)




Code
print(kw_decomp)


Kw decomposition: background vs. biotic extinction
--------------------------------------------------
Model:              kw ~ chla + turbidity
n used:             142 (5 dropped for missing values)
R^2 / adj R^2:      0.067 / 0.054

Coefficients (p-value):
  (Intercept)     0.36815   (p = 0.0013)
  chla            0.00705   (p = 0.1669)
  turbidity       0.12692   (p = 0.0165)

Mean total Kw:      0.707 m^-1
Mean biotic Kw:     0.339 m^-1 (48% of total)
Mean background Kw: 0.382 m^-1 (intercept = 0.368)

NOTE: 26 of 142 background estimates were below the 0.020 m^-1 floor and
were clipped (see `$data$background_kw_raw` for the unclipped values) — this can
indicate the regression is over-attributing extinction to the biotic term on
some dates (e.g. collinearity, or a bloom event outside the fitted range).

Use `$data$background_kw` (dated) as the GLM `Kw_file` forcing when running with
AED's bioshade_feedback on. To check whether it should be static, monthly, or
fully dated, pass it on to:
  recommend_light_parameterisation(date = x$data$date, kw = x$data$background_kw)


Two fits were run against the real data as the join was corrected:


Code
plot(kw_decomp)











Code
print(kw_decomp)
