--------------------------------------------------
Model:              kw ~ chla + turbidity
n used:             142 (5 dropped for missing values)
R^2 / adj R^2:      0.067 / 0.054

Coefficients (p-value):
  (Intercept)     0.36815   (p = 0.0013)
  chla            0.00705   (p = 0.1669)
  turbidity       0.12692   (p = 0.0165)

Mean total Kw:      0.707 m^-1
Mean biotic Kw:     0.339 m^-1 (48% of total)
Mean background Kw: 0.382 m^-1 (intercept = 0.368)

NOTE: 26 of 142 background estimates were below the 0.020 m^-1 floor and
were clipped (see `$data$background_kw_raw` for the unclipped values) — this can
indicate the regression is over-attributing extinction to the biotic term on
some dates (e.g. collinearity, or a bloom event outside the fitted range).

Use `$data$background_kw` (dated) as the GLM `Kw_file` forcing when running with
AED's bioshade_feedback on. To check whether it should be static, monthly, or
fully dated, pass it on to:
  recommend_light_parameterisation(date = x$data$date, kw = x$data$background_kw)



Interpretation

Even after fixing the join (pseudo-replication), R² = 0.067 — Chla and turbidity together explain under 7% of Kd variance. Chla alone is not significant (p = 0.167); only turbidity clears p < 0.05, and its large coefficient combined with an 18% floor-clipping rate suggests the fit is being pulled around by a handful of high-turbidity events rather than reflecting a stable relationship.
aed_noncohesive is active in this AED configuration, computing its own suspended-sediment-driven extinction (Ke_ss(i) * SS_conc(i)) dynamically — so, unlike a setup with phytoplankton feedback alone, both the Chla- and turbidity-attributable terms are legitimately things AED will reconstruct, and both are fair to remove from the prescribed background. (Caveat: aed_noncohesive’s simulated SS is a mass concentration state, not the same quantity as measured NTU turbidity — the decision to exclude it is justified, but there’s no guarantee the simulated SS dynamics reproduce the same magnitude/timing the regression attributed to turbidity.)
The intercept is the one robust number here: 0.368 m⁻¹ at p = 0.0013, much better constrained than either slope, since intercepts are anchored by the bulk of the data rather than a weak covariate relationship.
The Secchi–Kd relationship was also noted as weak, reinforcing that this system’s optical signal is noisy relative to the predictors available.

title: Rotorua Light
section: Recommendation for the climate scenario runs
text:
Recommendation for the climate scenario runs
For a climate scenario parameterisation (not a historical hindcast):

Do not use observed Kd. bioshade_feedback and aed_noncohesive are both active, so a Kw already containing today’s biotic/SS signal would be double-counted against AED’s own dynamic contribution.
Do not use a dated time-varying background. There is no calendar correspondence between a historical sampling date and a future scenario year — the “use the actual dated observations” option only applies to hindcast-style runs over the sampled period.
Do not build a monthly background climatology. The Chla/turbidity regression (R² = 0.067) and the Secchi–Kd relationship are both weak; imposing monthly structure on this background signal risks encoding noise as if it were a genuine recurring seasonal driver.
Use a static background Kw, set from the regression intercept (~0.37 m⁻¹) — the most robust single number the data support. Let bioshade_feedback (phytoplankton) and aed_noncohesive (suspended sediment) supply the dynamic, climate-responsive part of the light environment, rather than freezing it to the historical record. This is also the conceptually correct setup for a scenario run: it lets the lake’s optical response evolve mechanistically under whatever the scenario does to nutrients, temperature, and hydrology, instead of repeating today’s bloom/turbidity patterns indefinitely.

&light
   light_mode       = 0
   Kw               = 0.37   ! static background Kw (regression intercept)
   n_bands          = 2
   light_extc       = 1.0, 0.5
   energy_frac      = 0.5, 0.5
   Benthic_Imin     = 10
   albedo_mode      = 1
   albedo_mean      = 0.08
   albedo_amplitude = 0.02
/

title: Rotorua Light
text:
Sensitivity check
Before committing to this, a direct sensitivity comparison is worth running: static background Kw (0.37 m⁻¹) with bioshade_feedback on, vs. the old static observed mean Kw (0.71 m⁻¹) with bioshade_feedback off. If key scenario outputs (surface temperature, stratification onset/breakdown, chlorophyll, hypolimnetic DO) are not materially different between the two, the choice matters less than the analysis above might suggest; if they diverge substantially, it’s worth investing more in constraining the background estimate (e.g. more Chla/TSS sampling, a better SS-turbidity calibration for aed_noncohesive) before running the full scenario suite.
The chunks below are scaffolding only (eval: false) — wire in your own nml paths, glm.exe invocation, and output-reading (e.g. glmtools/ncdf4) to run them.


Code
lake_dir <- get_lake_dir(aeme)
model <- "glm_aed"
model_path <- file.path(lake_dir, model) # get_model_path(aeme)
tgt_vars <- c("HYD_temp", "PHY_tchla", "LKE_photic", "HYD_thmcln")
scenarios <- list(
  `Static - feedback` = list(
    Kw = 0.37, # static background Kw (regression intercept)
    bioshade_feedback = TRUE
  ),
  `Static - no feedback` = list(
    light_mode = 0,
    Kw = 0.71, # static observed mean Kw
    bioshade_feedback = FALSE
  )
)

  run_model_test(model = model, path = model_path, param_overrides = scenarios[[scn]], 
                 tgt_vars = tgt_vars)
})
names(out) <- names(scenarios)

    range(lst[[v]], na.rm = TRUE)
  })), na.rm = TRUE)

    lst <- out[[scn]]

title: Rotorua Light
text:
Summary







Question
Answer




Static vs. time-varying Kw (general)?
Time-varying is better if the seasonal signal is real and well-sampled; here, interannual variability (47% of variance) dominates over seasonality, so a pooled monthly climatology would misrepresent most years.


Does AED feedback interact with Kw?
Yes — bioshade_feedback (phytoplankton) and aed_noncohesive (suspended sediment) both add their own simulated extinction on top of the prescribed Kw, additively.


Should prescribed Kw include the biotic signal?
No, not when both feedbacks are active — it double-counts.


Can the biotic component be estimated from data?
Weakly. Kd ~ Chla + Turbidity gives R² = 0.067; only the intercept (background Kw ≈ 0.37 m⁻¹) is well-constrained.


Is calibrating AED’s biotic light coefficients a good idea?
Not as a first move — risks equifinality/circularity with growth and mortality parameters; better to fix it from the empirical estimate and reserve calibration for parameters not otherwise measurable.


What should the climate scenario runs use?
A static background Kw (~0.37 m⁻¹), with bioshade_feedback and aed_noncohesive supplying the dynamic, climate-responsive part of light extinction.

Section 9 introduces a continuous FRP inflow to the lake, which is more realistic than a closed system and directly mirrors the Rotorua setup where streams (Utuhina, Puarenga) supply FRP continuously. Three scenarios are tested: a no-dosing baseline to confirm the inflow load is represented correctly, S_ala surface dosing to quantify removal efficiency against the inflowing load, and alum dosed via the inflow concentration rather than S_ala to check whether the spatial entry point matters.
All three tests share the same inflow file and GLM configuration. Substitute the placeholder values below with your actual inflow data before running.


Inflow setup complete — check PLACEHOLDER values before running.



9.1 Constant FRP inflow — no dosing baseline
FRP enters via the inflow at a constant concentration; no alum applied. Expect: lake FRP rises toward a new equilibrium set by inflow load vs. outflow; ALU_uptake_w and ALU_uptake_s remain 0; all alum pools stay 0.

   S_ala                = 0.0

9.4 Entry-point comparison — inflow dosing vs. S_ala

No separate namelist — this test reuses out_dose from test 9.2 and out_inflow_dosed from test 9.3. Run those two tests first.

Directly compare removal efficiency between test 9.2 (S_ala surface dosing) and test 9.3 (inflow-concentration dosing) at equivalent total alum loads. Expect: both approaches remove FRP; any efficiency difference reflects the importance of where in the water column alum is introduced.

title: Data Inputs
text:
This page summarises the data inputs used in the targets pipeline for the Lake Rotorua modelling project (_targets.R), where each dataset comes from, and where it can be obtained.
A live, searchable version of this inventory (generated automatically from the pipeline) is available at data_inventory.html, built by the data_inventory_html target using render_data_inventory.R.

Access notes

LERNZMP API (https://api.limnotrack.com) — used for lake buoy data, lake shape/metadata, depth contours and the base AEME model object. Requires an API key stored in the LERNZMP_API (or LERNZMP_KEY) environment variable (see .Renviron, not committed to the repository).
BoPRC datasets (lake level, CTD, chemistry, alum dosing) are supplied directly by Bay of Plenty Regional Council as Excel/CSV exports and stored under data/raw/ (not version-controlled — see data-request.qmd for the running list of requested datasets).

CMIP6 / VCSN data is sourced from the Ministry for the Environment Climate Data Portal, with the bulk NetCDF archive mirrored on an institutional shared drive (Z:) due to its size (>4 TB nationally).
Processed/derived outputs (e.g. gcm_point_data_lake_11133.csv, cmip6_gcm_metadata.csv, rotorua_light_data.csv) are written to data/processed/ by the pipeline and are reproducible from the raw inputs above.

title: CSPS Evaluation Framework for Lake Rotorua
text:
The calibration so far scores the model on state variables (temperature, oxygen, nutrients, chlorophyll-a). A model can match those concentrations for the wrong reasons, particularly in a shallow lake where one parameter such as wind scaling can compensate for several errors (see the mixing section of the staged calibration). This page defines a metrics system based on the CSPS framework (Concept, State, Process, System; Hipsey et al. 2020), built from what the observations can actually support, and aimed at four things the model must get right:

Polymixis: a lake that stratifies for days to weeks and mixes again, many times a year.
Bottom-water anoxia: short, episodic and variable between years.
Internal loading: nutrient release from the sediment into stratified bottom water.
Seasonal phytoplankton dynamics: the magnitude, variability and timing of chlorophyll-a.

The code is in calibration/csps_metrics.R. calibration/csps_build_targets.R writes the observed targets to calibration/csps_targets.csv.

title: CSPS Evaluation Framework for Lake Rotorua
text:
2 What the observations support



Observation inventory used to build targets.


Data
Period
Use




Temperature profile
2003 to 2026 (daily from 2007)
Polymixis, mixing events, state


Dissolved oxygen profile
2003 to 2026 (daily from 2007)
Anoxia frequency and duration, oxygen demand, state


Chlorophyll-a profile
2003 to 2025 (monthly, more often from 2015)
Seasonality, bloom size, state


TP, TN, FRP, NH4, NO3 (lab, depth profile)
1990 to 2023 (monthly or bi-monthly; deep samples to 2020)
Internal loading (bottom to surface contrast), state


Secchi depth
1982 to 2023
Trophic state, light climate


Stratification flag, Schmidt stability, thermocline depth
2003 to 2026
Derived from the same profiles, so not used independently


TLI3, TLI4
1990 to 2023
System-level trophic check





Lessons from the data that shape the targets:

The lake is polymictic. Surface minus bottom temperature (17 m and deeper) exceeds 1 °C on about 22% of days (35% from December to April, almost never in winter). Spells last a median of 2 days, with a 90th percentile of 17 days and about 9 spells a year. The model must produce frequent short stratification and mixing, not a seasonal thermocline.
Anoxia is episodic and uneven between years. Bottom oxygen is below 2 mg/L on about 11% of December to April days, but from 0% (2014, 2022, 2023) to 33% (2010) of days between years, and 83% of years have at least one event.
Internal loading shows as a bottom to surface contrast in the stratified season. Bottom ammonium is a median 7 times the surface value, FRP 2.6 times and TP 1.4 times. It is only measured at depth to 2020.
Chlorophyll-a has weak seasonality. The median is about 9 mg m-3, the summer to winter ratio is close to 1, and the signal is irregular blooms (the 90th percentile is about 20) rather than a regular spring peak. Matching a seasonal cycle would reward the wrong behaviour, so the targets use the distribution, bloom frequency and the annual peak.

title: CSPS Evaluation Framework for Lake Rotorua
text:
3 The framework





Level
Question
How it is assessed




0 Concept
Is the model structure appropriate for these questions?
Checklist (table below), reviewed before each scenario use


1 State
Do simulated concentrations match observations?
Bias, MAE, RMSE, correlation and KGE by variable and layer (log scale for chlorophyll and nutrients), plus seasonal correlation


2 Process
Is the model producing the observed behaviour through the right processes?
Signatures of mixing, oxygen demand and nutrient gradients, with tolerances from the interannual spread


3 System
Does the whole lake respond as observed?
Trophic state (TLI3), chlorophyll to TP relation, response to alum dosing and to wet and dry years






3.1 Level 0: concept checklist







Question
Status




Does the hydrodynamic model resolve rapid mixing and stratification cycles (hourly forcing, wind-driven mixing)?
Yes with hourly forcing; the daily-forced base is a coarser test


Is sediment oxygen demand and nutrient release linked to bottom-water oxygen?
Sediment release and oxygen demand are parameterised by zone (fsed_*, ksed_*); the oxygen dependence needs checking in the AED sediment settings


Are the 21.5 m basin and the deeper pit (to 27 m) represented?
No. The model uses hyps_no_hole. Observed ammonium is highest at 21 to 25 m, so this is a known structural gap


Is phytoplankton resolved by group (cyanobacteria, diatoms, green algae)?
Yes, but only total chlorophyll-a is observed


Are alum dosing and its effect on phosphorus represented?
Yes (aed_alum, stage 4), with dose and efficiency uncertain


Is rainfall, river inflow and nutrient loading consistent with the lake budget?
Water balance calibrated; nutrient loads and the organic share are assumptions


Does the forcing carry the climate-scenario signal at the time scale the lake responds to (days)?
Delta-change on hourly corrected ERA5; daily weather variability is preserved





3.2 Level 1: state metrics
For each variable and layer (surface 0 to 2 m, middle, bottom 17 m and deeper, and bottom from December to April) the scorecard reports bias, MAE, RMSE, correlation, KGE and the correlation of the monthly climatology. Chlorophyll-a and nutrients are compared on the log scale. These replace a single pooled error score: a model that gets the surface right and the bottom wrong is visible.


3.3 Level 2 and 3: signatures
Every signature is computed by one function on the observations and on the model, using only days on which an observation exists. This removes the effect of sampling. The tolerance for each signature is the standard deviation of that signature between observed years (at least 10% of the value; 50% for signatures with fewer than five usable years). A model is inside tolerance when it lands within one standard deviation of the observed value, and the score falls from 1 to 0 between one and three standard deviations.

title: CSPS Evaluation Framework for Lake Rotorua
text:
4 Observed year-to-year range
The tolerances come from how much the lake itself varies between years:

title: CSPS Evaluation Framework for Lake Rotorua
text:
5 Calibration, validation and scoring

Calibration window. The current PEST windows (2 to 3 years inside 2017 to 2020) fit states. They are not long enough to score signatures that depend on rare events (spells, years with anoxia).
Validation. Score the calibrated model on all other years that have daily temperature and oxygen (2007 to 2016, 2021 to 2025) and on the 1992 to 2006 nutrient record from the daily-forced run. The signatures are the validation targets; a model that passes state metrics but fails signatures is not accepted for scenarios.
Ensembles. Run the signature scorecard on each realisation of the final PEST ensemble, and report the range, not only the best run.
Using signatures inside PEST. The signatures can be added as observation groups in the next calibration round. The first candidates are mix_f_strat_summer and mix_spell_median_d in stage 2 (they separate wind scaling from mixing coefficients), and anox_f_lt2_summer, anox_do_decline_strat and the load_*_ratio set in stage 3. They have to be computed over windows long enough to hold several spells, so the calibration window would need to extend to about one full year.

title: CSPS Evaluation Framework for Lake Rotorua
text:
6 Gaps in the data

Process rates (sediment fluxes, productivity, denitrification) are measured only as the zone sediment fluxes in meas_param, with unconfirmed units, so the process level for internal loading relies on concentration gradients, not fluxes.
Nutrients are not measured at depth after 2020, so internal loading signatures are scored on 11 to 14 years.
TLI4 needs a simulated Secchi depth, which GLM-AED does not output; TLI3 is used instead.
Cyanobacteria and phytoplankton group data would test whether the right groups bloom in the right season; only total chlorophyll-a is available.
The deep pit (to 27 m) is outside the model.

title: CMIP 6 Processing
text:
Currently the CMIP6 data we have is in NetCDF format, which is not directly compatible with our model input requirements. Therefore, we need to preprocess this data to extract the relevant variables and reformat them appropriately.
Also there are >4 TB of data for all of New Zealand on a daily timestep, at a 5x5 km resolution. This is too large to process directly, so we will need to subset the data spatially and temporally.

title: CMIP 6 Processing
text:
Metadata
We have gathered metadata for the CMIP6 datasets available on the shared drive, including information on the variables, scenarios, models, and bias correction methods used.
Further details can be found here.

title: CMIP 6 Processing
text:
File access
The CMIP6 data is stored on a shared drive (Z: drive) accessible within our institutional network. The files are organized by variable, scenario, model, region, timestep, spatial resolution, and bias correction method e.g “hurs_historical_ACCESS-CM2_CCAM_daily_NZ5km_raw.nc”. This corresponds to relative humidity (hurs) for the historical scenario from the ACCESS-CM2 GCM, downscaled using the CCAM model over New Zealand at a daily timestep and 5 km spatial resolution, without bias correction.
Loading and reading data from these NetCDF files can be done using the ncdf4 package in R. However, reading large datasets can be time-consuming, so we have implemented a function which uses a grid reference system to efficiently extract only the required data points.
This provided as the VCSN agent data. This contains a grid of points at 5 km resolution covering New Zealand, with each point having a unique coordinate index. We use this grid to identify which points fall within our area of interest, and then extract only those points from the NetCDF files.

title: CMIP 6 Processing
text:
Create an area of interest
If you do not have a shapefile of your area of interest (AOI), you can easily generate one with the mapedit package.


Code
x <- mapedit::drawFeatures()


Save the drawn features for future use:


Code
saveRDS(x, here::here("data", "processed", "rotorua_area.rds"))

title: CMIP 6 Processing
text:
Processing function
The process_cmip6 function takes in a spatial polygon (defining the area of interest), the VCSN grid points, the path to a NetCDF file, and an output file path. It extracts the relevant data points from the NetCDF file based on the area of interest, and saves the processed data to a new NetCDF file.

title: Climate-Change Impact Strategy for Lake Rotorua
text: Status: draft strategy. It builds on components that already exist in this project and lists what still has to be done before the projections can be trusted. Numbers marked estimate are my planning figures, not measurements.

title: Climate-Change Impact Strategy for Lake Rotorua
text:
1 Purpose and questions
The aim is to estimate how climate change alters nutrient dynamics and the trophic state of Lake Rotorua, and how much alum dosing could offset it. Three questions drive the design:

Climate effect. With catchment loads and alum dosing held as they are now, how do water temperature, stratification, bottom-water oxygen, internal P release, chlorophyll-a and LKE_tli4 change by mid and late century, and how large is that change compared with year-to-year variability?
Management response. How does the effect of alum dosing (present operations, more, less, none) change under each climate? Put another way, how much more or less alum is needed to hold LKE_tli4 at a chosen target?
Uncertainty. How much of the spread comes from the GCM, the emissions pathway, the catchment response, the alum behaviour, and the model parameters?

title: Climate-Change Impact Strategy for Lake Rotorua
text:
4 Design

4.1 Overview





flowchart LR
  A[ERA5 baseline<br/>bias-corrected] --> C[Scenario forcing<br/>GCM x SSP x window]
  B[CMIP6 monthly deltas] --> C
  D[Historical inflows<br/>1959-2022] --> E[Inflow adaptation<br/>flow, load, temperature]
  C --> E
  C --> F[GLM-AED runs]
  E --> F
  G[Alum scenarios] --> F
  H[Parameter ensemble<br/>from calibration] --> F
  F --> I[Daily output<br/>nutrients, DO, TLI4]
  I --> J[Annual and seasonal metrics<br/>variance partitioning]








4.2 Climate forcing

Use the existing delta-change forcing (scenario_hourly_met). It keeps real weather sequences and shifts their statistics, which suits a model that needs realistic storms and calm spells.
Use 30-year time slices, not 10 or 15 years (see the next subsection for why and for the cost). The weather baseline for a slice is the 1991 to 2020 ERA5 climate normal (taken from the 1988 to 2024 record), with each GCM/SSP/window delta applied to it.
How the ERA5 record maps to the climate windows. The window (2015–2040, 2041–2070, 2071–2100) only selects which monthly delta is applied; it does not select ERA5 years. Every window uses the same 30 ERA5 weather years (1991–2020), so differences between windows are purely the climate signal. The deltas are relative to the CMIP6 1995–2014 reference (scenario_ref_years), which sits at the same centre (about 2005) as the 1991–2020 baseline, so the two are consistent. Keep the original ERA5 dates (1991–2020) in the model and label the run by window; relabelling the years to 2041–2070 gains nothing and causes leap-year problems (for example 2100 is not a leap year).
The remaining ERA5 years are not wasted: 1988–1990 can serve as spin-up weather, and 2021–2024 can be used for hindcast checks. Optionally run the full 37 years once as a robustness test of the baseline choice.
NZESM (360-day calendar). No long transient run is needed. Delta-change uses only 12 monthly factors per variable, and these are applied to the Gregorian ERA5 days, so the GCM calendar never enters the model. The one thing to verify is that metscale::climate_point_monthly_climatology() assigns NZESM days to calendar months correctly (the repository already handles 360-day time in R/summarise_gcm_ts.R and R/standardise_to_gregorian.R). NZESM contributes monthly means only; its daily variability is not used, as for the other GCMs.
Keep hindcast (no delta) as the reference, and compare future windows with it, not with observations.
Use all 7 GCMs for the main set, because GCM spread dominates (annual warming for SSP585 by 2071 to 2100 ranges from +2.8 to +4.6 °C). Do not rely on NorESM2-MM alone, which is at the low end.
Assumption to state clearly: delta-change keeps present variability and sequences, so it will not capture changes in the frequency of persistent calm spells beyond what the monthly means imply. The extreme-event indices are used to check this.



4.3 Simulation length
A 10-year run is too short for climate statements, and the 15 years of bias-corrected hourly ERA5-Land (2011 to 2026) that the pipeline uses today is also short. The reasons:

Variability. Rainfall, inflow and bloom years in the Rotorua catchment swing with ENSO and decadal climate. A single decade can sit in one phase, so a 10-year difference between scenarios can reflect the weather sequence, not the climate signal. Thirty years is the standard averaging period and gives a much smaller sampling error on annual metrics such as TLI4 (about 40% smaller than for 10 years, as the error falls with the square root of the number of years).
Rare events. Storms, heatwaves, calm spells and the blooms and anoxic periods that follow them need long samples to estimate how often they occur.
Slow state variables. Sediment P pools, benthic alum pools and the legacy effect of stopping or changing dosing evolve over 10 to 30 years, so they need a spin-up of 5 to 10 years and, for the alum questions, runs long enough to see the response.

What is needed to get 30 years:








Item
Status
Action




Weather baseline 1991 to 2020
The corrected daily series covers only 2011 to 2026; ERA5 for 1988 to 2024 is now available but not bias-corrected
Apply the same daily bias correction (fitted on the buoy overlap, assumed stationary) to the 1988 to 2024 record, then disaggregate to hourly using the 2011 to 2025 hourly donor. Fix the rainfall units first (gap 5)


Inflows
The historical inflow series covers 1959 to 2022, so 1991 to 2020 is available
None, but check the inflow record is consistent through the period


Alum dosing in the baseline
Dosing history starts in 2006 and 2010
Use a constant present-day dose for the slices (scenario A1) rather than the history



Time slices or transient runs. Use 30-year time slices (a stationary climate per window, 5 to 10 years of spin-up) as the main design. Add a small number of transient runs for the alum questions that depend on timing and legacy: for example 2 to 3 GCMs under SSP245 and SSP585, run continuously from 2015 to 2100 with the monthly deltas interpolated between windows. A slice cannot show how long P from a stopped dose lingers or how fast the benthic alum pool builds.
Cost. Thirty years roughly doubles the 15-year cost per run, so the full design below needs about 20 hours rather than about 11. A tiered plan keeps it manageable: 30-year slices for the core scenarios and the hindcast, and 15-year slices (the 2011 to 2025 weather) for the large sweeps over alum parameters and inflow tiers. Check the two give the same signal on the pilot set before relying on the shorter runs.
Do we need 1970 to 2100 runs? No, not for the main questions. With delta-change, a continuous run to 2100 would need a trend in the forcing that the monthly-window deltas do not provide, and the slices already answer “what is the lake like under climate X”. Transient runs are only justified for timing and legacy questions (A4 below), and are optional for now.


4.4 Spin-up and equilibrium
How long a run must be depends on which state variable carries memory:








Component
Memory
Consequence




Water column nutrients, chlorophyll-a, temperature
Months to about 1 to 2 years (residence time; check against modelled outflow)
A 2 to 3 year spin-up is enough


Sediment P pools, benthic alum pools
Many years
5 to 10 years of spin-up, and this is what matters for alum



For the alum on/off comparison the question decides the design:

Equilibrium contrast (A0 versus A1, each in its own steady state): spin each case up under its own dosing, then run the 30 years. This is the default for the slices, and it needs the full 5 to 10 year spin-up because the sediment and alum pools differ between the cases. Spin up by looping the first 5 to 10 years of the baseline weather (or using 1988 to 1990 plus a loop).
Transient response (what happens after dosing stops from today’s state): needs a continuous run from the present state and a long enough record to see the legacy P decline. Keep this as the small optional set (A4).

Check that the spin-up is adequate empirically, once, on the pilot: run a slice twice back to back and compare the first and last 10 years of annual LKE_tli4, sediment P and benthic alum pools. If the drift is small relative to the climate signal and to the A0–A1 difference, the spin-up is sufficient.


4.5 Inflows (three tiers)
Initial phase. Climate-adjusted inflows do not exist yet, so the first runs use T1 only (historical 1991 to 2020 inflows, which are coherent with the ERA5 weather years) with two alum cases: A0 (none) and A1 (present flow-paced dose). Optionally shift stream temperature with the air-temperature delta (T1+, a cheap and defensible adjustment). State plainly that flow and load are unchanged while rainfall changes, so results are a lower bound on the catchment-driven change. T2 and T3 and alum cases A2 to A5 are later phases.
Climate also changes what enters the lake, and this is likely to matter as much as in-lake warming for nutrients.








Tier
Inflow treatment
Purpose




T1
Historical inflows unchanged
Isolates the direct lake response to weather and temperature


T2
Scale flow with the rainfall delta (with a runoff elasticity) and the evapotranspiration implied by the temperature delta; scale loads with flow through a load–discharge exponent; shift stream temperature with air temperature
Plausible catchment response without a catchment model


T3
Drive a catchment model with the scenario forcing (if the catchment model used to make the 1959 to 2022 inflow series can be run)
Best available, and the way to test T2



Run T1 and T2 for the full ensemble and T3 for a subset if available. The alum dose is proportional to flow in the dosed streams, so T2 also changes the alum delivered, which is a real climate–management interaction and is kept.


4.6 Alum scenarios
Built on scale_alum_inflows(); efficiency uses the factor already defined as ratio_al_p.








Code
Dosing
Rationale




A0
None
Counterfactual


A1
Present operations (Utuhina and Puarenga, flow-paced at about 1 mg Al/L)
Business as usual


A2
A1 with doubled dose
Management response


A3
A1 with half dose
Reduced effort


A4
Dosing stops at a set date
Legacy P release from sediment


A5
Adaptive dose: increases when modelled lake TLI4 or FRP is above a target
Inverse question: dose needed to hold the target



Alum behaviour is treated as an uncertainty dimension, using the thesis-based ranges in the thesis notes and the calibration page: floc settling 0.3 to 1.5 m/d, binding efficiency (Al:P) from 0.15 (field, about 7:1) to 1.4 (jar test, 0.7:1), resuspension on or off. The stage 4 sensitivity check showed that, in the calibrated model, the FRP fit is nearly insensitive to the alum parameters within their ranges and that removing the dose raises mean FRP by only about 30%. The alum response in the projections is therefore uncertain and should be explored through these ranges, not taken from a single fitted value.


4.7 Parameter and structural uncertainty

Use a small parameter ensemble from the calibration posterior (about 5 members from the final pestpp-ies ensemble), plus the alum efficiency and settling range above.
Add structural checks: switch temperature dependence of sediment P release and mineralisation (theta_*) between default and a stronger response; test phytoplankton T_opt shifts, since adaptation is unknown.
Do not tune the model to future conditions. Parameters stay fixed at their calibrated values.



4.8 Metrics








Group
Variables
Reported as




Trophic state
LKE_tli4, LKE_tlic, LKE_tlin, LKE_tlip, LKE_tlise
Annual mean, change from hindcast, probability of exceeding the management target (BOPRC’s target for Lake Rotorua is 4.2; verify)


Nutrients
TP, TN, FRP, ammonium, nitrate (epilimnion and bottom)
Annual and seasonal means; TN:TP


Phytoplankton
Chlorophyll-a, cyanobacteria
Annual mean, days above bloom threshold, bloom timing


Oxygen and stratification

title: Climate-Change Impact Strategy for Lake Rotorua
text:
5 Experimental design and compute budget
Initial phase (current scope): 83 GCM × SSP × window combinations × 2 alum cases (A0, A1) × T1 inflows = 166 runs, plus the hindcast. At 5 to 6 minutes per 30 + 5 year run and about 2 runs per minute on six workers this is roughly 3 to 4 hours of wall time; pilot with 3 GCMs first (about 36 runs). The phases below are the fuller design for when inflow scenarios exist.
Estimate: a 15 + 3 year run takes about 1 minute of GLM time plus 1 to 2 minutes to read the output when only the needed variables are requested, so about 3 minutes per run, and a 30 + 5 year run about 5 to 6 minutes. Six workers give about 2 runs per minute for 15-year runs. The table below uses 15-year runs for the sweeps; the core scenarios and the hindcast use 30-year slices (see Simulation length).

Use a crew controller with a worker count below the physical core count.

title: Climate-Change Impact Strategy for Lake Rotorua
text:
6 Analysis plan

Hindcast check. Compare the 2011 to 2022 hindcast (the period with water-quality observations) annual TLI4 and components with observed, per year. State the skill and bias explicitly and carry them into the interpretation.
Climate signal. For each metric, compute future minus hindcast per run. Report the ensemble median, the GCM range, and the fraction of runs agreeing in sign.
Signal against variability. Compare the climate change with the spread of annual values within the hindcast (internal variability). A change smaller than that is reported as such.
Variance partitioning. Decompose the spread into GCM, SSP, window, inflow tier, alum scenario and parameter member (ANOVA or mixed model). This answers question 3.
Alum response curves. For each climate, plot TLI4 and FRP against alum dose multiplier and efficiency, and read off the dose that holds the target. Report the extra dose required by climate.
Process attribution. Compare T1 and T2 inflows and A0 and A1 alum to separate in-lake warming, catchment input and alum effects. Use simple factorial contrasts.
Event view. Link the extreme-event indices (storms, heatwaves) to bloom and anoxia days in the runs where those change most.

title: Climate-Change Impact Strategy for Lake Rotorua
text:
7 Deliverables and layout

scenarios/ with scripts 10_build_scenario_aeme.R (forcing, inflows, alum, parameter set → Aeme object), 11_run_scenarios.R (targets-based, one branch per run, daily lake-mean and epilimnion/hypolimnion series only), 12_metrics.R (annual and seasonal metrics, TLI), and 13_analysis.R.
Summary tables as CSV in data/processed/scenarios/ so the website pages do not re-run models.
Quarto pages: results by metric, alum response curves, uncertainty partitioning, and a short non-technical summary.

text:
9 Sequence

Close the open calibration gaps (TP, TN and Secchi targets, ammonium, stage 3 with alum on) and fix the rainfall units and the aemetools unit bug at source.
Hindcast and TLI4 validation (P1). Go or no-go on skill before continuing.

title: Climate-Change Impact Strategy for Lake Rotorua
text:
10 Open questions

Which TLI4 target or threshold should be used for management (for example BOPRC’s 4.2), and is annual mean TLI4 the right headline metric?
Is a catchment model available that can be driven with the scenario forcing (T3), and who owns the 1959 to 2022 inflow series?
Are there planned changes in dosing locations, dose rates or the Ōhau weir operation that should be scenarios in their own right?
For alum on/off, is the equilibrium contrast (each case spun up under its own dosing) the question of interest, or the transient response after stopping from today’s state?
Should land-use or point-source changes (WWTP, geothermal) be included, or is the question climate only?

title: Calibration Step 1: Physics and Oxygen
text: This is the first step of the staged plan that follows the sensitivity analysis: calibrate the physics and the oxygen dynamics together, using the process signatures of the CSPS framework as well as state errors, with the alum module off, because alum does not change physics or oxygen. The target behaviour is a polymictic lake that stratifies for days at a time, mixes again, and develops short bottom-water anoxia.

title: Calibration Step 1: Physics and Oxygen
text: This is the first step of the staged plan that follows the sensitivity analysis: calibrate the physics and the oxygen dynamics together, using the process signatures of the CSPS framework as well as state errors, with the alum module off, because alum does not change physics or oxygen. The target behaviour is a polymictic lake that stratifies for days at a time, mixes again, and develops short bottom-water anoxia.

title: Calibration Step 1: Physics and Oxygen
text:
2 Set-up

Forcing: the hourly bias-corrected ERA5 series. The sensitivity analysis showed that daily forcing has less mixing energy, so mixing parameters fitted on it would not transfer.
Wind is not scaled. The wind is measured on the lake, so the wind scaling factor is fixed at 1 (earlier calibrations settled on 1.64, which was compensating for other errors). Heat and mixing errors are absorbed by the heat-flux coefficients and mixing coefficients instead.
Alum off: the dosed inflow concentration is set to zero. Phytoplankton and the other biogeochemical parameters are held at the earlier calibrated values (the phytoplankton parameters are calibrated in the next step).
Period: 2012-07 to 2022-06, the span with both hourly forcing and the inflow series, plus a 540-day spin-up. Calibration window 2012-07 to 2018-12; the years 2019-01 to 2022-06 are held out and are only used to check the result.
Free parameters (27): the radiation, air-temperature and humidity scalings; the heat-flux coefficients ce, ch, cd; the light extinction Kw; five mixing coefficients (coef_mix_shear is inert and fixed); the sediment oxygen demand in four zones with ksed_oxy and theta_sed_oxy; and eight organic-matter parameters (mineralisation and hydrolysis rates, their temperature coefficients and half-saturations, f_an, particle settling w_pom).
What is fitted (28 residuals, each in units of the lake’s tolerance or a fixed scale, so every metric counts equally):

16 process signatures: stratified fraction (all year, summer, winter), temperature difference statistics, spells per year, spell length, bottom temperature, anoxic fraction (below 2 and 1 mg/L), bottom oxygen statistics, the share of years with anoxia, and the oxygen decline rate in stratified spells.
Bias and RMSE of temperature and oxygen in the surface, middle and bottom layers.

Method: an ensemble smoother with multiple data assimilation (ES-MDA), 80 members, 6 assimilation steps, run in parallel (560 model runs). It gives an ensemble rather than one parameter set.

title: Calibration Step 1: Physics and Oxygen
text:
6 Limitations

The residual stratification excess (summer fraction, spell frequency) is not removed by any of the bounded parameters, so it is probably structural (for example the missing deep pit). This was not tested here.
Surface oxygen is biased low; this is an air-water exchange and production issue.
Phytoplankton, nitrogen and phosphorus parameters were held at their earlier values, so the oxygen parameters may be compensating for phytoplankton oxygen production and respiration. They should be re-checked after the phytoplankton step.
Three and a half years are held out, which is short for the signatures that depend on rare events (anoxic years).

Calibrate the alum parameters on the dosed years with everything else fixed.

title: Proposed Alum Model for AED
text:
NoteSummary



This document summarises a simple process representation of alum–phosphorus interactions for integration into GLM-AED. The formulation is intended to capture the main management-relevant processes in Lake Rotorua:

alum delivery from treated inflows,
SRP uptake in the water column,
settling of remaining reactive material,
continued uptake at the sediment–water interface,
a gradual loss of reactivity through ageing, and
a bell-shaped pH response included as a pragmatic modifier of binding efficiency.





The schematic below shows how the simplified module fits together. Treated inflows add effective reactive capacity to the pelagic pool, which removes SRP while suspended. Remaining capacity then settles to the bed, where it continues to suppress SRP in the bottom layer. Ageing reduces reactivity in both compartments.







Conceptual process diagram of the simplified alum–phosphorus module.







Reactive suspended alum capacity in the water column, \(C_w\) (mg P m−3), removes dissolved reactive phosphorus, SRP (mg P m−3). The uptake rate is controlled by a pelagic kinetic coefficient, \(k_w\) (d−1), the pH modifier, \(f_\text{pH}\) (−), and a saturating uptake term governed by \(K_P\) (mg P m−3). The saturating form ensures uptake increases with SRP but levels off as SRP becomes small relative to \(K_P\).

\[
\frac{dSRP}{dt} = -k_w f_{pH} C_w \frac{K_P \, SRP}{K_P + SRP}
\tag{1}\]




The pelagic reactive-capacity pool, \(C_w\) (mg P m−3), increases with alum input from the treated inflows, represented by \(J_\text{cap}\) (mg P d−1), and decreases through three pathways: SRP uptake, settling to the bed, and ageing. The volume term, \(V\) (m3), converts inflow capacity into a concentration-based state variable. \(J_\text{set}\) (mg P m−3 d−1) is the settling loss from the water column, while \(k_{\text{age},w}\) (d−1) controls the exponential decline in pelagic reactivity.
\[
\frac{dC_w}{dt} = \frac{J_\mathrm{cap}}{V} - k_w f_\mathrm{pH} C_w \frac{K_P\,\mathrm{SRP}}{K_P + \mathrm{SRP}} - J_\mathrm{set} - k_{\mathrm{age},w}\,C_w
\tag{2}\]



Once alum settles, the remaining reactive capacity at the bed, \(C_s\) (mg P m−2), continues to remove SRP from the bottom computational layer, \(\text{SRP}_b\) (mg P m−3). The benthic uptake rate is controlled by \(k_s\) (d−1), the same pH modifier, and the same saturating uptake term. The factor \(1/h_b\) converts an areal benthic sink into a concentration change in the bottom water layer of thickness \(h_b\) (m).
\[
\frac{d\mathrm{SRP}_b}{dt} = -\frac{1}{h_b}\,k_s f_\mathrm{pH} C_s \frac{K_P\,\mathrm{SRP}_b}{K_P + \mathrm{SRP}_b}
\tag{3}\]



The benthic reactive-capacity pool, \(C_s\) (mg P m−2), increases through settling input from the pelagic compartment, \(J_\text{set}^\text{area}\) (mg P m−2 d−1), and decreases through bottom-water uptake, ageing, and burial or permanent isolation from exchange. The terms \(k_{\text{age},s}\) (d−1) and \(k_\text{bur}\) (d−1) therefore represent two separate loss pathways: gradual deactivation of reactivity and physical removal from the active sediment–water interface, respectively.
\[
\frac{dC_s}{dt} = J_\mathrm{set}^\mathrm{area} - k_s f_\mathrm{pH} C_s \frac{K_P\,\mathrm{SRP}_b}{K_P + \mathrm{SRP}_b} - k_{\mathrm{age},s}\,C_s - k_\mathrm{bur}\,C_s
\tag{4}\]



The pH modifier, \(f_\text{pH}\) (−), is represented as a bell-shaped response centred on the optimal pH, \(\text{pH}_\text{opt}\) (−). The parameter \(\sigma_\text{pH}\) (−) controls the width of the response. This is not a full chemical equilibrium model; it is a practical way of reducing effective uptake when pH moves away from the range where alum is expected to bind phosphorus most efficiently.
\[
f_\mathrm{pH} = \exp\!\left[-\frac{(\mathrm{pH} - \mathrm{pH_{opt}})^2}{2\,\sigma_\mathrm{pH}^2}\right]
\tag{5}\]




Ageing is represented as a first-order exponential loss of reactivity. Here, \(A(t)\) denotes the remaining reactive fraction at time \(t\) and \(A_0\) is the initial reactive fraction. For the current implementation, the ageing parameter is chosen so that 95% of reactive uptake capacity is lost after 30 days. This gives \(k_\text{age} \approx 0.10\) d−1. In practice, this same logic is applied to the pelagic and benthic ageing terms, \(k_{\text{age},w}\) and \(k_{\text{age},s}\).
\[
A(t) = A_0\,e^{-k_\mathrm{age}\,t} \qquad k_\mathrm{age} = -\frac{\ln(0.05)}{30} \approx 0.10 \ \mathrm{d}^{-1}
\tag{6}\]




The table below lists the state variables, fluxes, and parameters used in the simplified model. All symbols referenced in the equations are included here so the document can be read either as a stand-alone concept note or as a guide for module implementation.

A practical first implementation in GLM-AED could introduce two new state variables: a pelagic reactive-capacity pool (\(C_w\)) and a benthic reactive-capacity pool (\(C_s\)). The main calibration priorities are likely to be the dose-to-capacity conversion (\(J_\text{cap}\)), the pelagic and benthic kinetic coefficients (\(k_w\) and \(k_s\)), the settling transfer, and the pH response parameters. For ageing, the intended behaviour is simple exponential loss of reactivity rather than a more complex multi-pool formulation.

title: Proposed Alum Model for AED
text:
The schematic below shows how the simplified module fits together. Treated inflows add effective reactive capacity to the pelagic pool, which removes SRP while suspended. Remaining capacity then settles to the bed, where it continues to suppress SRP in the bottom layer. Ageing reduces reactivity in both compartments.







Conceptual process diagram of the simplified alum–phosphorus module.

title: Proposed Alum Model for AED
text:
Reactive suspended alum capacity in the water column, \(C_w\) (mg P m−3), removes dissolved reactive phosphorus, SRP (mg P m−3). The uptake rate is controlled by a pelagic kinetic coefficient, \(k_w\) (d−1), the pH modifier, \(f_\text{pH}\) (−), and a saturating uptake term governed by \(K_P\) (mg P m−3). The saturating form ensures uptake increases with SRP but levels off as SRP becomes small relative to \(K_P\).

\[
\frac{dSRP}{dt} = -k_w f_{pH} C_w \frac{K_P \, SRP}{K_P + SRP}
\tag{1}\]




The pelagic reactive-capacity pool, \(C_w\) (mg P m−3), increases with alum input from the treated inflows, represented by \(J_\text{cap}\) (mg P d−1), and decreases through three pathways: SRP uptake, settling to the bed, and ageing. The volume term, \(V\) (m3), converts inflow capacity into a concentration-based state variable. \(J_\text{set}\) (mg P m−3 d−1) is the settling loss from the water column, while \(k_{\text{age},w}\) (d−1) controls the exponential decline in pelagic reactivity.
\[
\frac{dC_w}{dt} = \frac{J_\mathrm{cap}}{V} - k_w f_\mathrm{pH} C_w \frac{K_P\,\mathrm{SRP}}{K_P + \mathrm{SRP}} - J_\mathrm{set} - k_{\mathrm{age},w}\,C_w
\tag{2}\]



Once alum settles, the remaining reactive capacity at the bed, \(C_s\) (mg P m−2), continues to remove SRP from the bottom computational layer, \(\text{SRP}_b\) (mg P m−3). The benthic uptake rate is controlled by \(k_s\) (d−1), the same pH modifier, and the same saturating uptake term. The factor \(1/h_b\) converts an areal benthic sink into a concentration change in the bottom water layer of thickness \(h_b\) (m).
\[
\frac{d\mathrm{SRP}_b}{dt} = -\frac{1}{h_b}\,k_s f_\mathrm{pH} C_s \frac{K_P\,\mathrm{SRP}_b}{K_P + \mathrm{SRP}_b}
\tag{3}\]



The benthic reactive-capacity pool, \(C_s\) (mg P m−2), increases through settling input from the pelagic compartment, \(J_\text{set}^\text{area}\) (mg P m−2 d−1), and decreases through bottom-water uptake, ageing, and burial or permanent isolation from exchange. The terms \(k_{\text{age},s}\) (d−1) and \(k_\text{bur}\) (d−1) therefore represent two separate loss pathways: gradual deactivation of reactivity and physical removal from the active sediment–water interface, respectively.
\[
\frac{dC_s}{dt} = J_\mathrm{set}^\mathrm{area} - k_s f_\mathrm{pH} C_s \frac{K_P\,\mathrm{SRP}_b}{K_P + \mathrm{SRP}_b} - k_{\mathrm{age},s}\,C_s - k_\mathrm{bur}\,C_s
\tag{4}\]



The pH modifier, \(f_\text{pH}\) (−), is represented as a bell-shaped response centred on the optimal pH, \(\text{pH}_\text{opt}\) (−). The parameter \(\sigma_\text{pH}\) (−) controls the width of the response. This is not a full chemical equilibrium model; it is a practical way of reducing effective uptake when pH moves away from the range where alum is expected to bind phosphorus most efficiently.
\[
f_\mathrm{pH} = \exp\!\left[-\frac{(\mathrm{pH} - \mathrm{pH_{opt}})^2}{2\,\sigma_\mathrm{pH}^2}\right]
\tag{5}\]




Ageing is represented as a first-order exponential loss of reactivity. Here, \(A(t)\) denotes the remaining reactive fraction at time \(t\) and \(A_0\) is the initial reactive fraction. For the current implementation, the ageing parameter is chosen so that 95% of reactive uptake capacity is lost after 30 days. This gives \(k_\text{age} \approx 0.10\) d−1. In practice, this same logic is applied to the pelagic and benthic ageing terms, \(k_{\text{age},w}\) and \(k_{\text{age},s}\).
\[
A(t) = A_0\,e^{-k_\mathrm{age}\,t} \qquad k_\mathrm{age} = -\frac{\ln(0.05)}{30} \approx 0.10 \ \mathrm{d}^{-1}
\tag{6}\]

title: Proposed Alum Model for AED
section: 2.1 Kinetic formulation, AED units and notation
text:
2.1 Kinetic formulation, AED units and notation
This document presents a simplified process representation of alum–phosphorus interactions for integration into GLM-AED as the module aed_alum. SRP uptake is represented as a kinetic rate process. Units, variable notation, and parameter conventions follow aed_phosphorus and the AED framework. A sediment resuspension term is included but disabled by default via a logical switch.
The module is intended to capture the main management-relevant processes for Lake Rotorua:

alum capacity delivery from treated inflows,
kinetic uptake of dissolved reactive phosphorus in the water column,
settling of remaining reactive material to the bed,
continued kinetic uptake at the sediment–water interface,
a gradual loss of reactivity through ageing,
optional resuspension of settled alum, and
a bell-shaped pH response as a pragmatic modifier of binding efficiency.

title: Proposed Alum Model for AED
text:
2.2 Structural decisions and open questions
The formulation below resolves several structural issues identified while reviewing the original concept note against the AED framework and the aed_phosphorus, aed_silica, and aed_tracer modules. The items still requiring confirmation are listed first.

2.2.1 Open — still requiring a decision

Numerical behaviour of kinetic uptake. SRP uptake is represented as a kinetic rate (Equation 1). Alum P-binding is physically fast, so a realistic k_w may be large enough to introduce stiffness and overshoot in an explicit ODE step. This needs to be checked in testing; if it proves unstable, the alternative is an equilibrium partition computed in an equilibrate routine, as aed_phosphorus does for adsorption.
Does ageing release or trap bound phosphorus? Ageing reduces binding capacity, but whether it also releases already-bound P depends on the physical interpretation — occlusion (P trapped) versus floc dissolution (P returned to frp). The “trapped” interpretation is adopted here (no ageing term on the bound pools), but should be confirmed against data from Lake Rotorua.
Alum delivery mechanism. Delivering alum capacity by dividing an inflow load by a fixed receiving-layer volume is fragile, because GLM places inflows by density and the receiving layer changes over time. The recommended approach is to deliver alum as an inflow water-quality concentration and let GLM distribute it, retaining the explicit S_ala term only for direct dosing. This needs to be confirmed against how GLM-AED handles inflow WQ variables.



2.2.2 Resolved in this formulation

Phosphorus mass closure. Phosphorus removed from frp is tracked in explicit bound-P pools (alp, ben_alp) rather than disappearing from the budget.
Settling as one coupled flux. Settling is handled by the mobility routine and AED transport, not as separate hand-coded volumetric and areal terms.
Benthic pools as sheet variables. ben_ala and ben_alp are registered with aed_define_sheet_variable. This deliberately extends beyond the aed_phosphorus template, which carries no benthic adsorbed-P state variable.
pH dependency. pH is sourced from aed_carbon (CAR_pH), with a configurable variable name and an f_pH = 1 fallback when unavailable.
Units and rate conventions. Phosphorus is in mmol P m⁻³ / m⁻², matching frp; namelist rates are per-day and converted to per-second on read.
Bottom-water SRP. Bottom-water SRP is frp evaluated in the bottom layer, not a separate state variable.
Resuspension. An optional, switch-gated resuspension term is included (Equation 7), disabled by default.

title: Proposed Alum Model for AED
text:
2.3 Notation and unit conventions

Phosphorus concentrations are in mmol P m⁻³ (pelagic) or mmol P m⁻² (benthic), consistent with aed_phosphorus. Where alum delivery is quoted as a mass dose, convert using a molar mass of P of 30.97 g mol⁻¹.
All rate parameters are supplied in the namelist per day and converted to per second on read in aed_define_alum (division by secs_per_day), following the AED convention.
Settling velocity w_ala is supplied in m day⁻¹ and converted to m s⁻¹ on read.
Fluxes applied to frp are in mmol P m⁻³ s⁻¹ (pelagic) or mmol P m⁻² s⁻¹ (benthic).
The equations below are written with rates in per-day units for readability; the implementation uses the per-second equivalents.

title: Proposed Alum Model for AED
text:
2.5 Core equations

2.5.1 Equation 1. Water-column SRP uptake
Reactive suspended alum capacity ala removes dissolved reactive phosphorus frp. The uptake rate U_w is controlled by the pelagic kinetic coefficient k_w, the pH modifier f_pH, and a Michaelis–Menten saturation term governed by the half-saturation constant K_P.
\[
\frac{d\,\mathrm{frp}}{dt} = -\,U_w
\]
\[
U_w = k_w\, f_\mathrm{pH}\, \mathrm{ala}\;\frac{\mathrm{frp}}{K_P + \mathrm{frp}}
\]
U_w has units of (d⁻¹)(−)(mmol P m⁻³)(−) = mmol P m⁻³ d⁻¹. The saturation term is linear at low frp and saturates at 1 at high frp. Uptake is linear in ala, so there is no saturation in available binding capacity.


2.5.2 Equation 2. Suspended alum capacity
ala is replenished by alum input S_ala, consumed one-to-one as it binds phosphorus, and lost through ageing. Settling is handled by transport via the mobility routine and does not appear as an explicit term.
\[
\frac{d\,\mathrm{ala}}{dt} = S_\mathrm{ala} - U_w - k_{age,w}\,\mathrm{ala}
\]
S_ala (mmol P m⁻³ d⁻¹) is the alum capacity input. It is best delivered as an inflow water-quality concentration so GLM distributes it by density; an explicit S_ala term is only needed for direct (non-inflow) dosing into a named layer.


2.5.3 Equation 3. Suspended alum-bound phosphorus
Phosphorus removed from frp enters the bound pool alp, preserving the phosphorus mass balance. alp settles with the same velocity w_ala as ala.
\[
\frac{d\,\mathrm{alp}}{dt} = U_w
\]
No ageing term is applied to alp: under the “trapped phosphorus” interpretation, ageing occludes binding sites but does not release already-bound phosphorus. If ageing were instead taken to represent floc dissolution, a term returning phosphorus to frp would be required. The trapped interpretation is the more conservative management assumption and is adopted here.


2.5.4 Equation 4. Bottom-water SRP uptake
Settled alum capacity ben_ala continues to remove frp from the bottom computational layer. The benthic uptake rate U_s is areal because ben_ala is areal; the factor 1/h_b converts it to a concentration change in the bottom layer of thickness h_b.
\[
\frac{d\,\mathrm{frp}_b}{dt} = -\frac{U_s}{h_b}
\]
\[
U_s = k_s\, f_\mathrm{pH}\, \mathrm{ben\_ala}\;\frac{\mathrm{frp}_b}{K_P + \mathrm{frp}_b}
\]
U_s has units of mmol P m⁻² d⁻¹; 1/h_b (m⁻¹) converts it to mmol P m⁻³ d⁻¹. frp_b is frp in the bottom layer, not a separate state variable.


2.5.5 Equation 5. Settled alum capacity
ben_ala gains the settling flux F_ala of ala arriving at the bed, and loses capacity through bottom-water uptake, ageing, burial, and optional resuspension.
\[
\frac{d\,\mathrm{ben\_ala}}{dt} = F_\mathrm{ala} - U_s - k_{age,s}\,\mathrm{ben\_ala} - k_\mathrm{bur}\,\mathrm{ben\_ala} - R_\mathrm{ala}
\]
F_ala (mmol P m⁻² d⁻¹) is supplied by AED’s vertical transport, not hand-coded. R_ala is the resuspension loss defined in Equation 7.


2.5.6 Equation 6. Settled alum-bound phosphorus
ben_alp gains the settling flux F_alp of alp, gains phosphorus bound at the bed (U_s), and loses mass through burial and optional resuspension.
\[
\frac{d\,\mathrm{ben\_alp}}{dt} = F_\mathrm{alp} + U_s - k_\mathrm{bur}\,\mathrm{ben\_alp} - R_\mathrm{alp}
\]
No ageing term is applied to ben_alp, consistent with the trapped-phosphorus interpretation in Equation 3.


2.5.7 Equation 7. Resuspension of settled alum (optional)
When simResuspension is enabled, a fraction of settled alum is returned to the water column. The resuspension fluxes R_ala and R_alp (mmol P m⁻² d⁻¹) are controlled by a resuspension coefficient k_res:
\[
R_\mathrm{ala} = \delta_\mathrm{res}\;k_\mathrm{res}\,\mathrm{ben\_ala},
\qquad
R_\mathrm{alp} = \delta_\mathrm{res}\;k_\mathrm{res}\,\mathrm{ben\_alp}
\]
where δ_res is 1 when simResuspension = .true. and 0 otherwise. The resuspended capacity and bound phosphorus are added back to the pelagic pools ala and alp in the bottom layer (divided by h_b to convert the areal flux to a concentration change). By default simResuspension = .false., so R_ala = R_alp = 0 and Equations 5 and 6 reduce to their non-resuspension form.
A more physically based option is to scale k_res by bottom shear stress relative to a critical threshold (as in aed_tracer), or to link to an external sediment-resuspension diagnostic (as the resus_link mechanism does in aed_phosphorus). The constant-coefficient form above is the minimal default; either extension can replace k_res later without changing the equation structure.


2.5.8 Equation 8. Bell-shaped pH modifier
The pH modifier f_pH is a bell-shaped response centred on the optimal pH, pH_opt, with width controlled by sigma_pH. It is a pragmatic efficiency modifier, not a chemical equilibrium model.
\[
f_\mathrm{pH} = \exp\!\left[-\frac{(\mathrm{pH} - \mathrm{pH_{opt}})^2}{2\,\sigma_\mathrm{pH}^2}\right]
\]
pH is obtained from the AED carbon-chemistry module, by default the variable CAR_pH, located with aed_locate_variable. The variable name is configurable via the namelist (pH_variable).


2.5.9 Equation 9. Ageing coefficient
Ageing is a first-order exponential loss of reactive capacity. Choosing the coefficient so that 95% of capacity is lost after 30 days gives:
\[
A(t) = A_0\, e^{-k_\mathrm{age}\, t},
\qquad
k_\mathrm{age} = -\frac{\ln(0.05)}{30} \approx 0.0998 \ \mathrm{d}^{-1}
\]
The same logic applies to the pelagic and benthic ageing coefficients k_age_w and k_age_s. The value 0.0998 d⁻¹ is the namelist value; internally it is converted to ≈ 1.16 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹.

title: Proposed Alum Model for AED
text:
2.6 Phosphorus mass balance
With the trapped-phosphorus interpretation, total phosphorus is conserved. Every term leaving frp enters a bound pool (alp or ben_alp); settling transfers ala and alp to ben_ala and ben_alp; resuspension transfers them back; and only burial (k_bur) permanently removes phosphorus from the modelled system. Retaining an ageing term on a bound pool without a compensating release term would introduce a silent phosphorus sink and should be avoided.

title: Proposed Alum Model for AED
text:
2.9 Calibration priorities
The main calibration targets are likely to be the dose-to-capacity conversion feeding S_ala (or the inflow alum concentration), the pelagic and benthic kinetic coefficients k_w and k_s, the settling velocity w_ala, and — if the pH modifier is enabled — pH_opt and sigma_pH. Ageing is intended as a simple first-order loss rather than a multi-pool formulation, and k_age_w and k_age_s can reasonably be fixed at the 30-day value unless data suggest otherwise. Resuspension is off by default; if enabled, k_res becomes an additional calibration parameter.

title: GLM-AED Sensitivity Analysis and Calibration Plan
text:
3 How SA and calibration relate

Screening SA (e.g. Morris / elementary effects). Run over the full parameter union below with wide ranges. Fix stoichiometry and most Arrhenius (theta_*) terms. Goal: discard parameters with negligible influence on the four targets.
Variance-based SA (e.g. Sobol) — optional. Run on the ~10–15 survivors with ranges tightened to roughly ±25–50 % of the expected value. Goal: rank interactions and first-order effects per target metric.
Calibration. Tune only the high-ranking, poorly-constrained, identifiable subset (Section 5). Typically 12–18 parameters.

Order matters. Get temperature/stratification and DO right first: the redox switches controlling NH4 and FRP sediment release (ksed_amm, ksed_frp) are gated on the simulated O2 field, so calibrating them before DO is closed will bias them.

title: Simplified Alum–Phosphorus Module for GLM-AED
text:
To maintain mechanistic defensibility while keeping the implementation simple, we propose a minimal two-state kinetic model representing alum–phosphorus (Al–P) interactions in the water column.
The model captures:

pH-dependent aluminium hydrolysis and reactivity

Phosphate sorption onto amorphous Al(OH)₃ flocs

Temperature effects on reaction kinetics

Rapid settling of aluminium flocs (~10 m d⁻¹)

Optional slow aging (loss of reactivity)

This structure is designed for scenario testing of alum dosing strategies.

title: Simplified Alum–Phosphorus Module for GLM-AED
text:
Water Column

\(Al_r\) — Reactive aluminium floc (g Al m\(^{-3}\))

\(P_{Al}\) — Phosphorus bound to aluminium floc (g P m\(^{-3}\))

Coupled to existing AED variable:

\(PO_4\) — Dissolved reactive phosphorus (FRP)

title: Simplified Alum–Phosphorus Module for GLM-AED
text:
1. Reactive Aluminium
Alum added via inflows is assumed to rapidly hydrolyse to reactive floc.
\[
\frac{d Al_r}{dt} =
L_{Al,in}
- k_{age} Al_r
- R_{bind}
- settling
\]
Where:

\(L_{Al,in}\) = alum loading from inflow forcing

\(k_{age}\) = first-order aging constant (loss of reactivity)

\(R_{bind}\) = phosphate binding rate

text:
2. Phosphate (FRP)
\[
\frac{d PO_4}{dt} = - R_{bind}
\]

\[
\frac{d P_{Al}}{dt} =
+ R_{bind}
- settling

title: Alum Dosing in Lake Rotorua
text:
Source: Sanila, S. (2026). Evaluation of Aluminium–Phosphorus Binding and pH Responses to Alum Dosing of Three New Zealand Lakes. MSc thesis, University of Waikato.



This thesis evaluates the effectiveness of alum (aluminium sulphate, Al₂(SO₄)₃) as a tool for reducing dissolved reactive phosphorus (DRP) across five New Zealand waters: Lake Rotorua, the Utuhina and Puarenga Streams, Lake Ōkaro, and Lake Moawhitu. The study was motivated by a recognised gap in site-specific, controlled evidence for Al:P binding behaviour across the Rotorua catchment lakes, despite many years of operational dosing.
The methodology centred on standardised 3-hour jar tests, with acid titrations used to quantify buffering capacity at each site. For Lake Rotorua specifically, video-based settling measurements and stereomicroscopy were used to characterise the physical properties of alum floc — providing the most detailed floc data available for this lake.
Across all sites, alum reduced DRP, but the magnitude of removal and pH response varied considerably. Al:P molar ratios ranged from 0.7:1 to 15.1:1 depending on site chemistry, and pH behaviour was governed primarily by alkalinity rather than dose rate. Lake Rotorua and the Puarenga Stream had the lowest alkalinity (~19 mg CaCO₃ L⁻¹) and showed the weakest pH recovery after dosing. Lake Moawhitu, with the highest alkalinity (~67 mg CaCO₃ L⁻¹), recovered most strongly.




The following sections draw directly on thesis findings to inform parameterisation of the &aed_alum module for Lake Rotorua. Parameters are addressed in thematic groups.



The jar-test Al:P molar ratio for Lake Rotorua was 0.7:1 (mass ratio 0.6:1), based on a dose of 1.0 mg Al L⁻¹ and a measured DRP removal of 1.60 ± 0.008 mg L⁻¹ from a pre-treatment spiked concentration of 1.62 mg L⁻¹. This near 1:1 molar performance is consistent with the lake’s characteristically low dissolved organic carbon (~2 mg L⁻¹), which reduces competition for Al(OH)₃ surface sites and allows a high proportion of added aluminium to remain available for phosphate binding.
It is important to note that this represents a best-case, laboratory-derived estimate. Operational field dosing on the Utuhina and Puarenga inflows has historically required substantially higher effective ratios (~7:1 Al:P; McDowell & Hawke, 2006), reflecting the effects of turbulence, short flocculation contact times, and hydrodynamic losses in the stream environment.
Regarding binding kinetics, DRP removal appeared rapid under jar-test conditions — pH dropped within the first five minutes of dosing, and most removal was complete within the first 20 minutes of the 3-hour experiment. This is qualitatively consistent with a fast water-column binding rate (k_w), though no explicit first-order rate constant was fitted in the thesis. The near-complete removal of 1.62 mg P L⁻¹ (~52 mmol P m⁻³) at a 1 mg Al L⁻¹ dose suggests binding was not substrate-limited at that concentration, which is consistent with a relatively low half-saturation constant (K_P). The default value of 0.3 mmol P m⁻³ is not contradicted by the data, though it cannot be independently confirmed from this study.




The thesis provides the most quantitatively useful constraints for this parameter. Settling velocities were measured for 89 individually tracked flocs under low-turbulence conditions:



Floc size class
Typical settling velocity




< 1,000 µm
< 40 m day⁻¹


1,500–2,500 µm
50–80 m day⁻¹


> 3,000 µm
~100 m day⁻¹



The fitted linear regression across all flocs was: velocity (m day⁻¹) = 0.0324 × diameter (µm) − 0.94, with R² = 0.69. The median Martin diameter was 1,290 µm and the mean was 1,442 µm. Applying the fitted relationship to Lake Rotorua’s bathymetry, settling through the mean depth (10.8 m) is estimated at 0.2–0.7 days (5–17 hours), and through the maximum depth (45 m) at 0.9–3.0 days under quiescent conditions.
The bulk of the floc population clustered in the 20–60 m day⁻¹ range. A representative central estimate for w_ala of ~0.5 m day⁻¹ (the current default) is physically defensible and consistent with median floc behaviour. A range of 0.3–1.5 m day⁻¹ could be justified depending on whether conservative or mean settling is targeted. These estimates should be treated as upper bounds, as wind-driven mixing in the lake is expected to interrupt settling and prolong suspension.




Microscopic image analysis of 1,094 fine floc particles revealed:

Equivalent diameters ranged from 25 to 240 µm
87% of particles were below 120 µm; only 13% exceeded this
Mean equivalent diameter: 77.5 µm; median: 69.3 µm
Distribution was right-skewed (skewness = 0.95), dominated by small aggregates

The larger settling aggregates tracked in video (median ~1,290 µm) are composite structures built from these fine sub-units. The thesis notes that alum flocs are inherently fragile and can release stable fine particles under gentle shear — a characteristic relevant to resuspension behaviour under wave action in the lake.




The thesis provides strong qualitative support for enabling resuspension in Lake Rotorua models. Sediment surveys (Tempero & Hamilton, 2016; Tempero, 2019) consistently show that amorphous Al(OH)₃ is concentrated in near-shore areas close to the Utuhina and Puarenga discharge zones, with limited accumulation in the deeper basin sediments. The thesis interprets this pattern as a consequence of fast near-shore settling (consistent with the 0.2–0.7 day estimate to mean depth) combined with subsequent wind-driven resuspension that prevents widespread offshore redistribution.
On this basis, simResuspension = .true. is recommended for Lake Rotorua, particularly in models that resolve spatial differences between near-shore and offshore zones. No quantitative value for k_res is derivable from the thesis; the authors recommend future wave-flume experiments to constrain this parameter.




The thesis provides directly relevant pH observations for Lake Rotorua:

Pre-treatment pH ranged from 6.9 to 7.9 across sites, with Lake Rotorua at the lower end
Following alum addition, pH dropped by up to 2.11 units within 10–20 minutes, then stabilised with minimal recovery (< 0.1 units over 3 hours)
Post-treatment pH in jar tests therefore sat persistently in the ~5–6 range
Alkalinity was the lowest of all sites at 19.20 mg CaCO₃ L⁻¹, providing very limited buffering against acidification
Al(OH)₃ is most stable and P-binding most effective in the pH 6–8 window; efficiency declines below pH 6 and Al³⁺ toxicity becomes a concern below pH 4.5

Since operational dosing is applied via the Utuhina and Puarenga inflows rather than directly to the open lake, pH in the lake body should remain close to ambient (~7–8) rather than dropping to the jar-test minimum. Under open-lake conditions, the pH efficiency modifier is therefore less critical than it would be for a direct-dosing scenario.
If ads_use_pH is activated, a pH_opt of 7.0 would better represent open-lake conditions than the default of 6.0. A sigma_pH of 1.0 is consistent with the observed ±1–2 unit swings recorded during dosing events.




Operational alum dosing has been applied continuously to the Utuhina Stream since 2006 and the Puarenga Stream since 2010, at a target rate of approximately 1 mg Al L⁻¹, adjusted automatically to stream flow. Cumulative aluminium applied reached 1,071 tonnes by end of 2024, at a long-term mean rate of 158.1 kg Al day⁻¹. Peak application occurred during 2011–2012 when more than 2,000 tonnes per year were applied.
Converting the mean operational rate to a whole-lake surface dose: 158.1 kg Al day⁻¹ ÷ 26.98 g mol⁻¹ = ~5,860 mol Al day⁻¹. At the observed 0.7:1 Al:P molar ratio, this binds approximately 8,370 mol P day⁻¹, or ~8.37 × 10⁶ mmol P day⁻¹. Distributed over Lake Rotorua’s surface area (80.6 km² = 80.6 × 10⁶ m²), this gives an indicative whole-lake mean of:

S_ala ≈ 0.10 mmol P m⁻² day⁻¹

Peak dosing years would yield approximately double this value. Note that this is a spatially averaged estimate; in practice, alum enters via discrete inflow points and is not uniformly distributed across the lake surface.




The thesis does not report explicit rate constants for the loss of binding capacity or burial of settled floc. It does confirm that sediment aluminium persists in near-shore zones over multi-year timescales, implying some long-term retention, but quantitative ageing or burial rates are not derivable from this study. The default values (k_age ~0.0998 day⁻¹, k_bur = 0.01 day⁻¹) cannot be validated or refuted from the available data and should be drawn from the broader literature or calibrated against monitoring data.

The jar-test Al:P ratios are best treated as site-specific indicators of performance under idealised, controlled conditions, not as fixed stoichiometric targets for field dosing. Operational experience consistently shows higher effective Al:P requirements in flowing systems due to turbulence and incomplete flocculation. Settling velocity estimates are similarly best-case figures derived under low-turbulence laboratory conditions; wind-driven mixing in Lake Rotorua will extend effective settling times and promote near-shore deposition over basin-wide distribution. Periodic re-evaluation of jar-test response and alkalinity is recommended, as water chemistry can shift over time and alter both treatment performance and operational risk.

A range of 0.3–1.5 m day⁻¹ could be justified depending on whether conservative or mean settling is targeted. These estimates should be treated as upper bounds, as wind-driven mixing in the lake is expected to interrupt settling and prolong suspension.




Microscopic image analysis of 1,094 fine floc particles revealed:

Equivalent diameters ranged from 25 to 240 µm
87% of particles were below 120 µm; only 13% exceeded this
Mean equivalent diameter: 77.5 µm; median: 69.3 µm
Distribution was right-skewed (skewness = 0.95), dominated by small aggregates

The larger settling aggregates tracked in video (median ~1,290 µm) are composite structures built from these fine sub-units. The thesis notes that alum flocs are inherently fragile and can release stable fine particles under gentle shear — a characteristic relevant to resuspension behaviour under wave action in the lake.




The thesis provides strong qualitative support for enabling resuspension in Lake Rotorua models. Sediment surveys (Tempero & Hamilton, 2016; Tempero, 2019) consistently show that amorphous Al(OH)₃ is concentrated in near-shore areas close to the Utuhina and Puarenga discharge zones, with limited accumulation in the deeper basin sediments. The thesis interprets this pattern as a consequence of fast near-shore settling (consistent with the 0.2–0.7 day estimate to mean depth) combined with subsequent wind-driven resuspension that prevents widespread offshore redistribution.
On this basis, simResuspension = .true. is recommended for Lake Rotorua, particularly in models that resolve spatial differences between near-shore and offshore zones. No quantitative value for k_res is derivable from the thesis; the authors recommend future wave-flume experiments to constrain this parameter.




The thesis provides directly relevant pH observations for Lake Rotorua:

Pre-treatment pH ranged from 6.9 to 7.9 across sites, with Lake Rotorua at the lower end
Following alum addition, pH dropped by up to 2.11 units within 10–20 minutes, then stabilised with minimal recovery (< 0.1 units over 3 hours)
Post-treatment pH in jar tests therefore sat persistently in the ~5–6 range
Alkalinity was the lowest of all sites at 19.20 mg CaCO₃ L⁻¹, providing very limited buffering against acidification
Al(OH)₃ is most stable and P-binding most effective in the pH 6–8 window; efficiency declines below pH 6 and Al³⁺ toxicity becomes a concern below pH 4.5

Since operational dosing is applied via the Utuhina and Puarenga inflows rather than directly to the open lake, pH in the lake body should remain close to ambient (~7–8) rather than dropping to the jar-test minimum. Under open-lake conditions, the pH efficiency modifier is therefore less critical than it would be for a direct-dosing scenario.
If ads_use_pH is activated, a pH_opt of 7.0 would better represent open-lake conditions than the default of 6.0. A sigma_pH of 1.0 is consistent with the observed ±1–2 unit swings recorded during dosing events.




Operational alum dosing has been applied continuously to the Utuhina Stream since 2006 and the Puarenga Stream since 2010, at a target rate of approximately 1 mg Al L⁻¹, adjusted automatically to stream flow. Cumulative aluminium applied reached 1,071 tonnes by end of 2024, at a long-term mean rate of 158.1 kg Al day⁻¹. Peak application occurred during 2011–2012 when more than 2,000 tonnes per year were applied.
Converting the mean operational rate to a whole-lake surface dose: 158.1 kg Al day⁻¹ ÷ 26.98 g mol⁻¹ = ~5,860 mol Al day⁻¹. At the observed 0.7:1 Al:P molar ratio, this binds approximately 8,370 mol P day⁻¹, or ~8.37 × 10⁶ mmol P day⁻¹. Distributed over Lake Rotorua’s surface area (80.6 km² = 80.6 × 10⁶ m²), this gives an indicative whole-lake mean of:

S_ala ≈ 0.10 mmol P m⁻² day⁻¹

Peak dosing years would yield approximately double this value. Note that this is a spatially averaged estimate; in practice, alum enters via discrete inflow points and is not uniformly distributed across the lake surface.




The thesis does not report explicit rate constants for the loss of binding capacity or burial of settled floc. It does confirm that sediment aluminium persists in near-shore zones over multi-year timescales, implying some long-term retention, but quantitative ageing or burial rates are not derivable from this study. The default values (k_age ~0.0998 day⁻¹, k_bur = 0.01 day⁻¹) cannot be validated or refuted from the available data and should be drawn from the broader literature or calibrated against monitoring data.
