title: Alum Dosing in Lake Rotorua
text: The jar-test Al:P ratios are best treated as site-specific indicators of performance under idealised, controlled conditions, not as fixed stoichiometric targets for field dosing. Operational experience consistently shows higher effective Al:P requirements in flowing systems due to turbulence and incomplete flocculation. Settling velocity estimates are similarly best-case figures derived under low-turbulence laboratory conditions; wind-driven mixing in Lake Rotorua will extend effective settling times and promote near-shore deposition over basin-wide distribution. Periodic re-evaluation of jar-test response and alkalinity is recommended, as water chemistry can shift over time and alter both treatment performance and operational risk.

title: Benthic Nutrient Fluxes in Lake Rotorua (Burger et al. 2007)
text:
Reference: Burger, D.F., Hamilton, D.P., Pilditch, C.A. & Gibbs, M.M. (2007). Benthic nutrient fluxes in a eutrophic, polymictic lake. Hydrobiologia 584: 13–25. doi:10.1007/s10750-007-0582-0
This page summarises the paper and tabulates its chamber data so the fluxes can be used to characterise, and later constrain, the sediment-release terms in the Lake Rotorua GLM-AED model. Data are in data/burger2007_chamber_fluxes.csv and data/burger2007_bottom_water.csv, transcribed from Tables 1 and 2 of the paper.

title: Benthic Nutrient Fluxes in Lake Rotorua (Burger et al. 2007)
text:
Aim and approach
The authors measured sediment release of soluble reactive phosphorus (SRP) and ammonium (NH4), and sediment oxygen demand (SOD), using in situ benthic chambers at three sites in Lake Rotorua. They then compared internal (sediment) loads with the external catchment load.

Lake: 79.8 km², mean depth 10.5 m, polymictic, eutrophic. Annual mean TP 0.055 mg L⁻¹, TN 0.814 mg L⁻¹. Catchment 425 km² (48% agriculture, 23% plantation forestry). Wastewater was discharged to the lake until 1991 (about 35 t TP and 150 t TN per year).
Sites: Site 1 (7 m, well mixed and oxygenated), Site 2 (14 m, periodically stratified) and Site 3 (20 m, periodically stratified and anoxic).
Timing: four deployments: 10 Feb 2003, 13 Aug 2003, 4/10 Nov 2003 and 27 Jan 2004.
Chambers:

Acrylic and PVC cylinders of about 0.11 m² and 17–18 L, pushed 80 mm into the sediment by divers.
Duplicate light and dark chambers at Sites 1 and 2. Only light chambers at Site 3, where light was below 1% of surface PAR.
Pumped for 5 s per minute. Sampled about four times a day for 2 days.
Fluxes come from linear regression of concentration against time, corrected for dilution, with control bottles subtracted.
The 48 h deployment was long enough to make the chambers anoxic at Sites 2 and 3 in summer, which mimics natural stratification events.

title: Benthic Nutrient Fluxes in Lake Rotorua (Burger et al. 2007)
text:
Key findings

SRP release was large and mostly independent of oxygen. Rates were 2.1–85.6 mg P m⁻² d⁻¹, and concentrations rose linearly in the chambers (mean R² = 0.93) regardless of chamber DO. This is above the 7–50 mg m⁻² d⁻¹ typical of other eutrophic lakes. The authors link it to high organic matter deposition and microbial P cycling at the sediment surface, rather than to Fe-P redox release alone.
NH4 release had two phases.

A very high initial rate over 0–12 h of up to about 2,200 mg N m⁻² d⁻¹.
A lower secondary rate over 12–48 h of up to about 270 mg N m⁻² d⁻¹ (maximum 283 in the dark chambers).
The authors suggest the initial burst may partly be a chamber or porewater disturbance artefact, and that the secondary rate better represents natural organic matter degradation under low DO.

Release peaks in summer and in deep water. The pattern held for SRP, NH4 and SOD. August (winter, about 10 °C) rates were the lowest, and Site 3 (20 m) had the highest SRP and NH4 release. Site 3 SRP (mean 44.3 mg m⁻² d⁻¹) was significantly higher than Sites 2 (9.3) and 1 (7.7) in all periods except August. Temperature and the organic matter supply rate (sedimentation) are the proposed drivers.
Light and dark chambers differed little at Site 1. Site 2 dark chambers had higher initial NH4 release and, in Feb 2003, about three times higher SRP release (29.4 vs 9.0 mg m⁻² d⁻¹), so benthic primary production appears to matter little for fluxes.
The chamber rates agree with whole-lake estimates. For the 19-day stratification event starting 1 Feb 2003:

SRP release from chambers, interpolated by depth below the thermocline, was 17.4 mg m⁻² d⁻¹. The independent hypolimnetic mass balance gave 13.8.
NH4 release from the chambers’ secondary rate was 131 mg m⁻² d⁻¹. The hypolimnion accumulation gave 63.9, so the chambers over-estimate NH4 by about 2× (they miss nitrification and benthic uptake).

Internal load exceeds external load. Mean sediment SRP and NH4 release were at least three times the mean daily external load. At Site 3, SRP release exceeded the TP sedimentation rate. The authors expect high release to continue because of the large legacy sediment nutrient pool, and say only a severe reduction in external load would “break” the depositional cycle.

title: Benthic Nutrient Fluxes in Lake Rotorua (Burger et al. 2007)
text:
Caveats stated or implied

Only SRP and NH4 were measured. Dissolved organic P and N, porewater release by resuspension (important in the shallows), and water-column denitrification are not included.
NO3 fluxes were not calculated because chamber concentrations were below 5% of NH4 and often below detection.
The sample size is small (n = 2 chambers per site and period, 4 in Jan 2004 at Site 3), and Site 3 has no dark chambers.
The text says TP sedimentation was 0.5–2.7 g m⁻² d⁻¹. That is inconsistent with the 13–29 mg m⁻² d⁻¹ shown in Fig. 6, so it is probably a units slip in the paper.

title: Benthic Nutrient Fluxes in Lake Rotorua (Burger et al. 2007)
text:
Recommended flux ranges

SRP: 2–14 mg P m⁻² d⁻¹ in the shallow and mid-depth regions (Sites 1–2) and about 6–86 mg P m⁻² d⁻¹ at 20 m. Winter (about 10 °C) is the low end and summer stratification the high end. About 17 mg m⁻² d⁻¹ is a reasonable mean beneath the thermocline in summer, based on the paper’s own validation.
NH4: use the secondary (12–48 h) rate, 33–283 mg N m⁻² d⁻¹, which the authors argue is more representative. The initial burst (up to 2,213) should not be used directly. Even the secondary rate over-estimates the hypolimnion mass balance by about 2×, so treat it as an upper bound.
SOD: 0.3–4.0 g O2 m⁻² d⁻¹, with lake-wide means of about 0.9 / 1.5 / 1.9 g m⁻² d⁻¹ at 7 / 14 / 20 m.

section: Comparison with the current model settings
text:
Comparison with the current model settings
The current aed.nml sets fsed_amm = 6.654, 2.408, 0.616, fsed_frp = 0.0602, 0.0657, 0.0254 and fsed_oxy = -30.1, -30.1, -23.33 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹. I have not checked which sediment zone each entry maps to.

fsed_oxy is in the same range as the chamber SOD (about 27 / 47 / 60 mmol O2 m⁻² d⁻¹ at 7 / 14 / 20 m). Chamber SOD is somewhat larger at depth.
fsed_amm is within the chamber range for the first zone (6.65 against 6.6 mmol N m⁻² d⁻¹ at Site 1), but the other two zones (2.4 and 0.6) are well below the secondary chamber rates (about 4.4 at 14 m and 9.7 at 20 m).
fsed_frp is much lower than the chamber SRP rates (0.25 / 0.30 / 1.43 mmol P m⁻² d⁻¹ at 7 / 14 / 20 m). The model values are about 4–50 times smaller.

Whether that gap is a calibration artefact or a real model–observation mismatch depends on how the model treats other P sources. These include phytoplankton and POP settling and mineralisation, and the alum-bound P pool in the alum module. In AED the sediment fluxes also scale with temperature (theta_sed_frp, theta_sed_amm) and with a DO half-saturation (ksed_frp, ksed_amm). The paper’s finding that SRP release was largely independent of DO argues against making the P flux strongly oxygen-dependent.

title: Climate-Scenario Extreme & Storm-Event Analysis
text:
climate-scenario-workflow.qmd builds scenario_hourly_met – the AEME MET_*-formatted hourly forcing for every GCM x SSP x future-window combination (7 GCMs x 4 SSPs x 3 windows, minus NZESM/ssp585 = 81 branches), by applying each GCM/scenario’s monthly delta-change signal to the bias-corrected daily ERA5 baseline and disaggregating back to hourly against the bias-corrected hourly ERA5 record.
This page uses that same hourly forcing to ask a narrower question: how does the frequency and intensity of extreme/storm-scale events change, not just the monthly-mean climate? Sub-daily (hourly) data matters here because heavy-rain intensity, wind-storm duration and short heatwaves are sub-daily-to-daily phenomena that a monthly delta-change factor alone cannot resolve – they only show up once the delta has been re-expanded to hourly.
This is a rebuild of an earlier version of this page, incorporating two changes made since:

title: Climate-Scenario Extreme & Storm-Event Analysis
text:
Method
For every branch of scenario_hourly_met, and separately for the bias-corrected historical baseline (era5_corrected_hourly, 1995-2014), compute_annual_extreme_indices() (R/summarise_climate_extremes.R) computes one row per calendar year for:







Index
Definition




rx1day
Annual maximum daily rainfall (mm)


heavy_rain_days
Days/year with daily rainfall above the p95 (wet days only)


extreme_rain_days
Days/year above the p99


hot_days
Days/year with daily maximum air temperature above the historical p95


wsdi
Warm-spell duration index: days/year in spells of >=3 consecutive hot days


max_wind
Annual maximum hourly wind speed (m/s)


storm_wind_hours
Hours/year with hourly wind speed above the historical p95


severe_wind_hours
Hours/year above the historical p99


storm_events
Number of separate contiguous spells/year above the wind p95 threshold



Thresholds (compute_extreme_thresholds()) are fixed once and applied unchanged to every future branch, so “heavy rain” and “storm wind” mean the same absolute thing in every period – a change in frequency is then a genuine intensification/frequency signal, not an artefact of a moving definition. Wind and temperature thresholds still come from the bias-corrected ERA5 hourly baseline (1995-2014) – there’s no long-record alternative for those at this site. Rainfall thresholds now come from the 125-year Whakarewarewa daily rain-gauge record (compute_long_rain_thresholds(), on pc10_climate_met) rather than the 20-year ERA5 window: 20 years is thin for estimating a p95/p99 event, and the long, independently-measured record is unaffected by anything in the reanalysis/bias-correction/delta-change chain the scenarios themselves are built from.

These are a fixed, historically-grounded reference point – e.g. how the scenario ensemble’s projected rx1day (below) compares to a present-day 1-in-20 or 1-in-50 year event – independent of any GCM or bias-correction choice made elsewhere in this pipeline.
Each scenario_hourly_met branch’s 20-30 annual values are then averaged into one mean-annual number per GCM/scenario/window (summarise_branch_extremes()), and the figure/tables below summarise those 81 branch-means as a GCM-ensemble mean and range per scenario/window, against the same baseline period’s mean-annual values (dashed line in the figure).

title: Climate-Scenario Extreme & Storm-Event Analysis
text:
Discussion
Rainfall. heavy_rain_days and extreme_rain_days increase modestly and roughly monotonically with emissions scenario and window, consistent with a warmer atmosphere holding more moisture – but the ensemble range across GCMs is wide relative to the mean shift, and for rx1day several GCMs project little change or a slight decrease at some windows (the ratio-based delta-change method rescales the historical daily rainfall sequence rather than restructuring its day-to-day intermittency, so it cannot invent a heavier single-day extreme than proportional scaling of the historical record allows – see the stationarity caveat in climate-scenario-workflow.qmd). Anchoring the rainfall thresholds to the 125-year Whakarewarewa record instead of the 20-year ERA5 window matters here specifically because a 20-year sample gives a noisy p95/p99 estimate – with a long, independent record the “heavy”/“extreme” definitions themselves are far more stable, so a projected change in frequency is more trustworthy as an actual signal rather than partly an artefact of which 20 years happened to set the threshold.
Heat. hot_days and wsdi (warm-spell duration) show the clearest, most consistent scenario/window gradient of the three groups – both increase substantially and near-monotonically from ssp126 to ssp585 and from the near-term to the end-of-century window, with comparatively narrow GCM spread. This is the expected signature of a monotonic mean-warming delta applied to a fixed threshold: as the whole distribution shifts up, an increasing share of days cross a fixed, historical p95 threshold.
Wind storms. With the vector-disaggregation fix, wind speed is now shaped directly from the donor’s own hourly wind-speed pattern rather than being recomputed from reshaped u/v components, removing the disaggregation-side inflation flagged in the previous version of this page (disaggregated hourly wind no longer runs systematically higher than its own delta-adjusted daily target). The wind-storm indices above should now be read as a direct read on the GCM ensemble’s wind delta-change signal, which – per gcm_monthly_deltas_df – is close to 1 (little change) for most GCM/scenario combinations, with a modest number of outlier models/months driving any larger shifts. Wind remains the index group with the least physical basis for a strong climate-change signal at monthly delta-change resolution, since storm-scale wind events are a synoptic-scale phenomenon that a monthly mean factor is a weak proxy for.
Practical implication for lake modelling. Heavy-rain and warm-spell frequency both increase with scenario severity in a way that is directionally robust across the GCM ensemble, and both are levers on lake response that matter beyond the monthly-mean forcing already explored in climate-scenario-workflow.qmd: more frequent heavy-rain days translate to more frequent high-inflow/nutrient-loading pulses, and longer warm spells extend the window over which thermal stratification can strengthen and hypolimnetic anoxia can develop. The return-level table above gives a fixed, long-record reference point (e.g. a 1-in-50-year daily rainfall total) against which to judge whether a given scenario/window’s mean rx1day represents a meaningfully more frequent extreme, rather than reasoning from the 20-30 year scenario windows alone.

title: Climate-Scenario Extreme & Storm-Event Analysis
text:
Caveats
In addition to the caveats already noted in climate-scenario-workflow.qmd (stationarity of the bias-correction and delta-change transfer functions, the short buoy overlap period, and the known MET_prsttn unit issue) and met-source-comparison.qmd (PC10’s weak day-to-day correlation with the buoy for rainfall, r ~ 0.12 – a long-run climatology/threshold use like this is far less sensitive to that than a day-by-day bias-correction reference would be):

The Whakarewarewa gauge is a land station, not over the lake; its absolute rainfall total may differ from true over-lake rainfall even though its long-run climatology is the best available basis for a stable extreme-event threshold at this site.
The Gumbel method-of-moments fit is a simple, standard estimator but not the only reasonable choice (e.g. GEV with a shape parameter, or L-moments); treat the return-level table as indicative rather than a design-standard flood estimate.
Wind and temperature thresholds still come from only 20 years of ERA5 (1995-2014) – no equivalently long, independent wind/temperature record exists at this site the way it does for rainfall.
Extreme indices here are derived from the delta-changed reanalysis sequence, not from the GCM’s own extremes – by construction they inherit the historical record’s actual extreme events (dates, storm tracks, event structure), rescaled by a smooth monthly climate signal, so they cannot represent a genuinely new type of extreme event outside the historical envelope.

title: Climate-Scenario Meteorology Workflow
text:
cmip6-processing.qmd and cmip6-visualisation.qmd extract and plot the raw, absolute CMIP6/CCAM values at the lake point (gcm_point_data_df). Raw GCM output is not suitable for directly driving a sub-daily lake model: it carries its own absolute-level biases (mean offset, distorted seasonal cycle, wrong wind climatology) that would land straight in simulated stratification, ice and evaporation, and it is daily on a coarse grid with no sub-daily information.
This page instead builds the meteorological forcing the lake model actually uses, following the metscale package’s bias-correct → delta-change → disaggregate workflow (vignette("scenario-workflow", package = "metscale"), vignette("climate-extremes") for storm/heatwave-focused alternatives):
The corrected reanalysis carries real weather — genuine day-to-day persistence, event structure and a real diurnal cycle, all on actual calendar dates. Warping it with a model’s own future-vs-historical change (which is far more reliable than the model’s absolute output) keeps that physical realism while shifting its statistics onto each scenario. See the vignette for the full reasoning and the calendar-handling details (NorESM2-MM runs a 365_day calendar, NZESM a 360_day calendar – metscale::climate_point_monthly_climatology() decodes each correctly before averaging).
These steps are wired into _targets.R as era5_hourly_met → era5_bias_correction → era5_corrected_hourly / era5_corrected_daily_baseline → gcm_monthly_deltas_df → scenario_daily_met → scenario_hourly_met, added alongside (not replacing) the existing raw gcm_point_data* targets.

Air temperature, wind speed, shortwave radiation and relative humidity all improve out-of-sample after the monthly scale correction (day-of-year loess-smoothed offset). Station pressure (MET_prsttn) is a known data issue, not yet resolved: the raw bias between ERA5 (Pa) and the buoy’s PrBaro field is ~96 kPa, an order of magnitude larger than the ~3 kPa elevation-offset effect the metscale vignette describes for its own site – this looks like a unit mismatch in buoy_to_aeme_met() (PrBaro likely arrives in hPa, not Pa) rather than a real atmospheric difference, and should be checked before MET_prsttn from this workflow is trusted.
Update: rainfall (MET_pprain) is now included in this correction, having previously been left uncorrected on the assumption that the buoy gauge was an unreliable target. A multi-source comparison (buoy vs. airport vs. ERA5 vs. BOPRC/PC10 stations – see met-source-comparison.qmd) found no evidence the buoy under-reads rain relative to the land stations, but did surface a real unit bug: the raw ERA5-Land CSV stores MET_pprain in mm/hour, not the m/hour every other source in this pipeline uses, which was silently inflating ERA5 rainfall ~1000x wherever it passed uncorrected. That’s fixed at the source in read_era5_hourly_met(). The buoy’s rain record is still noisier than its other variables (weak correlation with the long land records), so treat the corrected MET_pprain here with more caution than temperature/humidity/wind – see the comparison page for the numbers.
Further update – found and fixed: comparing the raw buoy PpRain record against its own known climatology surfaced a systematic ~10x inflation from the start of the record (Feb 2022) through October 2023 – mean daily rain of ~47 mm/day (annualising to ~17,000 mm/yr, physically impossible for Rotorua) versus ~4 mm/day (~1,500 mm/yr, matching raw ERA5 and the 125-year Whakarewarewa gauge closely) from late October 2023 onward. The root cause is a recording-unit change at the buoy on 2023-10-23, not an instrument calibration drift: before that date PpRain was logged in mm/10min (not mm) and WndSpd in knots (not m/s). Both are now converted in rotorua_buoy_met_data (_targets.R) – PpRain / 10 and WndSpd * 0.514444 – for the pre-2023-10-23 rows before being combined with the already-correct-unit rows after it, so era5_bias_correction now fits against a consistently-unit’d buoy record across its full span. The plots below reflect whatever era5_bias_correction/era5_corrected_hourly build was current when last rendered – re-render this page after a fresh tar_make() to confirm the corrected distribution’s tail now tracks the buoy/long-record rainfall instead of overshooting it.

Bias-correction diagnostics: wind speed and rainfall
The skill table above summarises cross-validated numeric performance; the figures below show what the correction is actually doing to the daily time series and distribution, for the two variables most consequential downstream (wind drives the storm indices in climate-extreme-events.qmd, rainfall drives the heavy-rain indices there).


















Wind speed is expected to be the cleaner case: the corrected series should track the buoy’s day-to-day variability more closely than raw ERA5 does, and the corrected distribution should sit closer to the buoy’s than the raw distribution – check the two plots above confirm that once rendered from a build that includes the rotorua_buoy_met_data knots-to-m/s fix above.


















Rainfall is the variable to check most carefully here, given the buoy unit issue above: if these plots were last rendered from a build of era5_bias_correction/era5_corrected_hourly that predates the rotorua_buoy_met_data unit fix, expect the corrected distribution’s upper tail to sit well beyond both the raw ERA5 and the buoy’s own post-fix distribution, and the time series to show the correction pulling rainfall up hardest during the pre-October-2023 window. A rebuild after the fix should bring the corrected distribution back in line with raw ERA5 and the long-record rainfall data – re-render this page after tar_make() and check these two plots specifically before trusting MET_pprain downstream.

section: 3. CMIP6 monthly delta-change factors, and inter-GCM variability
text:
3. CMIP6 monthly delta-change factors, and inter-GCM variability
For each of the 7 downscaled GCMs (ACCESS-CM2, AWI-CM-1-1-MR, CNRM-CM6-1, EC-Earth3, GFDL-ESM4, NZESM, NorESM2-MM) and each SSP (ssp126/ssp245/ssp370/ssp585, NZESM has no ssp585 run), compute_gcm_monthly_deltas() reads that GCM’s own already-cropped netCDFs directly at the lake point and computes a monthly change factor – additive for temperature and shortwave, multiplicative (ratio) for the bounded/skewed fields (rainfall, wind, humidity) – for three future windows against a 1995-2014 historical reference.
The dominant source of uncertainty in this workflow, once the downscaling chain and delta-change method are fixed, is which GCM drives the projection. The figure below makes that spread explicit for the end-of-century window:



Inter-GCM spread in monthly delta-change factors, 2071-2100. Thin lines are individual GCMs, the shaded band spans the GCM min-max range, and the thick line is the GCM mean, for each SSP.


The spread is not uniform across variables. Annual-mean warming under ssp585 ranges from +2.8 °C (NorESM2-MM) to +4.6 °C (ACCESS-CM2) by 2071-2100 – a ~1.8 °C spread from GCM choice alone, on top of the ~3.5 °C spread already visible between the lowest (ssp126) and highest (ssp585) emissions pathway. Shortwave and rainfall change factors span, and in some months straddle, both sides of no-change (ratio = 1 / delta = 0) across the GCM ensemble, meaning some models project a drier or cloudier Rotorua in a given month under the same scenario that others project the opposite sign for. Wind and humidity changes are comparatively modest and more consistent in sign across GCMs. The mid-century window shows the same pattern at reduced magnitude:



Inter-GCM spread in monthly delta-change factors, 2041-2070.


Collapsing each GCM’s 12 monthly values into a single box per model makes the same GCM-consensus-vs-disagreement question easier to read at a glance, independent of the seasonal cycle:



GCM consensus in delta-change factors, 2071-2100. Each box summarises one GCM’s 12 monthly values; overlapping boxes indicate GCM consensus, separated boxes indicate disagreement between models.

title: Climate-Scenario Meteorology Workflow
text:
4. Delta-changed baseline and hourly disaggregation
scenario_daily_met applies each GCM/scenario/window’s monthly deltas to the corrected daily baseline (apply_gcm_delta_to_baseline()), and scenario_hourly_met disaggregates the result to hourly with metscale::disaggregate_met_to_hourly(), borrowing the within-day shape of era5_corrected_hourly (method of fragments) and reconstructing shortwave from clear-sky solar geometry – identical to steps 3-4 of vignette("scenario-workflow"), just run once per combination of scenario_delta_grid (7 GCM × 4 SSP × 3 windows, minus NZESM/ssp585 = 83 combinations).
That is enough runs (each disaggregating 20-30 years to hourly) that, like gcm_ts_summary and tutira_cmip6_files elsewhere in this pipeline, both targets are gated with cue = tar_cue(mode = "never") so a routine tar_make() does not trigger them. Build them explicitly with:
targets::tar_make(names = c("scenario_daily_met", "scenario_hourly_met"))
or invalidate just the combinations that changed with tar_invalidate() / tar_cue(mode = "always") per branch.
These time-slice runs are the fixed-climate set: each window is a snapshot of one climate state on the same ERA5 weather, with no trend inside it. They are the right tool for asking “what does the lake look like in a 2071-2100 climate?”, but not for the long-term nutrient-loading question, which is covered next.

title: Climate-Scenario Meteorology Workflow
section: 5. Transient scenarios for long-term nutrient-loading runs
text:
5. Transient scenarios for long-term nutrient-loading runs
The lake’s response to a nutrient reduction (e.g. an N cut from 2032) is path-dependent: sediment legacy stores, alum dosing and flushing mean the state in any year depends on the whole history of loads and climate before it. Three disconnected time slices cannot represent that – stitching them together would also put steps in the forcing at the window boundaries. The transient workflow instead builds one continuous 2005-2099 series per GCM/SSP (2005-2014 is the 10-year spin-up before sim_periods$ssp$start), so the climate warms gradually while the loads change. It runs alongside the time-slice set, which stays as the fixed-climate sensitivity.
It follows the same bias-correct → delta-change → disaggregate chain, with three changes, all in R/scenario_climate_workflow.R:

Weather: build_transient_year_map() assigns every simulated year a real, complete ERA5 baseline year (complete_years(); shuffled cycles, so every source year is used about equally often and a weather year is not repeated at a fixed lag the way a simple loop would). Leap-year targets only draw leap-year sources, so no 29 February is invented or dropped. The mapping depends only on transient_weather_seed, so every GCM/SSP sees identical weather and differences between runs are the climate signal alone. build_transient_weather() stitches the years together on the target dates.
Deltas that evolve: compute_gcm_transient_deltas() replaces the three fixed windows with a 30-year window sliding along each GCM’s own historical → SSP run, giving a monthly delta for every year, against the same 1995-2014 reference as the slices. It reads each GCM’s point series once and averages locally, rather than re-reading the netCDFs per year.
A no-delta control: scenario = "control" applies no deltas to the same weather sequence (stationary baseline climate), the reference for separating a nutrient effect from a climate effect.

apply_transient_deltas_to_baseline() then applies the year-and-month delta to each day (the same add/ratio rules, clipping and expand_met() as the slices), and disaggregate_scenario_met() disaggregates to hourly with wind handled as a plain scalar, exactly as in step 4.

Build the hourly set explicitly, and invalidate it first after any change to the daily met:
targets::tar_invalidate("scenario_transient_hourly_met")
targets::tar_make(names = "scenario_transient_hourly_met")
Things to keep in mind when reading transient runs:

Weather sampling noise is real. Decadal means from a single shuffled 95-year sequence wander by roughly ±0.3 °C and ±15% in rainfall relative to the long-term mean, purely from which ERA5 years land in which decade. Compare each scenario against the control (same weather), never against the observed record.
The weather is synthetic, including the spin-up decade. 2005-2014 uses shuffled ERA5 years with small deltas (about +0.1 to +0.5 °C by 2014, from the GCMs’ own historical-to-SSP run), not the actual weather of those years. The transient runs therefore cannot be validated against observations; the calibration/validation period stays on the real ERA5/buoy forcing.
The trajectory lags at the end. The sliding window is truncated at 2100 rather than shifted, so the final years are averaged over fewer years (down to ~16 at 2099, see n_years) and lag the underlying trend by up to ~6 years of change. Shifting the window back instead held the last ~15 years flat and under-warmed the end of the run by ~0.6 °C under ssp585, which is why it was changed. Rainfall, wind and shortwave deltas also get noisier over those final years.
tas/pr stop at 2099-12-31 while other variables run to 2100-11, so the 2071-2100 end windows average 29 years for temperature and rainfall (extract_climate_point() warns “NA after merge” for those dates; this is expected).
Deltas are piecewise-constant by month, as in the slices, so there is a small step at each month boundary.
One GCM member per GCM: the 30-year window averages out most, but not all, of each model’s internal variability.

title: Climate-Scenario Meteorology Workflow
section: How this feeds into the lake model
text:
How this feeds into the lake model
For long-term nutrient-loading questions, use scenario_transient_hourly_met, one branch per row of transient_delta_grid. scenario_hourly_met (one branch per GCM/scenario/window) remains the input for fixed-climate sensitivity runs. The intended path from here into a model run is:

AEME::add_met(aeme, met = scenario_transient_hourly_met[[i]]), where i is the row of transient_delta_grid for the GCM/SSP of interest (e.g. which(grid$gcm == "ACCESS-CM2" & grid$scenario == "ssp245")), in place of the placeholder gcm_point_data_std_df-based forcing in setup_aeme().
AEME::set_time() with sim_periods$ssp (2015-07-01 to 2099-06-30, 10-year spin-up – the met starts in 2005 so the spin-up is covered).
AEME::build_aeme() / AEME::run_aeme() as for the calibration runs in aeme_glm4.

What is still missing before a transient simulation is meaningful for nutrients: the met is only half the forcing.

Inflows and loads for 2005-2099. setup_aeme() currently removes the inflows, so a run built that way has no catchment loading at all. A transient run needs a flow and nutrient-load series for the whole period, including the N-reduction pathway (e.g. a step from 2032), and a decision on how stream flows respond to the rainfall deltas (for example scaling the historical flow series by the same monthly rainfall ratio, or modelling it explicitly).
Alum dosing after the calibration period needs a defined assumption.
Lake level / outflow handling over 95 years should be checked in a short run first.

A sensible first set of test simulations is the control plus one GCM under a low and a high SSP (e.g. ssp126 and ssp585), first over a short horizon (say 2015-2040) with loads held at the present baseline, to check the runs are stable and the climate signal comes through in the temperature and stratification output. The 2032 N-reduction step and the long-horizon runs can follow once the inflow/loads series exist. With 28 branches the same pattern = map(transient_delta_grid) branching extends to a per-branch AEME::run_aeme() target, and the GCM-variability figure above is then the basis for interpreting how much of the simulated spread is driven by GCM choice, scenario, or the nutrient pathway versus lake-model internal dynamics.

title: Climate-Scenario Meteorology Workflow
text:
Caveats
Both the bias-correction and the delta-change step assume stationarity – a transfer function fitted on the ERA5/buoy overlap period is asserted to hold under a future climate, and the scale method used here rescales the observed daily sequence rather than reshaping its day-to-day variability (see ?metscale::scenario_workflow). The buoy overlap (2022-2026) is short relative to the vignette’s recommendation of a long reanalysis record and 20-year climate windows; the ERA5-only record (2011-2026) is longer and used for the daily baseline and hourly donor, but the fit of the bias correction itself is necessarily anchored to the shorter buoy overlap. Treat the across-scenario spread as a lower bound on total uncertainty, and fix the MET_prsttn unit issue noted in step 1 before using corrected station pressure downstream.

title: Visualise CMIP6
text:
After processing the CMIP6 data for the Rotorua catchment, we can visualise the results.
We present both the spatial summary and time series summary for each GCM and scenario. This allows us to inspect how the different models and scenarios represent climate variables over the catchment area.

title: Visualise CMIP6
text:
CMIP6 Variable Plots

Air Temperature (2 m above ground level)
The annual mean 2 m air temperature anomalies show robust warming across all CMIP6 models and emissions scenarios, although the magnitude and rate of warming vary among models. Historical simulations indicate a modest warming of ~0.5–1 °C relative to the mid-20th-century baseline, with relatively small inter-model spread during this period.
From ~2020 onward, the scenarios diverge and uncertainties increase. Under SSP1-2.6, most models project warming that stabilises at around 1–1.5 °C above the historical mean by mid-century, with limited additional warming thereafter. The ensemble spread remains comparatively narrow in this scenario, reflecting greater model agreement under strong mitigation.
Under SSP2-4.5, temperatures continue to increase throughout the century, reaching approximately 2.5–3 °C by 2100. Inter-model variability broadens slightly over time, but the overall warming trajectory remains consistent across the ensemble.
The higher-emission scenarios show both stronger warming and greater uncertainty. SSP3-7.0 produces accelerated warming after 2050, with end-of-century anomalies near 4 °C, although individual model projections span a wider range. SSP5-8.5 exhibits the largest spread and steepest trend, with most models exceeding 5 °C by 2100, but with notable divergence in the upper tails of the ensemble.
Despite year-to-year variability and differences among models, all scenarios show statistically robust warming relative to the historical period. The increasing separation of scenario trajectories after ~2040 highlights both the importance of emissions pathway choice and the expanding uncertainty associated with long-term climate projections.

title: Rotorua Lake Modelling – PC10 Support
text:
The Rotorua Lake model will be updated to GLM-AED, an open-source hydrodynamic–ecological model that enables improved simulation of vertical mixing, nutrient cycling, and management interventions under variable climate conditions.
This upgrade will allow long-term scenario testing and a more flexible, modular architecture.

title: Rotorua Lake Modelling – PC10 Support
text:
🔍 Overview
Key enhancements over previous Lake Rotorua models will include:

Dynamic sediment–water feedback to better represent internal nutrient loading and delayed responses to external inputs.

Support for climate change scenarios, enabling projections of lake responses over decadal scales.

Mechanistic simulation of alum dosing, which is currently conducted in two inflows on a near-daily basis.

Active and ongoing development of model software and related tools.

title: Rotorua Lake Modelling – PC10 Support
text:
⚗️ Alum–Phosphorus Modelling
One important improvement will be incorporating a mechanistic representation of Al–P interactions.
Current models do not explicitly simulate alum chemistry or its interaction with phosphorus.
Model description here.
We are engaging with the University of Western Australia (UWA) to explore support for code modification within the AED structure.
The proposed model will simulate:

Hydrolysis of dosed alum and speciation of aluminium (e.g. Al³⁺, Al(OH)₃)

pH and temperature dependence of phosphate binding efficiency

Sediment-mediated sorption and variable effectiveness depending on depth, organic content, and redox state

Aging or decay of reactive Al over time to simulate persistence of alum effects

Dosing through inflow boundary conditions, allowing for flexible scenario testing


If this collaboration is not confirmed, alternate pathways for implementing alum dynamics will be explored to maintain model delivery timelines.

title: Rotorua Lake Modelling – PC10 Support
text:
🗓️ Timeline and Resources

The model upgrade and calibration will begin in September 2025, using existing University of Waikato resources.

Initial climate change scenarios will be prioritised and delivered by September 2026, with alum scenario testing dependent on code development.

This lake modelling work will proceed independently of catchment model scaling, ensuring continuity regardless of SWAT-MODFLOW outcomes.

Comparing the raw sources against the buoy
met_source_comparison aggregates all five sources to daily values and scores the NIWA airport, MetService airport, ERA5 and PC10 against the buoy — the only source with a direct claim to being “true” lake conditions — over whatever window each pair overlaps, for temperature, humidity, rainfall, wind speed, shortwave radiation and station pressure. Since the old buoy data were added (all_buoy_met_data), that window reaches back to mid-2007, so most comparisons rest on up to ~16 years of daily pairs.






Note



Wind units. Buoy wind is in m/s and is extrapolated to 10 m (from 2 m on the new buoy and 1.5 m on the old one). A duplicated knots→m/s conversion was being applied to buoy wind that was already in m/s, scaling it by 0.514; it was removed in buoy_to_aeme_met() (and the old-buoy equivalent) in October 2026. Before the fix the buoy’s mean 10 m wind was ~2.8 m/s; it is now ~5.4 m/s. That change moves ERA5’s apparent wind bias from ~−0.2 m/s to ~−2.8 m/s, so every wind result on this page reflects the corrected series, and earlier versions of this page that reported a small ERA5 wind bias were wrong. Separately, the buoy’s own rain had a unit bug, fixed in rotorua_buoy_met_data: before 2023-10-23 it logged rain in mm/10 min, while later records use mm.

What this shows (ERA5 now covers 1988–2025, so ERA5 comparisons span the whole buoy record, 2007–2025):

The offset is stable year to year (ERA5 − buoy is −1.2 to −1.7 °C in every full year 2007–2025), so it is a real and consistent difference between lake-surface air and land/grid-cell air rather than drift. ERA5 tracks the buoy’s day-to-day shape best (r ≈ 0.99); both airports follow at r ≈ 0.98; PC10 is weakest (r ≈ 0.86, MAE ≈ 1.9 °C).
Relative humidity — all sources read more humid than the buoy: ERA5 +7.0 %, NIWA airport +6.4 %, MetService +6.1 %, PC10 +3.1 %. This is not simply a lake effect: the land station and ERA5 agree with each other (hourly ERA5 − MetService is +1.6 % over 1993–2023), and the buoy’s offset is not constant — the annual ERA5 − buoy RH bias is +2–3 % in 2022–23, +9.5 % in 2024, +13 % in 2025 and +48 % in the 2026 data (buoy mean RH 47 %). The buoy RH sensor looks drifty or faulty, particularly from 2024 on (see the hourly section). PC10 RH has very weak correlation with the buoy (r ≈ 0.32).
Rainfall — mean daily totals agree well. The MetService gauge matches the buoy almost exactly (bias ≈ 0, r ≈ 0.86, the best rain agreement of any source), ERA5 is next (bias ≈ 0, r ≈ 0.76), then the NIWA airport (r ≈ 0.59, biased low because its daily rain is incomplete), and PC10 is essentially uncorrelated day to day (r ≈ 0.06) despite agreeing on long-run totals — consistent with real small-scale spatial variability in rain rather than a PC10 error.
Wind speed — the buoy (10 m) averages ~5.4 m/s, well above every other source: MetService airport −1.7 m/s (r ≈ 0.89), NIWA airport −2.1 m/s (r ≈ 0.82, only 679 days), and ERA5 −2.9 m/s (r ≈ 0.89, 6,071 days), i.e. about 53 % below the buoy. Even against the land MetService station ERA5 is ~1.1 m/s low on matched hours, so ERA5 under-reads wind generally and the buoy is windier than both land stations (open-water fetch plus the 2 m → 10 m extrapolation). PC10 has no wind station.
Shortwave radiation — only the MetService airport (r ≈ 0.97, bias −5 W/m² over 469 days of overlap with the new buoy, Feb 2022–Jun 2023) and ERA5 (r ≈ 0.84, bias −10 W/m² over 1,404 days) can be compared; the NIWA airport has no overlap with the buoy.
Station pressure — all sources differ from the buoy by a nearly constant offset (r ≥ 0.996): MetService −0.13 kPa, ERA5 −1.10 kPa and NIWA airport +3.29 kPa. MetService (station height 285 m) is by far the closest.


Hourly comparison: buoys, MetService airport and ERA5
The daily comparison scores sources against a single combined buoy series. This section looks at hourly resolution and brings in four series: the old buoy (2007–22), the new buoy (2022–), ERA5 (1988–2025), and the MetService airport record (1993–Jun 2023), which is the only independent, complete hourly station in the set and overlaps the old buoy for 16 years. ERA5 now covers the whole MetService record, so ERA5 − MetService statistics below use 30 years (~265,000 hours) rather than 12. The section answers three questions the daily view cannot: (1) can the two buoy loggers be treated as one record?, (2) what are ERA5’s biases on matched hours, variable by variable, including shortwave, pressure and wind direction? and (3) is the buoy itself a trustworthy reference for each variable? The old and new buoys never overlap in time, so they are compared with each other through their distributions and indirectly through ERA5 and MetService.
All series are floored to the hour (the old buoy logs every 15 minutes, so the :00 record is kept) and duplicate hours are dropped, keeping the first value so wind direction is never averaged arithmetically. MetService rain, wind and radiation are hour-ending values (they describe the hour preceding the stamp); MetService wind is the hourly mean where recorded and the 10-minute mean otherwise.

prep <- function(df) {
  for (v in setdiff(vars, names(df))) df[[v]] <- NA_real_

    mutate(Date = lubridate::floor_date(Date, "hour")) |>

The two buoy loggers are statistically interchangeable for temperature, wind and pressure. Mean air temperature (14.0 °C both), 10 m wind speed (5.45 vs 5.34 m/s) and pressure (98.34 kPa both) match to within about 2 %, so there is no sign of a step change at the 2022 handover, and ERA5’s matched-hour offsets for these variables are nearly identical against each logger (below). Relative humidity is the exception (see the annual-bias table). Full-record means for ERA5 are not directly comparable with the buoys because ERA5 spans 1988–2025, but they show the same character: ERA5 is cooler (12.2 °C, SD 4.6 vs 14.0 °C, SD 4.0), more humid (mean 83 % vs 75 %; median 87 % vs 77 %) and much less windy (2.51 vs ~5.4 m/s). The MetService airport sits in between on wind (3.58 m/s), is cooler than the buoys (12.7 °C, with a much wider range of −5 to 30 °C), is more humid (81 %), and reads 98.20 kPa station pressure (the buoys 98.34 kPa). Shortwave means agree across the three sources that measure it (new buoy 165, ERA5 169, MetService 167 W/m²).


Is the buoy a stable reference? Annual bias by year
Because ERA5 and the MetService airport are independent of the buoy and of each other, year-by-year bias against them shows whether a buoy sensor has drifted. A real, physical offset (such as lake vs. land air temperature) should be steady; sensor drift should not.


Code
b_all <- bind_rows(dfs_h[["Buoy (old, 2007-22)"]], dfs_h[["Buoy (new, 2022-)"]])
era5_h <- dfs_h[["ERA5"]]
ms_h   <- dfs_h[["MetService airport"]]

yr_bias <- function(ref, test, v, lab) {
  inner_join(select(ref, Date, ref = all_of(v)),
             select(test, Date, test = all_of(v)), by = "Date") |>
    filter(!is.na(ref), !is.na(test)) |>
    mutate(yr = lubridate::year(Date)) |>
    group_by(yr) |>
    summarise(bias = mean(test - ref), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(comparison = lab, variable = v)
}

annual_bias <- bind_rows(
  yr_bias(b_all, era5_h, "MET_tmpair", "ERA5 - buoy"),
  yr_bias(b_all, era5_h, "MET_humrel", "ERA5 - buoy"),
  yr_bias(b_all, era5_h, "MET_wndspd", "ERA5 - buoy"),
  yr_bias(ms_h,  era5_h, "MET_tmpair", "ERA5 - MetService"),
  yr_bias(ms_h,  era5_h, "MET_humrel", "ERA5 - MetService"),
  yr_bias(ms_h,  era5_h, "MET_wndspd", "ERA5 - MetService")
) |>
  mutate(variable = factor(variable, levels = vars, labels = var_labels[vars]))

annual_bias |>

  arrange(variable, yr) |>

Temperature and wind offsets are steady; the RH offset is not. ERA5 − buoy temperature stays between −1.2 and −1.7 °C in every full year 2007–2025 (−2.1 °C in the partial 2026 data), and ERA5 − MetService stays between −0.3 and −0.8 °C across all 31 years, so those are stable properties of the sources. ERA5 − buoy wind is −2.6 to −3.4 m/s every year. ERA5 − MetService wind is steadier in sign but drifts from about −0.8 to −1.0 m/s in the 1990s to −1.3 to −1.5 m/s in 2019–2023, so part of the ERA5 wind deficit against the land station has grown over time (a MetService sensor or ERA5 change, not the buoy). ERA5 − MetService RH is typically +0 to +2.5 %, but larger in the mid-1990s (+7 to +9 % in 1994 and 1996), which is the one place the land record disagrees with ERA5. Against the buoy, the RH bias is +3.6 to +5.2 % in 2007–10, wanders from +5 % to +9.5 % through 2011–2020, falls to +2–3 % in 2022–23, then rises to +9.5 % (2024), +13 % (2025) and +48 % in 2026, when the buoy reports a mean RH of only 47 %. That pattern points to calibration drift or a failing sensor rather than a lake effect.

Rainfall
Rainfall is zero-inflated, so it is compared by wet-hour fraction and by the distribution of non-zero hours rather than by mean and SD alone.
All four series are now in the same unit (m/hour — the old buoy’s maximum is 0.046 m/hr and the MetService maximum 0.047 m/hr, in line with the others), so no rescaling is needed; rain_scale is kept at 1 as a hook in case that changes.


Code
rain_scale <- c("Buoy (new, 2022-)"   = 1,
                "Buoy (old, 2007-22)" = 1,
                "ERA5"                = 1,
                "MetService airport"  = 1)    # edit once units are confirmed

rain <- met_all |>
  filter(!is.na(MET_pprain)) |>
  mutate(rain = MET_pprain * rain_scale[as.character(source)])

rain |>
  group_by(source) |>
  summarise(
    n_obs        = n(),
    wet_fraction = mean(rain > 0),

Matched-hour comparison: ERA5, MetService and the buoys
To remove sampling differences between periods, series are paired on hours where both have valid data: ERA5 against each buoy, ERA5 against the MetService airport, and MetService against each buoy. Bias is the second-named series minus the first-named reference, i.e. ERA5 − buoy, ERA5 − MetService, and MetService − buoy, so a negative wind bias means the first series reads low.


Code
paired <- function(ref, test, vars) {
  inner_join(
    ref  |> select(Date, all_of(vars)),
    test |> select(Date, all_of(vars)),
    by = "Date", suffix = c("_ref", "_test")
  ) |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(-Date, names_to = c("variable", "which"),
                        names_pattern = "(.*)_(ref|test)$", values_to = "value") |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = which, values_from = value) |>
    filter(!is.na(ref), !is.na(test))
}

lag_r <- function(ref, test, v, k) {
  t2 <- test
  t2$Date <- t2$Date - k * 3600
  d <- inner_join(select(ref, Date, a = all_of(v)), select(t2, Date, b = all_of(v)), by = "Date")
  d <- filter(d, !is.na(a), !is.na(b))
  cor(d$a, d$b)
}

A real bug this comparison caught
Running this comparison surfaced a unit mismatch that a single-source sanity check would have missed: ERA5-Land’s raw MET_pprain column is stored in mm/hour, while every other source in this pipeline (buoy, airport, PC10) is in m/hour/m-day, the AEME convention. Uncorrected, ERA5’s rainfall was reading roughly 1000x too high in the shared units (mean 0.18 vs. the buoy’s 0.0008 m/hr) — and because era5_bias_correction originally excluded MET_pprain from correction (rainfall was assumed to be a poor target due to buoy-gauge reliability, not a units problem), that inflated value would have flowed straight through era5_corrected_hourly into every scenario baseline.
Fixed in two places:

read_era5_hourly_met() now converts MET_pprain mm/hour → m/hour at read time, so the fix applies everywhere the ERA5 series is used, not just here.
MET_pprain is now included in both era5_bias_correction and era5_bias_correction_extended’s vars, using the same method = "scale" day-of-year correction as the other variables — see the comparison above for why this is reasonable (no evidence of a buoy under-catch, just noise), while still treating the buoy’s rain series with more caution than its temperature/RH/wind.

Fixing ERA5 rainfall: quantile mapping vs. scaling
The default method = "scale" rain correction is only a monthly multiplier on totals, so it cannot touch the drizzle problem found above. metscale::fit_met_bias_correction() also offers empirical quantile mapping ("eqm") and quantile delta mapping ("qdm"), which remap the whole ERA5 distribution — zeros included — onto the buoy distribution month by month. Four ERA5 rain variants are compared here, all fit against all_buoy_met_data:

raw — uncorrected ERA5.
scale — the current era5_bias_correction approach (monthly multiplier).
eqm — quantile mapping (100 quantiles), which also adjusts wet-hour frequency and intensity.
eqm+scale — eqm, then a second monthly scale fit on the eqm output to put the total back on the buoy’s.

qdm was also fitted and gives numbers identical to eqm on the historical period (it only differs when extrapolating a trend), so it is not shown separately.


Code
all_buoy_met_data <- tar_read(all_buoy_met_data)

fit_rain <- \(e, m) metscale::fit_met_bias_correction(
  e, all_buoy_met_data, vars = "MET_pprain", method = m,
  nquantiles = 100, verbose = FALSE)
apply_rain <- \(e, f) metscale::apply_met_bias_correction(e, f, verbose = FALSE)

f_scale <- fit_rain(era5_hourly_met, "scale")
f_eqm   <- fit_rain(era5_hourly_met, "eqm")
e_eqm   <- apply_rain(era5_hourly_met, f_eqm)
f_es    <- fit_rain(e_eqm, "scale")

rain_variants <- list(
  raw         = era5_hourly_met,
  scale       = apply_rain(era5_hourly_met, f_scale),
  eqm         = e_eqm,
  `eqm+scale` = apply_rain(e_eqm, f_es)
)

# Cross-validated (leave-one-year-out) skill. For eqm+scale this is the
# second-stage fit only (scored against the eqm output); the first-stage
# skill is in the "eqm" row.
bind_rows(
  raw         = f_scale$skill |> filter(stage == "cv_raw"),
  scale       = f_scale$skill |> filter(stage == "cv_corrected"),
  eqm         = f_eqm$skill   |> filter(stage == "cv_corrected"),
  `eqm+scale` = f_es$skill    |> filter(stage == "cv_corrected"),

Buoy: eqm+scale matches the buoy’s annual total (1,397 vs. 1,393 mm/yr), p95 (20.2 vs. 20.2 mm/day) and maximum (278 vs. 281 mm/day); raw ERA5 has 44 % wet days against the buoy’s 27 %, and the eqm-based variants 24–25 %. The upper tail is slightly over-stretched (p99 70 vs. 62 mm/day).
MetService airport (independent hourly gauge) is the strongest check, because it shares no instrument with the buoy. Over its 1993–2023 record it reads 1,397 mm/yr on matched days (11,059 days); on matched hours its wet-hour fraction is 12.0 %, mean wet-hour rain 1.33 mm/hr and p95 5.0 mm/hr. eqm+scale gives 15.1 %, 1.01 and 5.0 mm/hr and a total of 1,342 mm/yr, i.e. ~4 % below MetService, whereas raw ERA5 is 9 % above it (1,528 mm/yr, 41 % wet hours, 0.42 mm/hr wet-hour intensity). At daily resolution eqm+scale approaches the MetService p95 (19.6 vs. 21.2 mm/day) but under-counts wet days (24.4 % vs. 32.6 %) and over-stretches the extreme tail (p99 70 vs. 52 mm/day; maximum 232 vs. 167 mm/day). The shortfall arises because the correction is fit to the 2007–2025 buoy record while MetService covers 1993 onward, so any difference between the early (1993–2006) ERA5 and the buoy-era ERA5 is not corrected.
PC10 (Whakarewarewa gauge) reads 1,449 mm/yr over 13,880 days, so eqm+scale (1,340) is ~8 % below it and raw ERA5 (1,535) 6 % above. Its p95 (20.5 mm/day) is close to eqm+scale (19.6). PC10’s wet-day fraction (37 %) is the highest of the gauges, but a once-daily reading probably smears wet days across two calendar days and inflates the count. Its daily correlation with ERA5 is very low in every case (r ≈ 0.05–0.10), as in the source comparison above. Together the buoy, MetService and PC10 bracket the true Rotorua total at roughly 1,400–1,450 mm/yr, with raw ERA5 sitting 6–12 % above all three.
NIWA airport: this check remains unreliable. Its daily rainfall averages only about 920 mm/yr on days it is “valid” — roughly a third below every other gauge — so its rain series appears incomplete (many days probably contain only some of the 3-hourly observations) and cannot be used to judge totals or wet-day frequency. The MetService record now fills that role.
Daily skill: all eqm variants have slightly lower daily correlation than scale or raw ERA5 against the buoy (r 0.75 vs. 0.76), consistent with the hourly double penalty.

Recommendation (now implemented in the pipeline): use MET_pprain = "eqm" followed by a monthly scale for the historical ERA5 baseline. That fixes drizzle frequency, wet-hour intensity and the bulk of the tail and keeps the total on the buoy. The land gauges read 4–8 % higher than the corrected series (MetService −4 %, PC10 −8 %), and raw ERA5 reads 6–12 % higher than all three, so the corrected total is probably a slight underestimate rather than an overestimate. Because the second stage is fit on the output of the first, it needs two chained calls rather than a single method = vector:
In _targets.R this is era5_rain_eqm_correction → era5_hourly_met_rainqm (stage 1), then era5_bias_correction fitted on era5_hourly_met_rainqm (stage 2, together with the other variables), with era5_corrected_hourly and era5_corrected_daily_baseline built from era5_hourly_met_rainqm. The equivalent standalone code is:


Code
# 1. quantile-map rain onto the buoy distribution
bc_rain_eqm <- metscale::fit_met_bias_correction(
  era5_hourly_met, all_buoy_met_data, vars = "MET_pprain",
  method = "eqm", nquantiles = 100, verbose = FALSE)
era5_eqm <- metscale::apply_met_bias_correction(era5_hourly_met, bc_rain_eqm)

# 2. restore the buoy's total with a monthly ratio
bc_rain_scale <- metscale::fit_met_bias_correction(
  era5_eqm, all_buoy_met_data, vars = "MET_pprain",
  method = "scale", by = "doy-loess", verbose = FALSE)
era5_rain_corrected <- metscale::apply_met_bias_correction(era5_eqm, bc_rain_scale)








Note



expand_met() rounding (fixed). metscale::expand_met() previously rounded every column to 3 decimals. Rain is in m/hr, so that quantised it to whole millimetres: in testing it cut the corrected wet-hour fraction from 15.2 % to 4.9 % and erased all the drizzle correction (and coarsened earlier era5_corrected_hourly rain). It now rounds to 6 decimals and the pipeline calls apply_met_bias_correction(expand = TRUE) directly. era5_corrected_daily_baseline rounds daily totals to 6 decimals too, so it is unaffected.


Caveats: hourly timing is unchanged (r stays ≈ 0.5) — this corrects the distribution, not when rain falls. The quantile map caps ERA5 extremes at the buoy’s observed maximum, and the extreme daily tail ends up somewhat heavier than the MetService gauge shows.




How this improves lake model forcing

The buoy reference is now ~19 years, not ~4.5, and ERA5 now spans 1988–2025. Adding the old buoy lets the day-of-year corrections in era5_bias_correction and niwa_to_buoy_bias_correction train on ~140,000 hourly pairs instead of ~40,000, and the hourly comparison shows the two loggers agree on temperature, wind and pressure. The longer ERA5 record also overlaps the whole MetService record, so ERA5 can now be checked against an independent station for 30 years.
Caught a forcing bug before it reached the model. The ERA5 rain unit error above would have meant every ERA5-driven scenario — including every future GCM projection, since deltas are applied to the ERA5 baseline — ran with rainfall roughly 3 orders of magnitude too high. A single-source pipeline has no way to notice this; comparing independent sources does.
Wind is the largest bias in the forcing, and it is now correctly sized. With the doubled unit conversion removed, ERA5 reads ~2.9 m/s (~53 %) below the buoy’s 10 m wind, not ~0.2 m/s. Wind drives mixing and surface heat flux directly, so era5_bias_correction’s MET_wndspd scale correction (cross-validated RMSE 3.59 → 2.11 m/s, KGE 0.18 → 0.71) is one of the most consequential steps in the pipeline. The land stations cannot substitute: the MetService airport also reads 1.7 m/s below the buoy, so the correction really is a land/reanalysis → lake transfer and depends on the buoy’s 2 m/1.5 m → 10 m extrapolation being right.
The buoy → airport extension now supports every variable it needs. niwa_to_buoy_bias_correction trains on the buoy overlap (2007–present) and cuts NIWA-airport-vs-buoy RMSE from 2.02 → 1.74 °C (temperature); wind is corrected for bias (−2.3 → −0.1 m/s) with a modest RMSE gain (3.18 → 2.94 m/s, r ≈ 0.63), while humidity, which uses the 2022–23 buoy only in this fit, shows no cross-validated gain (RMSE 5.7 → 6.6 %). Because ERA5 now reaches back to 1988, era5_bias_correction_extended has far more paired data than before (~140,000–165,000 hours for temperature, humidity and wind) and cuts ERA5 RMSE for temperature from 2.08 → 1.45 °C, wind from 4.26 → 2.51 m/s (KGE 0.10 → 0.65), and humidity from 7.3 → 7.0 %.
A second, independent hourly station is now available. The MetService airport record (1993–Jun 2023) has a real rain gauge, shortwave and wind, and agrees with ERA5 on temperature (−0.6 °C), humidity (+1.6 %) and shortwave (+2 W/m²). It validates the rain correction independently of the buoy, exposes the buoy RH drift, supplies the humidity correction, and is a candidate for extending reference records back before 2007 (for variables where it agrees well with the buoy: temperature, pressure, rain).
PC10’s 1901–present rainfall record is the longest available context for Rotorua rainfall, over 40 years longer than the airports’. That’s directly useful for summarise_climate_extremes.R / climate-extreme-events.qmd’s historical-extremes framing, and as a long-run independent check on whatever ERA5 rainfall climatology ends up driving the historical baseline and scenario deltas. Its weak daily correlation with the buoy for RH and rain (r ≈ 0.32 and 0.06) means it shouldn’t be used as a fit_met_bias_correction() reference for those variables.
Wind direction and shortwave timing check out. ERA5 reproduces the prevailing WSW–W flow (hourly mean absolute direction error ~39–60°) and the shortwave daily cycle (r = 0.91 against the new buoy and 0.95 against MetService), so ERA5-derived direction and radiation are defensible for the model.



Caveats

Buoy relative humidity is not a reliable reference, so ERA5 humidity is corrected against the MetService airport instead. The old buoy (2007–22) reads ~4–9.5 % below ERA5 and the MetService airport, and the new buoy’s offset drifts from +2–3 % in 2022–23 to +9.5 % (2024), +13 % (2025) and +48 % in 2026 (mean RH 47 %). era5_bias_correction therefore no longer corrects MET_humrel; era5_humrel_correction fits it to airport_met_aeme (1993–Jun 2023, so the fit covers ERA5 up to Jun 2023), and the correction is applied before the buoy-based one. buoy_met_fit_ref keeps buoy RH only for 2022-01-01 to 2023-12-31 for the remaining buoy-referenced fits (niwa_to_buoy_bias_correction and, through it, era5_bias_correction_extended, which still corrects humidity against that lake-equivalent series). all_buoy_met_data and the comparisons above still include all buoy RH. The airport station is a land station, so any lake effect on humidity (the buoy is the only lake-surface sensor) is not captured; the airport fit assumes the same land–lake humidity relationship ERA5 already has. ERA5 also runs 7–9 % more humid than MetService in 1994 and 1996, so the early-1990s ERA5 humidity deserves caution.
Station pressure (MET_prsttn). The buoys log sensible station pressure (~98.3 kPa on both loggers; the MetService airport 98.2 kPa). ERA5 reads a near-constant 1.1 kPa lower (r = 0.997), a grid-cell elevation difference of order 100 m, not a units error; the NIWA airport reads ~3.3 kPa higher. All offsets are removed by the scale corrections (ERA5 RMSE falls to ~57 Pa), but raw ERA5 and NIWA pressures should not be used uncorrected.
era5_bias_correction_extended radiation and wind reference caveats. Its shortwave reference is the NIWA airport’s radiation, which has no overlap with the buoy and so is not put through the buoy transfer function (niwa_to_buoy_bias_correction has no radiation model), and its wind reference is only weakly corrected (r ≈ 0.63 with the buoy). Prefer era5_bias_correction for MET_wndspd and MET_radswd. The comment in _targets.R that describes only 2 wind pairs and 0 radiation pairs predates the old buoy and the longer ERA5 and is worth updating.
Shortwave is validated on limited data. The old buoy has no shortwave, the NIWA airport has none that overlaps the buoy, and the MetService airport overlaps the new buoy only from Feb 2022 to Jun 2023 (~11,000 hours), so ERA5 shortwave rests on the new buoy (~30,000 hours) plus that MetService overlap (ERA5 versus MetService shortwave over 1993–2023 agrees to +2 W/m², r 0.95).
ERA5 wind deficit against MetService grows over time (from ~−0.8 m/s in 1993 to ~−1.5 m/s in 2023), which the buoy-only wind correction cannot see. If wind drives a historical simulation before 2007, the early-period correction is likely too small.
Sub-daily timing. The buoy stamps are offset from ERA5/MetService hour-ending stamps by roughly 30–60 minutes (see the diurnal section). This matters for hourly radiation and temperature, not for daily results.
ERA5 rain is wet too often (41 % of hours vs 12–16 %) with weak hourly intensity; fine for totals, less so for event-scale extremes. The current scale rain correction does not address this; eqm followed by scale does (see “Fixing ERA5 rainfall”). era5_bias_correction_extended still uses plain scale for rain.
PC10 has no radiation or wind data, so pc10_climate_met is a partial forcing (temp/RH/rain only) — useful for comparison and historical context, not as a standalone forcing source.
Hour-stamp de-duplication. prep() in the hourly section drops a large number of duplicated hour stamps (first value kept); the old buoy’s 15-minute rows are reduced to the :00 record. This is harmless for the comparisons here but means sub-hourly information is not used.

title: Meteorological Data Sources & Forcing Comparison
section: Hourly comparison: buoys, MetService airport and ERA5
text:
Hourly comparison: buoys, MetService airport and ERA5
The daily comparison scores sources against a single combined buoy series. This section looks at hourly resolution and brings in four series: the old buoy (2007–22), the new buoy (2022–), ERA5 (1988–2025), and the MetService airport record (1993–Jun 2023), which is the only independent, complete hourly station in the set and overlaps the old buoy for 16 years. ERA5 now covers the whole MetService record, so ERA5 − MetService statistics below use 30 years (~265,000 hours) rather than 12. The section answers three questions the daily view cannot: (1) can the two buoy loggers be treated as one record?, (2) what are ERA5’s biases on matched hours, variable by variable, including shortwave, pressure and wind direction? and (3) is the buoy itself a trustworthy reference for each variable? The old and new buoys never overlap in time, so they are compared with each other through their distributions and indirectly through ERA5 and MetService.
All series are floored to the hour (the old buoy logs every 15 minutes, so the :00 record is kept) and duplicate hours are dropped, keeping the first value so wind direction is never averaged arithmetically. MetService rain, wind and radiation are hour-ending values (they describe the hour preceding the stamp); MetService wind is the hourly mean where recorded and the 10-minute mean otherwise.


Code
era5_hourly_met          <- tar_read(era5_hourly_met)
airport_met_aeme         <- tar_read(airport_met_aeme)
old_buoy_met_hr_aeme     <- tar_read(old_buoy_met_hr_aeme)
rotorua_buoy_met_aeme_hr <- tar_read(rotorua_buoy_met_aeme_hr)

dfs <- list(
  "Buoy (new, 2022-)"   = rotorua_buoy_met_aeme_hr,
  "Buoy (old, 2007-22)" = old_buoy_met_hr_aeme,
  "ERA5"                = era5_hourly_met,
  "MetService airport"  = airport_met_aeme
)

# Variables shared by at least two sources (missing ones are filled with NA)
vars <- c("MET_tmpair", "MET_prsttn", "MET_wndspd", "MET_humrel",
          "MET_radswd", "MET_pprain", "MET_wnddir")

var_labels <- c(
  MET_tmpair = "Air temperature (°C)",
  MET_prsttn = "Station pressure (Pa)",
  MET_wndspd = "Wind speed (m/s)",
  MET_humrel = "Relative humidity (%)",
  MET_radswd = "Shortwave radiation (W/m²)",
  MET_pprain = "Rain (check units!)",
  MET_wnddir = "Wind direction (°)"
)

cols <- c("Buoy (new, 2022-)"   = "#1b9e77",
          "Buoy (old, 2007-22)" = "#d95f02",
          "ERA5"                = "#7570b3",
          "MetService airport"  = "#e7298a")

prep <- function(df) {
  for (v in setdiff(vars, names(df))) df[[v]] <- NA_real_
  out <- df |>
    mutate(Date = lubridate::floor_date(Date, "hour")) |>
    select(Date, all_of(vars)) |>
    arrange(Date)
  distinct(out, Date, .keep_all = TRUE)
}

The two buoy loggers are statistically interchangeable for temperature, wind and pressure. Mean air temperature (14.0 °C both), 10 m wind speed (5.45 vs 5.34 m/s) and pressure (98.34 kPa both) match to within about 2 %, so there is no sign of a step change at the 2022 handover, and ERA5’s matched-hour offsets for these variables are nearly identical against each logger (below). Relative humidity is the exception (see the annual-bias table). Full-record means for ERA5 are not directly comparable with the buoys because ERA5 spans 1988–2025, but they show the same character: ERA5 is cooler (12.2 °C, SD 4.6 vs 14.0 °C, SD 4.0), more humid (mean 83 % vs 75 %; median 87 % vs 77 %) and much less windy (2.51 vs ~5.4 m/s). The MetService airport sits in between on wind (3.58 m/s), is cooler than the buoys (12.7 °C, with a much wider range of −5 to 30 °C), is more humid (81 %), and reads 98.20 kPa station pressure (the buoys 98.34 kPa). Shortwave means agree across the three sources that measure it (new buoy 165, ERA5 169, MetService 167 W/m²).


Is the buoy a stable reference? Annual bias by year
Because ERA5 and the MetService airport are independent of the buoy and of each other, year-by-year bias against them shows whether a buoy sensor has drifted. A real, physical offset (such as lake vs. land air temperature) should be steady; sensor drift should not.


Code
b_all <- bind_rows(dfs_h[["Buoy (old, 2007-22)"]], dfs_h[["Buoy (new, 2022-)"]])
era5_h <- dfs_h[["ERA5"]]
ms_h   <- dfs_h[["MetService airport"]]

yr_bias <- function(ref, test, v, lab) {
  inner_join(select(ref, Date, ref = all_of(v)),
             select(test, Date, test = all_of(v)), by = "Date") |>
    filter(!is.na(ref), !is.na(test)) |>
    mutate(yr = lubridate::year(Date)) |>
    group_by(yr) |>
    summarise(bias = mean(test - ref), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(comparison = lab, variable = v)
}

  yr_bias(b_all, era5_h, "MET_humrel", "ERA5 - buoy"),
  yr_bias(b_all, era5_h, "MET_wndspd", "ERA5 - buoy"),
  yr_bias(ms_h,  era5_h, "MET_tmpair", "ERA5 - MetService"),

  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("ERA5 - buoy" = "#1b9e77", "ERA5 - MetService" = "#e7298a")) +

Temperature and wind offsets are steady; the RH offset is not. ERA5 − buoy temperature stays between −1.2 and −1.7 °C in every full year 2007–2025 (−2.1 °C in the partial 2026 data), and ERA5 − MetService stays between −0.3 and −0.8 °C across all 31 years, so those are stable properties of the sources. ERA5 − buoy wind is −2.6 to −3.4 m/s every year. ERA5 − MetService wind is steadier in sign but drifts from about −0.8 to −1.0 m/s in the 1990s to −1.3 to −1.5 m/s in 2019–2023, so part of the ERA5 wind deficit against the land station has grown over time (a MetService sensor or ERA5 change, not the buoy). ERA5 − MetService RH is typically +0 to +2.5 %, but larger in the mid-1990s (+7 to +9 % in 1994 and 1996), which is the one place the land record disagrees with ERA5. Against the buoy, the RH bias is +3.6 to +5.2 % in 2007–10, wanders from +5 % to +9.5 % through 2011–2020, falls to +2–3 % in 2022–23, then rises to +9.5 % (2024), +13 % (2025) and +48 % in 2026, when the buoy reports a mean RH of only 47 %. That pattern points to calibration drift or a failing sensor rather than a lake effect.

ERA5 gets the rain total right but not its character. Mean hourly rain is similar across sources (≈ 0.00014–0.00018 m/hr), but ERA5 is “wet” in 41 % of hours versus 12–16 % on both buoys and the MetService gauge, and its wet hours are weaker (mean 0.42 mm/hr vs 0.9–1.3 mm/hr; 95th percentile 2.0 vs 4.5–5.5 mm/hr; maximum 21 vs 28–47 mm/hr). That is the classic reanalysis drizzle pattern — light rain spread over too many hours with extremes smoothed away. The two buoys and the independent MetService gauge agree with each other, which is strong evidence that the buoy rain gauge is not the problem. For lake forcing this matters mostly for event-scale inflow and extremes; daily and longer totals are fine.

Matched-hour comparison: ERA5, MetService and the buoys
To remove sampling differences between periods, series are paired on hours where both have valid data: ERA5 against each buoy, ERA5 against the MetService airport, and MetService against each buoy. Bias is the second-named series minus the first-named reference, i.e. ERA5 − buoy, ERA5 − MetService, and MetService − buoy, so a negative wind bias means the first series reads low.


Code
paired <- function(ref, test, vars) {
  inner_join(
    ref  |> select(Date, all_of(vars)),
    test |> select(Date, all_of(vars)),
    by = "Date", suffix = c("_ref", "_test")
  ) |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(-Date, names_to = c("variable", "which"),
                        names_pattern = "(.*)_(ref|test)$", values_to = "value") |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = which, values_from = value) |>
    filter(!is.na(ref), !is.na(test))
}

pair_vars <- c("MET_tmpair", "MET_prsttn", "MET_wndspd", "MET_humrel",
               "MET_radswd", "MET_wnddir")

pairs_all <- bind_rows(
  list(
    "ERA5 vs new buoy" = paired(dfs_h[["Buoy (new, 2022-)"]],   dfs_h[["ERA5"]], pair_vars),

All four Date columns carry the same fixed-offset timezone (Etc/GMT-12, NZST, no daylight saving), so this is not a timezone mismatch in the stored data. lag_r <- function(ref, test, v, k) {
  t2 <- test
  t2$Date <- t2$Date - k * 3600
  d <- inner_join(select(ref, Date, a = all_of(v)), select(t2, Date, b = all_of(v)), by = "Date")
  d <- filter(d, !is.na(a), !is.na(b))
  cor(d$a, d$b)
}

title: Meteorological Data Sources & Forcing Comparison
section: A real bug this comparison caught
text:
A real bug this comparison caught
Running this comparison surfaced a unit mismatch that a single-source sanity check would have missed: ERA5-Land’s raw MET_pprain column is stored in mm/hour, while every other source in this pipeline (buoy, airport, PC10) is in m/hour/m-day, the AEME convention. Uncorrected, ERA5’s rainfall was reading roughly 1000x too high in the shared units (mean 0.18 vs. the buoy’s 0.0008 m/hr) — and because era5_bias_correction originally excluded MET_pprain from correction (rainfall was assumed to be a poor target due to buoy-gauge reliability, not a units problem), that inflated value would have flowed straight through era5_corrected_hourly into every scenario baseline.
Fixed in two places:

read_era5_hourly_met() now converts MET_pprain mm/hour → m/hour at read time, so the fix applies everywhere the ERA5 series is used, not just here.
MET_pprain is now included in both era5_bias_correction and era5_bias_correction_extended’s vars, using the same method = "scale" day-of-year correction as the other variables — see the comparison above for why this is reasonable (no evidence of a buoy under-catch, just noise), while still treating the buoy’s rain series with more caution than its temperature/RH/wind.

Note: the pipeline now quantile-maps rain before this fit (see “Fixing ERA5 rainfall”), so the raw rows for MET_pprain here and in the table below are the quantile-mapped series, and the skill shown is the second-stage monthly scale. With the units fixed, ERA5 rain now agrees with the buoys on mean totals (hourly r ≈ 0.52 overall). The scale correction leaves rain essentially unchanged — cross-validated KGE is marginally lower after correction (0.31 vs 0.34) — which is the expected outcome for a variable whose mismatch is in timing and intensity rather than in the mean. Rain correction is harmless but should not be credited with improving the forcing.

Wind is now the largest correction: bias −2.88 → 0.00 m/s, RMSE 3.59 → 2.11 m/s and KGE 0.18 → 0.71, with correlation unchanged (r ≈ 0.72) — a scale correction fixes the mean, not the hourly timing error visible in the matched-hour scatter.
Temperature and pressure improve a lot: temperature bias −1.48 → 0.00 °C and RMSE 2.01 → 1.34 °C; pressure bias −1,105 Pa → 0 and RMSE 1,107 → 57 Pa.
Humidity is fit to the MetService airport (airport_met_aeme, ~260,000 matched hours, 1993–Jun 2023) rather than the buoy, as a separate stage in front of era5_bias_correction (target era5_humrel_correction). Raw ERA5 already agrees with that station to within about 2 % (bias +1.6 %, r 0.77), so the correction is small: cross-validated RMSE 10.0 → 9.9 %, KGE 0.765 → 0.766, and the mean bias goes to zero (mean ERA5 RH 82.9 % → 81.3 %). It is essentially a bias removal, not a skill improvement.
Shortwave: already close to unbiased (+9 W/m²); correction gives only a small gain, and it is fit on the new buoy alone (~30,000 hours).
Rain: no gain from scale (above). Quantile mapping followed by a monthly scale does fix wet-hour frequency and intensity — see the next subsection.


Fixing ERA5 rainfall: quantile mapping vs. scaling
The default method = "scale" rain correction is only a monthly multiplier on totals, so it cannot touch the drizzle problem found above. metscale::fit_met_bias_correction() also offers empirical quantile mapping ("eqm") and quantile delta mapping ("qdm"), which remap the whole ERA5 distribution — zeros included — onto the buoy distribution month by month. Four ERA5 rain variants are compared here, all fit against all_buoy_met_data:

raw — uncorrected ERA5.
scale — the current era5_bias_correction approach (monthly multiplier).
eqm — quantile mapping (100 quantiles), which also adjusts wet-hour frequency and intensity.
eqm+scale — eqm, then a second monthly scale fit on the eqm output to put the total back on the buoy’s.

qdm was also fitted and gives numbers identical to eqm on the historical period (it only differs when extrapolating a trend), so it is not shown separately.


Code
all_buoy_met_data <- tar_read(all_buoy_met_data)

fit_rain <- \(e, m) metscale::fit_met_bias_correction(
  e, all_buoy_met_data, vars = "MET_pprain", method = m,
  nquantiles = 100, verbose = FALSE)
apply_rain <- \(e, f) metscale::apply_met_bias_correction(e, f, verbose = FALSE)

f_scale <- fit_rain(era5_hourly_met, "scale")
f_eqm   <- fit_rain(era5_hourly_met, "eqm")
e_eqm   <- apply_rain(era5_hourly_met, f_eqm)
f_es    <- fit_rain(e_eqm, "scale")

rain_variants <- list(
  raw         = era5_hourly_met,
  scale       = apply_rain(era5_hourly_met, f_scale),
  eqm         = e_eqm,
  `eqm+scale` = apply_rain(e_eqm, f_es)
)

# Cross-validated (leave-one-year-out) skill. For eqm+scale this is the

Cross-check against independent gauges
Because the corrections are fit to the buoy, the buoy cannot also validate them. The same variants are therefore scored at daily resolution against the buoy, the NIWA airport, the MetService airport and PC10 gauges (daily totals in mm), and at hourly resolution against the MetService gauge, which is the only fully independent hourly rain record.

Buoy: eqm+scale matches the buoy’s annual total (1,397 vs. 1,393 mm/yr), p95 (20.2 vs. 20.2 mm/day) and maximum (278 vs. 281 mm/day); raw ERA5 has 44 % wet days against the buoy’s 27 %, and the eqm-based variants 24–25 %. The upper tail is slightly over-stretched (p99 70 vs. 62 mm/day).
MetService airport (independent hourly gauge) is the strongest check, because it shares no instrument with the buoy. Over its 1993–2023 record it reads 1,397 mm/yr on matched days (11,059 days); on matched hours its wet-hour fraction is 12.0 %, mean wet-hour rain 1.33 mm/hr and p95 5.0 mm/hr. eqm+scale gives 15.1 %, 1.01 and 5.0 mm/hr and a total of 1,342 mm/yr, i.e. ~4 % below MetService, whereas raw ERA5 is 9 % above it (1,528 mm/yr, 41 % wet hours, 0.42 mm/hr wet-hour intensity). At daily resolution eqm+scale approaches the MetService p95 (19.6 vs. 21.2 mm/day) but under-counts wet days (24.4 % vs. 32.6 %) and over-stretches the extreme tail (p99 70 vs. 52 mm/day; maximum 232 vs. 167 mm/day). The shortfall arises because the correction is fit to the 2007–2025 buoy record while MetService covers 1993 onward, so any difference between the early (1993–2006) ERA5 and the buoy-era ERA5 is not corrected.
PC10 (Whakarewarewa gauge) reads 1,449 mm/yr over 13,880 days, so eqm+scale (1,340) is ~8 % below it and raw ERA5 (1,535) 6 % above. Its p95 (20.5 mm/day) is close to eqm+scale (19.6). PC10’s wet-day fraction (37 %) is the highest of the gauges, but a once-daily reading probably smears wet days across two calendar days and inflates the count. Its daily correlation with ERA5 is very low in every case (r ≈ 0.05–0.10), as in the source comparison above. Together the buoy, MetService and PC10 bracket the true Rotorua total at roughly 1,400–1,450 mm/yr, with raw ERA5 sitting 6–12 % above all three.
NIWA airport: this check remains unreliable. Its daily rainfall averages only about 920 mm/yr on days it is “valid” — roughly a third below every other gauge — so its rain series appears incomplete (many days probably contain only some of the 3-hourly observations) and cannot be used to judge totals or wet-day frequency. The MetService record now fills that role.
Daily skill: all eqm variants have slightly lower daily correlation than scale or raw ERA5 against the buoy (r 0.75 vs. 0.76), consistent with the hourly double penalty.
