Recommendation (now implemented in the pipeline): use MET_pprain = "eqm" followed by a monthly scale for the historical ERA5 baseline. That fixes drizzle frequency, wet-hour intensity and the bulk of the tail and keeps the total on the buoy. The land gauges read 4–8 % higher than the corrected series (MetService −4 %, PC10 −8 %), and raw ERA5 reads 6–12 % higher than all three, so the corrected total is probably a slight underestimate rather than an overestimate. Because the second stage is fit on the output of the first, it needs two chained calls rather than a single method = vector:
In _targets.R this is era5_rain_eqm_correction → era5_hourly_met_rainqm (stage 1), then era5_bias_correction fitted on era5_hourly_met_rainqm (stage 2, together with the other variables), with era5_corrected_hourly and era5_corrected_daily_baseline built from era5_hourly_met_rainqm. The equivalent standalone code is:


Code
# 1. quantile-map rain onto the buoy distribution
bc_rain_eqm <- metscale::fit_met_bias_correction(
  era5_hourly_met, all_buoy_met_data, vars = "MET_pprain",
  method = "eqm", nquantiles = 100, verbose = FALSE)
era5_eqm <- metscale::apply_met_bias_correction(era5_hourly_met, bc_rain_eqm)

# 2. restore the buoy's total with a monthly ratio
bc_rain_scale <- metscale::fit_met_bias_correction(
  era5_eqm, all_buoy_met_data, vars = "MET_pprain",
  method = "scale", by = "doy-loess", verbose = FALSE)
era5_rain_corrected <- metscale::apply_met_bias_correction(era5_eqm, bc_rain_scale)








Note



expand_met() rounding (fixed). metscale::expand_met() previously rounded every column to 3 decimals. Rain is in m/hr, so that quantised it to whole millimetres: in testing it cut the corrected wet-hour fraction from 15.2 % to 4.9 % and erased all the drizzle correction (and coarsened earlier era5_corrected_hourly rain). It now rounds to 6 decimals and the pipeline calls apply_met_bias_correction(expand = TRUE) directly. era5_corrected_daily_baseline rounds daily totals to 6 decimals too, so it is unaffected.


Caveats: hourly timing is unchanged (r stays ≈ 0.5) — this corrects the distribution, not when rain falls. The quantile map caps ERA5 extremes at the buoy’s observed maximum, and the extreme daily tail ends up somewhat heavier than the MetService gauge shows.

title: Meteorological Data Sources & Forcing Comparison
section: How this improves lake model forcing
text:
How this improves lake model forcing

The buoy reference is now ~19 years, not ~4.5, and ERA5 now spans 1988–2025. Adding the old buoy lets the day-of-year corrections in era5_bias_correction and niwa_to_buoy_bias_correction train on ~140,000 hourly pairs instead of ~40,000, and the hourly comparison shows the two loggers agree on temperature, wind and pressure. The longer ERA5 record also overlaps the whole MetService record, so ERA5 can now be checked against an independent station for 30 years.
Caught a forcing bug before it reached the model. The ERA5 rain unit error above would have meant every ERA5-driven scenario — including every future GCM projection, since deltas are applied to the ERA5 baseline — ran with rainfall roughly 3 orders of magnitude too high. A single-source pipeline has no way to notice this; comparing independent sources does.
Wind is the largest bias in the forcing, and it is now correctly sized. With the doubled unit conversion removed, ERA5 reads ~2.9 m/s (~53 %) below the buoy’s 10 m wind, not ~0.2 m/s. Wind drives mixing and surface heat flux directly, so era5_bias_correction’s MET_wndspd scale correction (cross-validated RMSE 3.59 → 2.11 m/s, KGE 0.18 → 0.71) is one of the most consequential steps in the pipeline. The land stations cannot substitute: the MetService airport also reads 1.7 m/s below the buoy, so the correction really is a land/reanalysis → lake transfer and depends on the buoy’s 2 m/1.5 m → 10 m extrapolation being right.
The buoy → airport extension now supports every variable it needs. niwa_to_buoy_bias_correction trains on the buoy overlap (2007–present) and cuts NIWA-airport-vs-buoy RMSE from 2.02 → 1.74 °C (temperature); wind is corrected for bias (−2.3 → −0.1 m/s) with a modest RMSE gain (3.18 → 2.94 m/s, r ≈ 0.63), while humidity, which uses the 2022–23 buoy only in this fit, shows no cross-validated gain (RMSE 5.7 → 6.6 %). Because ERA5 now reaches back to 1988, era5_bias_correction_extended has far more paired data than before (~140,000–165,000 hours for temperature, humidity and wind) and cuts ERA5 RMSE for temperature from 2.08 → 1.45 °C, wind from 4.26 → 2.51 m/s (KGE 0.10 → 0.65), and humidity from 7.3 → 7.0 %.
A second, independent hourly station is now available. The MetService airport record (1993–Jun 2023) has a real rain gauge, shortwave and wind, and agrees with ERA5 on temperature (−0.6 °C), humidity (+1.6 %) and shortwave (+2 W/m²). It validates the rain correction independently of the buoy, exposes the buoy RH drift, supplies the humidity correction, and is a candidate for extending reference records back before 2007 (for variables where it agrees well with the buoy: temperature, pressure, rain).
PC10’s 1901–present rainfall record is the longest available context for Rotorua rainfall, over 40 years longer than the airports’. That’s directly useful for summarise_climate_extremes.R / climate-extreme-events.qmd’s historical-extremes framing, and as a long-run independent check on whatever ERA5 rainfall climatology ends up driving the historical baseline and scenario deltas. Its weak daily correlation with the buoy for RH and rain (r ≈ 0.32 and 0.06) means it shouldn’t be used as a fit_met_bias_correction() reference for those variables.
Wind direction and shortwave timing check out. ERA5 reproduces the prevailing WSW–W flow (hourly mean absolute direction error ~39–60°) and the shortwave daily cycle (r = 0.91 against the new buoy and 0.95 against MetService), so ERA5-derived direction and radiation are defensible for the model.

title: Meteorological Data Sources & Forcing Comparison
text:
Caveats

Buoy relative humidity is not a reliable reference, so ERA5 humidity is corrected against the MetService airport instead. The old buoy (2007–22) reads ~4–9.5 % below ERA5 and the MetService airport, and the new buoy’s offset drifts from +2–3 % in 2022–23 to +9.5 % (2024), +13 % (2025) and +48 % in 2026 (mean RH 47 %). era5_bias_correction therefore no longer corrects MET_humrel; era5_humrel_correction fits it to airport_met_aeme (1993–Jun 2023, so the fit covers ERA5 up to Jun 2023), and the correction is applied before the buoy-based one. buoy_met_fit_ref keeps buoy RH only for 2022-01-01 to 2023-12-31 for the remaining buoy-referenced fits (niwa_to_buoy_bias_correction and, through it, era5_bias_correction_extended, which still corrects humidity against that lake-equivalent series). all_buoy_met_data and the comparisons above still include all buoy RH. The airport station is a land station, so any lake effect on humidity (the buoy is the only lake-surface sensor) is not captured; the airport fit assumes the same land–lake humidity relationship ERA5 already has. ERA5 also runs 7–9 % more humid than MetService in 1994 and 1996, so the early-1990s ERA5 humidity deserves caution.
Station pressure (MET_prsttn). The buoys log sensible station pressure (~98.3 kPa on both loggers; the MetService airport 98.2 kPa). ERA5 reads a near-constant 1.1 kPa lower (r = 0.997), a grid-cell elevation difference of order 100 m, not a units error; the NIWA airport reads ~3.3 kPa higher. All offsets are removed by the scale corrections (ERA5 RMSE falls to ~57 Pa), but raw ERA5 and NIWA pressures should not be used uncorrected.
era5_bias_correction_extended radiation and wind reference caveats. Its shortwave reference is the NIWA airport’s radiation, which has no overlap with the buoy and so is not put through the buoy transfer function (niwa_to_buoy_bias_correction has no radiation model), and its wind reference is only weakly corrected (r ≈ 0.63 with the buoy). Prefer era5_bias_correction for MET_wndspd and MET_radswd. The comment in _targets.R that describes only 2 wind pairs and 0 radiation pairs predates the old buoy and the longer ERA5 and is worth updating.
Shortwave is validated on limited data. The old buoy has no shortwave, the NIWA airport has none that overlaps the buoy, and the MetService airport overlaps the new buoy only from Feb 2022 to Jun 2023 (~11,000 hours), so ERA5 shortwave rests on the new buoy (~30,000 hours) plus that MetService overlap (ERA5 versus MetService shortwave over 1993–2023 agrees to +2 W/m², r 0.95).
ERA5 wind deficit against MetService grows over time (from ~−0.8 m/s in 1993 to ~−1.5 m/s in 2023), which the buoy-only wind correction cannot see. If wind drives a historical simulation before 2007, the early-period correction is likely too small.
Sub-daily timing. The buoy stamps are offset from ERA5/MetService hour-ending stamps by roughly 30–60 minutes (see the diurnal section). This matters for hourly radiation and temperature, not for daily results.
ERA5 rain is wet too often (41 % of hours vs 12–16 %) with weak hourly intensity; fine for totals, less so for event-scale extremes. The current scale rain correction does not address this; eqm followed by scale does (see “Fixing ERA5 rainfall”). era5_bias_correction_extended still uses plain scale for rain.
PC10 has no radiation or wind data, so pc10_climate_met is a partial forcing (temp/RH/rain only) — useful for comparison and historical context, not as a standalone forcing source.
Hour-stamp de-duplication. prep() in the hourly section drops a large number of duplicated hour stamps (first value kept); the old buoy’s 15-minute rows are reduced to the :00 record. This is harmless for the comparisons here but means sub-hourly information is not used.

Meeting with DO – 11 August 2026
Data & Setup The team reviewed data inputs for Lake Rotorua modelling, including a hypsograph (excluding the hole), hourly met data from NIWA (sourced from the airport), and existing inflow data. The plan is to calibrate against the historical period (2000–2010) and validate against contemporary data (2011–2026), with a water balance assessment using GLM v4’s diagnostic residual outflow.
Calibration Strategy (to be discussed further with Matt) Calibration will cover physical and biological parameters, including phytoplankton dynamics modelled across three groups: cyanobacteria (positively buoyant), diatoms, and chlorophytes (winter-dominant). Buoy data will be integrated to separate signal from noise, drawing on parameters from an old CAEDYM version.
Calibration Benchmarks Key performance indicators were identified, framed as important for climate adaptation conversations: - Trophic Level Index (TLI) and its components — TN, TP, chlorophyll-a, and Secchi depth - Anoxic duration, temperature, and stratification metrics - Phytoplankton timing - Outflow nutrient concentrations to the Ohau Channel - Alum dosing module — accounting for pH effects, TLI impact, and cost implications - Consideration of whether a simplified approach could achieve comparable results
Sediment Processes Discussion around fixed vs. dynamic sediment loading, potential looping of the spin-up period, and the associated trade-offs.
Other - Slides prepared for the MH update — to be retained for ongoing monthly meetings - Longwave radiation to be estimated using an algorithm

text:
28/04/26 - BoP PC10 Meeting

Summary: This PC10 meeting covered the science, monitoring, and economic dimensions of managing water quality in Lake Rotorua under climate change pressures. Key discussions centred on nitrogen reduction targets, groundwater lags, and the costs of mitigation options including constructed wetlands and riparian restoration. Data consistency, groundwater monitoring integration, and the validity of the TLI 4.2 target were debated, alongside updated nutrient accounting, internal loading measurements, and emerging restoration techniques such as ultrasonic cyanobacteria removal. An economic review and spatial planning work are ongoing to identify the most cost-effective pathways to meeting PC10 objectives. TALT engagement (via William) is ongoing with an update to follow, and strong turnout from the Rotorua Pastoral Collective reflects positive MoU partner engagement. A new NZ-based peer reviewer, Mike Scarsbrook (Waikato Regional Council), has been recommended by both LWQS and RPC and is expected to be confirmed within the next few weeks. The review must be completed by March 2027, with draft reports due September–December 2026, an October presentation to LWQS and RPC, and a final draft to council by January 2027.

title: Ōhau Channel Weir and GLM Outflow Setup
text:
Note



Lake Rotorua has a single surface outflow, the Ōhau Channel, which is controlled by a weir with removable stoplogs. GLM cannot represent a two-level crest with stoplogs, so we replace it with one equivalent crest (elevation, width, and a dimensionless factor) fitted to the gauged lake level and channel discharge. This page documents the physical weir, the data used, and how the GLM parameters are derived.

title: Ōhau Channel Weir and GLM Outflow Setup
text:
1. The physical weir
The weir spans the 26 m wide Ōhau Channel. It has two crest levels:

a narrow, deep lower crest (4.6 m wide, 278.166 m) in the centre of the channel, and
a higher upper crest (279.316 m) across the remaining 21.4 m.

Up to three stoplogs, each 0.270 m high, can be stacked on the lower crest to raise the low-flow control level. Their installation and removal are tied to lake-level triggers.

title: Ōhau Channel Weir and GLM Outflow Setup
text:
3. Physical weir rating curves
For each stoplog count the discharge is the sum of the flow over the lower and the upper sections, each treated as a broad-crested rectangular weir at critical flow:
\[
Q = 1.705\, C_d \Big[\, b_{low}\,(h - z_{low})_+^{3/2} + b_{up}\,(h - z_{up})_+^{3/2} \Big]
\]
where \(1.705 = \tfrac{2}{3}\sqrt{2g/3}\) is the critical-flow broad-crested weir coefficient (SI units), \(h\) is lake level, \(z_{low} = 278.166 + n \times 0.270\) is the lower crest with \(n\) stoplogs, \(z_{up} = 279.316\), \(b_{low} = 4.6\) m, \(b_{up} = 21.4\) m, and \(C_d =\) 0.565 is an empirical discharge coefficient. This is rotorua_weir_flow() / generate_rotorua_weir_curves() in R/rotorua_weir_flow.R, as used in compare_rating_curve.R.


Code
lvl_seq <- seq(upper_crest_m, max(fl$level, na.rm = TRUE) + 0.05, by = 0.01)
curves <- generate_rotorua_weir_curves(
  level_range_m = range(lvl_seq), by_m = 0.01, cd = cd
)




Code
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = slice_sample(fl, n = min(40000, nrow(fl))),
             aes(level, flow), size = 0.3, alpha = 0.3, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(data = curves,
            aes(level_m, flow_m3s, colour = factor(n_stoplogs)), linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(name = "Stoplogs") +
  labs(x = "Lake level (m a.s.l.)", y = "Discharge (m³/s)")





Gauged level–flow data (grey) with the physical weir rating curve for 0–3 stoplogs.

title: Ōhau Channel Weir and GLM Outflow Setup
text:
4. How GLM represents the outflow
GLM treats the lake outflow as a single rectangular broad-crested weir. When the water level \(h\) is above the crest, outflow is
\[
Q = \tfrac{2}{3}\, f_c \sqrt{2g}\; w_c\, (h - z_c)_+^{3/2}
\]
with three parameters in the .nml:








GLM parameter
Namelist entry
Meaning




Crest elevation \(z_c\)
&morphometry crest_elev
Height of the single equivalent crest (m a.s.l.)


Crest width \(w_c\)
&outflow crest_width
Width of the weir (m)


Crest factor \(f_c\)
&outflow crest_factor
Dimensionless discharge coefficient, a free scaling on flow



Because the physical weir has two crest levels and a stoplog configuration that changes through time, the GLM parameters are not measured, they are fitted so that the single crest reproduces the gauged rating.

Choices

Crest width is fixed at the full channel width, 26 m (ohau_weir_width target), so \(w_c\) is not fitted and the factor absorbs the loss in effective width.
Crest elevation and crest factor are fitted by least squares on all paired observations (flow >= 0, finite level and flow).
For any trial crest elevation \(z_c\) the best factor has a closed form. With \(q_i = \tfrac{2}{3}\sqrt{2g}\; w_c (h_i - z_c)_+^{3/2}\),

\[
f_c(z_c) = \frac{\sum q_i Q_i}{\sum q_i^2}
\]
and optimize() then searches \(z_c\) between the lower and upper physical crests (278.166–279.316 m) to minimise the sum of squared errors.
This is implemented in est_glm_weir_params() (R/est_glm_weir_params.R), run by the glm_weir_params target, and written to the model by format_weir_params().

Code

rating <- tibble::tibble(level = lvl_seq) |>
  mutate(flow = glm_weir_outflow(level, crest_factor, crest_elev, channel_width_m))

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = slice_sample(fl, n = min(40000, nrow(fl))),
             aes(level, flow), size = 0.3, alpha = 0.3, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(data = rating, aes(level, flow), colour = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = crest_elev, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#D55E00") +
  labs(x = "Lake level (m a.s.l.)", y = "Discharge (m³/s)")

Equivalent crest versus the real weir
The fitted crest (279.147 m) falls between the lower crest and the upper crest. This is expected: it is a flow-weighted compromise between a narrow section that passes water at low heads and a wide, higher section that dominates at high heads.


Code
patchwork::wrap_plots(
  plot_rotorua_glm_weir_comparison(crest_elev, crest_factor, n_stoplogs = 0),
  plot_rotorua_glm_weir_comparison(crest_elev, crest_factor, n_stoplogs = 2),
  ncol = 1, guides = "collect"
)





Actual weir (0 and 2 stoplogs) against the GLM single-crest approximation (dashed).




The crest factor does not move the drawn crest. It scales flow. Note the GLM equation uses \(\tfrac{2}{3}\sqrt{2g} = 2.953\) as its base coefficient, whereas the physical curves use \(1.705\,C_d\) = 0.963. Per metre of crest width at the same head, the fitted GLM coefficient is \(2.953 \times 0.362 = 1.069\), of similar magnitude to the physical 0.963. The GLM crest sits lower than the upper crest, so it compensates for the physical weir’s higher crest with a slightly higher unit coefficient over the full 26 m.


Rating comparison: physical vs GLM

            linewidth = 0.7) +

            colour = "red", linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(name = "Physical weir\nstoplogs") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("GLM single crest" = "dashed"), name = NULL) +

5. Writing the parameters into GLM
format_weir_params() returns the table that the calibration workflow applies to glm4.nml. The min and max columns are the parameter bounds for calibration: ±0.2 m on the crest elevation, and −0.1 / +0.2 on the factor.

Resulting namelist entries:
&morphometry
   crest_elev   = <crest_elev>      ! fitted
/
&outflow
   num_outlet   = 0                 ! surface weir only; no submerged outlet
   crest_width  = 26.0              ! channel width
   crest_factor = <crest_factor>    ! fitted
/

Caveats

One curve for all stoplog states. The fit pools all years and stoplog configurations; stoplog history is not used. The GLM rating is a compromise, so it will overpredict flow in periods when logs are in and underpredict when they are out (the scatter at a given level in the figure above shows this spread).
Pooled fit weights high flows. Least squares on flow is driven by the large discharges, so the low-head end of the rating is less well matched.
Fitted crest is an effective value. It should not be compared with a surveyed crest level, and the bounds for calibration (±0.2 m) are deliberately narrow around it.
Datum. Both level and crest elevations are in Moturiki datum, which must match the datum of the lake hypsograph used in GLM (see the crest_elev row in the config notes).

title: Overview of my Research
text:
Sensitivity analysis: which parameters matter?
Before calibrating, ask which parameters each target actually responds to.












Morris elementary effects: change one parameter at a time across its range, repeated along random trajectories
Effect size: in the lake’s own tolerance. 1 means the parameter, moved across its range, shifts the metric as much as the lake varies between years
Outputs: 33 process signatures (stratification, anoxia, internal loading, chlorophyll)


Source: sensitivity-csps.qmd. Morris screening of 121 GLM-AED parameters with ranges deliberately wider than the calibration bounds, 12 trajectories, 6 levels, 1,464 runs per setup. Daily-forced model with alum.

title: Overview of my Research
text:
Sensitivity results

Top six parameters for each target (mean effect across that target’s signatures, capped at 20). Dashed = effect of 1 tolerance. Wind and mixing parameters dominate stratification and anoxia; sediment oxygen demand in the deepest zone is the only biogeochemical lever of comparable size for oxygen. Internal loading responds weakly to everything (nothing above about 3). Chlorophyll is driven by the cyanobacteria group and the alum rates. Many chlorophyll effects come from runaway bloom regions of the sampled space.

title: Overview of my Research
section: How the screening shaped the calibration
text:
How the screening shaped the calibration







What the screening showed
Decision in the calibration




Wind scaling has the largest single effect on mixing, but wind is measured on the lake
Fix MET_wndspd at 1; put the adjustment in mixing and heat-flux coefficients (coef_wind_stir, cd, coef_mix_hyp)


Stratification and anoxia respond to the same mixing parameters
Calibrate physics and oxygen first (stage 1), so later stages inherit a sound mixing regime


Deep-zone sediment oxygen demand is the one biogeochemical lever for oxygen
Calibrate per-zone oxygen demand in stage 1, with the measured values as the prior and wider bounds




Sources: sensitivity-csps.qmd (findings by target, are the targets reachable), the staged calibration page and the wind and calibration plan memory. The screening used ranges wider than the calibration bounds, so it shows what the model can do, not what is plausible. The calibration then narrows bounds using measured values.

title: Overview of my Research
text:
Frequentist vs Bayes
Frequentist

There is one true value of the parameter, and we are trying to estimate it.

Bayesian

There is a distribution of possible values for the parameter, and we are trying to estimate that distribution.

title: Overview of my Research
Overview of my Research
text:
Reading the formula

Prior: what we believed before the data
Likelihood: how well each value explains the data
Posterior: our updated belief


The posterior is a compromise between the prior and the data.


The evidence term only rescales the result so the posterior integrates to 1. Spoken version: start with what you believed, weight it by how well each possibility explains the data, and renormalise.

title: Overview of my Research
text:
Bayes in lake calibration
Example parameter: sediment phosphorus release rate







Prior
Measured sediment P flux from [student]’s core incubations


Likelihood
How well simulated TP, chlorophyll-a and bottom oxygen match the lake monitoring data for each value


Posterior
The values consistent with both the experiment and the lake record




Prior: the student’s incubation experiment gives a measured release rate, with replicate-to-replicate spread. We widen it because cores are small, taken at a few sites, and incubated under controlled temperature and oxygen. Likelihood: run GLM-AED across candidate values and score the fit to monitoring data. Posterior: the combination. Do the two sources agree?

title: Overview of my Research
text:
Prior, likelihood and posterior

If the lake-only estimate and the experiment agree, we have independent support for the parameter. If they disagree, either the lab and lake conditions differ or the model is compensating for something else.

title: Overview of my Research
text:
Example: Linear regression
We have a set of data points (x, y) and we want to fit a linear model y = mx + b.
For the Frequentist approach, we would find the best-fit line that minimizes the sum of squared errors. We would then report the estimated slope (m) and intercept (b) along with confidence intervals.
For the Bayesian approach, we would specify prior distributions for m and b, and then use the data to update those priors to posterior distributions. We would then report the posterior distributions for m and b, which give us a range of plausible values for the parameters.

The likelihood is only as good as the data. It describes what the data say, not what is true. If I redid the experiment, the peak would move. The truth wouldn’t. The width tells you how much to trust the peak. A narrow curve means the data pin the slope down, and a wide one means they don’t.

Why is alum added to Lake Rotorua?



Too much phosphorus drives algal blooms and poor water quality
Rotorua’s two main inflows carry a large share of the P that reaches the lake
Alum (aluminium sulphate) added to the Utuhina and Puarenga streams binds P into particles that settle out, before it reaches the lake
It is one lever, alongside nitrogen reduction under Plan Change 10, for meeting the lake’s trophic target


The management question: how much does it help, and does that hold up under a warmer climate?

The “why” is general background: alum removes phosphorus in the streams so less reaches the lake; the wording on the share of P load and on alum as one lever alongside nitrogen management is not taken from the repo, so check it against BOPRC material before presenting.

title: Alum calibration: next steps
text:
The GLM-AED model has been calibrated with an alum setup that mixes treated and untreated inflow phosphorus (P) and leaves the stream reaction out. This page sets out what to change and in what order. It builds on the inflow and alum report summaries, which describe the reports and the inflow files.
What is wrong with the current setup

Utuhina is already treated. Its inflow P was measured downstream of the dosing point, but the alum module also acts on it in the lake, so part of the Utuhina removal is counted twice. The Puarenga inflow is untreated (sampled upstream). The “no alum” scenario runs also kept the Utuhina treatment.
The stream reaction is missing. Alum reacts with stream DRP in the 680 m (Puarenga) to 1360 m (Utuhina) of stream reach before the lake. Hamilton et al. (2015) found more than 80% removal in the Puarenga above 75 kg Al/d. The model sends the full upstream DRP into the lake and lets the lake kinetics do all of it.
The effect on the lake fit is small. Steps 1 and 2 (below) show that making the inflows consistent and adding the stream reaction changes surface TP by about 2% or less. The treatment is a fix for physical consistency and for clean scenarios, not for the fit. Once the refractory DOP (0.0046 g/m³, added to the model TP in the calibration objective) is included, the mean TP bias is within 3% for every variant and efficiency scale 0.85 to 1.0. An earlier efficiency sensitivity that left the offset out wrongly suggested a bias of about 23%.
The remaining misfit is elsewhere. Surface FRP is about 50% low (with the high-FRP episodes of 2005 to 2008 and 2020 to 2022 missed), chlorophyll is about 16% high, and TP is about 80% too high in 2017 to 2019 and too low in 2021 to 2022.

What to do

Use the no-alum inflow file for both streams, with the alum module on.
Add an in-stream reaction step in the inflow preparation: a fraction of the inflow FRP becomes suspended alum-bound P (ALU_alp) and the dosed capacity (ALU_ala) falls by the same amount.
Scale k_w and k_s by the mean pH efficiency (0.85) from the buoy pH record, and refit the rest of the alum parameters on the new inflows.
Compare the resulting in-lake removal with the independent evidence: the sediment aluminium survey (ERI 178) and the roughly 50% internal-load reduction found by Hamilton et al. and ERI 128.
Rerun the climate scenarios with the clean alum-on and alum-off inflows.

text:
3 Handling alum

3.1 In-stream reaction
Applied each day to the dosed streams before the inflow reaches the lake. With R the Al:DRP ratio (dosed capacity over inflow FRP, mol/mol):









Stream
Reach
Removal fraction f
Basis




Puarenga
about 680 m
0.9 × min(1, R / 23)
McIntosh paired up- and downstream samples (Hamilton et al. 2015, Fig 20): a ramp to a 90% cap at Al:DRP of about 23


Utuhina
about 1360 m
0.45 (range 0.40 to 0.52)
Measured downstream DRP against the reconstructed untreated DRP, dosed days 2007 onwards; the range reflects the reconstruction uncertainty



The bound P (f times FRP) enters the lake as ALU_alp, and the capacity ALU_ala is reduced by the same amount. Total P is conserved. The calibration build omits ALU_alp from the inflow variables (AEME calls it ALU_alap), so the column and the namelist entry are added by hand after the build.


3.2 Alum module in the lake

Efficiency. Scale k_w and k_s by 0.85, the mean pH efficiency from the buoy record (median pH 7.0, pH_opt 7, sigma_pH 1: about 0.88 in the water column, 0.77 in the bottom water in summer). A prescribed-pH fpH would need a libaed rebuild and changes little on average.
Parameters to refit (priors from the thesis): w_ala (settling, 0.3 to 1.5 m/d in the thesis, 2.8 fitted so far), K_P (about 0.3), k_w, k_s, k_age_w, k_age_s, k_bur, k_res.
Total P in the comparison. The model’s TP leaves out the suspended alum-bound pool, but observed TP includes floc-bound P. Include ALU_alp in the model TP when comparing, and test how much of the TP bias this explains.
In-lake effects. Hamilton et al. and ERI 128 both needed an additional effect after 2010: about 50% less sediment P release (about 16 t P/yr) and more flocculation of organic matter. Check whether the module’s settled-alum uptake already supplies this. If it does not, free the sediment P flux after dosing as its own stage.

title: Alum calibration: next steps
text:
4 Alum setup
This section sets out how alum enters the model, what the stream step does to the inflow, what each module parameter controls, and how the values compare with the Sanila (2026) thesis (thesis summary; the module equations are in the module description). The model carries alum as a phosphorus-binding capacity, not as aluminium mass.

4.1 From dose to binding capacity
Only the two dosed streams (Utuhina from 2006, Puarenga from 2010) carry alum. The daily liquid-alum volume V (L/d) becomes a capacity concentration in the inflow, ALU_ala (mmol P-binding capacity per m³ of inflow), in calc_alum_inflow():
\[
\text{ALU\_ala} = \frac{V \times 1.323\ \text{kg/L} \times 0.04263 \times 10^{6}}{26.98\ \text{g/mol} \times Q}\times r_{Al:P}, \qquad r_{Al:P} = 1
\]
with Q the stream flow (m³/d) and 4.263% Al by weight. The capacity ratio r_Al:P of 1 means 1 mmol of aluminium can bind 1 mmol of P at most. This is a ceiling, not an efficiency: the thesis gives 0.7:1 in the lake-water jar test and about 7:1 for field dosing in the streams (McDowell and Hawke, 2006), so the real binding is below the ceiling and the module kinetics (k_w, K_P, ageing) set how much of the capacity is used. The module’s direct surface dose S_ala is zero; the thesis-equivalent whole-lake dose of about 0.10 mmol P m⁻² d⁻¹ is delivered through the inflows instead.


4.2 Stream fractionation
Alum reacts with stream DRP in the stream reach between the dosing point and the lake (about 680 m on the Puarenga, 1360 m on the Utuhina). The model cannot resolve this reach, so the inflow is split into three pools before it enters the lake. Each day, for each dosed stream, a fraction f of the inflow FRP is bound to the dosed alum:









Inflow pool
Before the reaction
After the reaction
Meaning




PHS_frp (dissolved reactive P)
FRP
FRP − B
P still dissolved when it reaches the lake


ALU_ala (free capacity)
D
D − B
Dose that did not react in the stream and is still available in the lake


ALU_alp (alum-bound P)
0
B
P already bound to floc, delivered as a suspended particulate pool



Here D is the dosed capacity and B = min(f × FRP, D) is the bound P, all in mmol m⁻³ of inflow. Total P (FRP + ALU_alp) and total capacity (ALU_ala + ALU_alp) are both conserved, so the step moves P between pools without adding or removing any. Days with no dose or no FRP have f = 0. The removal fraction depends on the Al:DRP ratio of the day, R = D / FRP (mol/mol):








Stream
Removal fraction f
What it says




Puarenga
0.9 × min(1, R / 23)
Removal rises in proportion to R and reaches a 90% cap at R = 23 (McIntosh paired up- and downstream samples, Hamilton et al. 2015, Fig 20)


Utuhina
0.45
Constant, from measured downstream DRP against the reconstructed untreated DRP on dosed days from 2007; the measured removal is nearly flat with dose



Three points matter when reading the numbers:

The reaction is inefficient in capacity terms. Below R = 23 the Puarenga rule removes 0.9 R / 23 of the FRP, which uses D / B = 23 / 0.9 ≈ 26 mol of aluminium per mol of P removed. That is a derived number, not a reported one, and it is well above the roughly 7:1 field ratio and 0.7:1 jar-test ratio in the thesis. Most of the dosed capacity (about 96% at R = 7) therefore passes through the stream step unreacted and reaches the lake as ALU_ala, where the lake kinetics use it.
Variants. A multiplier m on f gives the three baseline variants: V0 (m = 0, no stream reaction), V1 (m = 1, as above) and V2 (m = 0.5). The lake data cannot separate them (Section 5, step 2), so V1 is kept on physical grounds. In V1 the bound P load is 1.15 t P/yr (Utuhina) and 1.75 t P/yr (Puarenga) over 2011 to 2017, and the suspended ALU_alp pool is only about 0.5% of lake TP.
Inflow P is the untreated series for both streams (the no-alum file; see Section 2). The stream step is therefore the only place where dosing lowers the inflow FRP, and the lake module acts only on what is left.



4.3 Alum in the lake
The module carries four pools: suspended capacity ala and suspended bound P alp (mmol P m⁻³, every layer), and the settled equivalents ben_ala and ben_alp (mmol P m⁻², bottom layer). The processes are:

Pelagic uptake. ala binds FRP at a rate k_w × f_pH × ala × FRP / (K_P + FRP). The bound P moves from frp to alp, and the capacity is used one for one.
Settling. Both suspended pools sink at w_ala and accumulate in the settled pools of the bottom layer.
Benthic uptake. Settled capacity keeps binding FRP of the bottom layer at k_s × f_pH × ben_ala × FRP_b / (K_P + FRP_b).
Ageing. Capacity (ala, ben_ala) loses reactivity by first-order decay at k_age_w and k_age_s.
Resuspension and burial. With simResuspension on, settled pools return to the bottom water at k_res. Burial at k_bur is the only process that removes P from the model for good.
pH. ads_use_pH is off, so f_pH is not computed. The mean pH efficiency (0.85, from the buoy pH record) is applied as a factor on k_w and k_s instead, and pH_opt = 7 and sigma_pH = 1 are recorded but inactive.



4.4 Parameters, thesis values and fitted values

Other thesis results are used outside the module parameters: pH after dosing fell by up to 2.1 units within 10 to 20 minutes in the jar tests but dosing is at the stream mouths, so lake pH stays near ambient (median 7.0 on the buoy), and the thesis suggests pH_opt 7.0 and sigma_pH 1.0 if the pH modifier is switched on. The floc images (87% of fine particles below 120 µm, fragile flocs that release fine particles under gentle shear) support resuspension being on.
How the fitted values sit against the thesis:

w_ala (1.84 m/d) is above the thesis range of 0.3 to 1.5 and about 3.7 times the 0.5 m/d default, but 10 to 30 times slower than the still-water floc speeds, so it describes effective settling in a wind-mixed lake. It would take about 6 days to cross the mean depth. Earlier stages reached 2.8 m/d. The ensemble is wide (0.32 to 4.4 m/d), so the lake data do not pin it down.
k_w (3.4 d⁻¹) is an effective lake rate, not a jar-test rate: minutes-scale removal would need tens per day. The ensemble (0.14 to 3.8 d⁻¹) is weakly constrained, and it is the parameter that shrank most (17% less spread) together with K_P.
K_P (0.80 mmol P/m³) is within a factor of three of the 0.3 default and inside the 0.05 to 1 range of the thesis-informed prior table in calibration/helpers.R; the ensemble spans 0.08 to 1.8.
k_age_w (0.39 d⁻¹) is four times the default, so unused capacity ages out in days. k_bur (0.13 d⁻¹) is 13 times the default and sits at 90% of its allowed range. Neither has thesis support. Fast ageing and burial mean settled alum is lost quickly, which fits the ERI 178 finding that alum-derived aluminium does not accumulate in the main basin, but it is a weak check because the data constrain neither parameter.
k_s (0.029 d⁻¹) is at the bottom of its range and below the 0.1 default, while the ensemble median is three times higher (0.092 d⁻¹): the best member and the ensemble disagree, so benthic uptake is not identified.
k_res (0.011 d⁻¹) is inside the 0.001 to 0.1 range of that table and consistent with the qualitative support for resuspension.

Figure 2: Objective by iteration for each stage (best member and ensemble median; free y-axis, so levels are not comparable across stages). Most stages gain little after the first or second iteration; stage s gains most because its prior ensemble was wide.







6.2 Efficiency sensitivity (old inflows)
The first sensitivity scaled k_w and k_s on the old (hybrid) inflows. Without the refractory DOP offset it suggested the alum was too efficient (best scale 0.3 to 0.4); that was an artefact. With the offset, the TP bias is -3% at the fitted efficiency and +5% at 0.7, so the fitted efficiency is about right for TP (Figure 3). Lower scales improve FRP (-51% to -20% from 1 to 0.3) but worsen TP (+25%) and chlorophyll, so FRP and TP pull in different directions.






Figure 3: Mean bias against the efficiency scale on k_w and k_s (old base).





6.3 In-stream reaction variants
V0 (no stream reaction), V1 (full: Puarenga ramp, Utuhina 0.45) and V2 (half) on the no-alum inflows, with k_w and k_s × 0.85, all fit about equally (Table 2 and Figure 4): the stream reaction changes surface TP by 2% or less, because total P is conserved and the lake module already removes the FRP quickly. The suspended alum-bound pool is only about 0.5% of TP, so adding it to the model TP changes nothing. The lake data therefore cannot identify the stream fractions; V1 is kept because it follows the reports. The ALU_alp delivery works: the column and namelist entry survive the run, the lake pool fills, and the bound P load matches the with-alum file (1.15 t P/yr Utuhina, 1.75 t P/yr Puarenga, 2011 to 2017).






Figure 4: Mean surface TP by period (observed: diamonds) for the old base and the three variants.





6.4 Lake TP follows the inflow load, the observations do not
The variants share a structured TP error. Across 2006 to 2021 the simulated annual TP is positively correlated with the annual inflow TP load (r = 0.56) while the observed TP is negatively correlated (r = -0.52); the error correlates with the load at r = 0.77 (Figure 5). The four wet years (2011, 2012, 2017, 2018; inflow volume above 580 hm³/yr and TP loads of 69 to 90 t against about 46 t in other years) are overestimated by 66% to 113%, while the observed TP is at its lowest. The extra load in wet years is mostly particulate P (about 37 t PIP and 10 t POP, against 13 and 3.5 t), and flood days (3 to 6% of days) carry 36% to 66% of the particulate P of the gauged streams. The 2021 to 2022 observed TP rebound occurs with low loads and is a separate, unexplained effect.






Figure 5: Left: simulated minus observed annual TP against the annual inflow TP load (V1). Right: annual TP, observed and simulated with flood-day particulate P scaled.

Removing the flood particulate P brings the wet years much closer (error +0.013 to +0.004 g/m³, year-to-year r 0.06 to 0.44) but lowers TP in the other years and worsens FRP (the particulate organic P is a source of FRP through hydrolysis). The fix is therefore how fast the event P leaves the water column, not removing the load. In the calibrated 2O member the particulate organic matter settles at only -0.019 m/d (about 580 days to settle across the mean depth) and these parameters were fixed in earlier stages, so event particulate P stays until the outflow flushes it (about 1.4 years).


6.6 What stage q calibrates
Stage q frees three lake-process parameters, not event-specific ones: the particulate organic matter settling velocity w_pom (range -1 to -0.005 m/d, now -0.019), the particulate organic P hydrolysis rate rpop_hydrol (0.002 to 0.3 /d, now 0.016) and the settling velocity of adsorbed P w_po4ads (-3 to -0.02 m/d, now -0.29). The wet years are where these rates can be identified because that is where the particulate load is large. The objective is the alum-stage objective (TP, FRP, chlorophyll, aluminium, temperature, oxygen guards, with calibration 2006 to 2018 and validation 2018 to 2022) plus two annual-TP terms: the mean wet-year bias (scale 0.005 g/m³) and the year-to-year correlation. The inflow flood scaling is not a free parameter, because it is an input correction that would trade off against settling; it is tested afterwards at fixed values (step 4). Parameters that influence oxygen (w_pom also settles the particulate carbon) are guarded by the oxygen and anoxia terms of the objective.


6.7 Stage q result
All 48 members ran in every iteration and the objective fell from 1.10 (start) to 0.95 (best). The best member has faster settling and hydrolysis: w_pom -0.019 to -0.105 m/d, rpop_hydrol 0.016 to 0.10 /d, w_po4ads -0.29 to -0.92 m/d. The top quarter of the final ensemble is tight on w_pom (-0.13 to -0.06) and rpop_hydrol (0.04 to 0.24) and wide on w_po4ads.

A modest gain. Faster particulate settling and hydrolysis cut the wet-year error from +0.013 to +0.010 g/m³ and lift the year-to-year correlation from 0.06 to 0.12. Scaling the flood particulate P as well brings it to +0.006 (× 0.5), but the other years then run low (-0.007) and the overall TP bias is about -17%.
Total N pays for it. Faster particulate settling also removes particulate N (w_pom settles carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus together), and the total N bias gets worse (the guard term went from -0.19 to -1.01 tolerance units). Chlorophyll is slightly worse and anoxic days are unchanged (243 to 255 against 239).
The wet-year excess is mostly dissolved P, not particulate. In the stage q run the top 5 m pools are higher in the wet years by about 0.0022 g/m³ for FRP (0.0022 to 0.0044), 0.0020 for dissolved organic P (0.0067 to 0.0087) and 0.0010 for diatom internal P, but only 0.0003 for particulate organic P. FRP reaches 0.009 g/m³ in 2017 against an observed 0.0015. Settling the particulates faster does not remove that: the event P is hydrolysed and mineralised to dissolved forms, and the alum capacity per unit of flow is smaller in wet years.

What this means. Particulate settling and hydrolysis are not the main lever for the wet-year TP error, and the parameters that help P hurt N. The better targets are the dissolved P pools in the wet years (FRP removal by the alum, DOP mineralisation) and, as an input uncertainty, the flood-day particulate load.


6.8 Refits after stage q
Four further stages followed, all on the V1 inflows (no-alum files, in-stream bound P) with 48 members and 4 iterations each. The alum-stage objective is used throughout, with the wet-year TP bias and year-to-year correlation terms added (S2_TPTERMS=1).

Stage q2. Intended as a narrower stage q (w_pom fixed), but a range helper in step2_common.R reset the limits after the freeze and left w_pom free, so it is stage q plus rdom_minerl (0.5 to 2 ×). Best member: w_pom -0.051, rpop_hydrol 0.21, w_po4ads -0.58, rdom_minerl 0.033. Total N is no worse than V1 this time.
Stage r. The eight alum parameters freed again (wide ranges), holding the stage o and q2 members.
Stage p2. The alum parameters plus the sediment P release (fsed_frp by zone, ksed_frp, theta_sed_frp). No improvement on r: objective 0.766 to 0.778.
Stages p3 and p4. The same joint refit on the base with flood-day particulate P × 0.5 (the input correction from step 4), so the wet years are handled by the input and the sediment P and alum parameters fit the other years. The objective fell from 0.73 to 0.58 in p3. p4 continued from it and changed nothing (0.580 to 0.577), so the ensemble has converged.

Figure 6: Annual mean surface TP by year for the stage o start member, the particulate stages and the flood × 0.5 refits, against the observations (grey: wet years).





Why these stages were designed this way. Figure 6 shows the problem that drove them: in the wet years (2011, 2012, 2017, 2018) the model’s annual TP is well above the observations, while in dry years it is slightly low, and the observations fall in wet years. Lake processes alone (q, q2, r, p2) reduced the overshoot but pushed the dry years lower. Halving the flood-day particulate P in the inflows (p3, p4) is an input correction that lets the lake parameters fit the dry years while the storm load is damped, which is why the refits were repeated on that base.
Result. p4 has the lowest annual TP error, the best year-to-year correlation and anoxic days within 3 of the observed 239. It keeps three misfits: surface TP about 17% low overall, FRP about 34% low and chlorophyll about 25% high. q2 fits FRP and the overall TP bias better (-16% and -6%) but at the price of a larger wet-year error and chlorophyll +29%. The two are the candidates for the scenarios; p4 is the working choice because the year-to-year behaviour is what drives the scenario contrasts, with q2 kept as a sensitivity member. The p4 parameters are in calibration/step2p4/runs/step2_best.rds, and the final ensemble is in step2_ies.rds in the same folder.
Caveats. The p4 best member rests on the flood-day particulate P × 0.5 correction, which is an input assumption and not a calibrated quantity; it must be carried into the scenario runs (build with STR_FLOODSCALE=0.5, as in calibration/alum/stream_variant.R). The alum parameters are poorly constrained across the top quarter of the ensemble (for example k_res 0.001 to 0.5 in stage r), so the scenario ensemble should draw members rather than use the best member alone. The surface FRP and chlorophyll misfits did not respond to any of these stages, which points at the phytoplankton uptake and the dissolved P cycling and not at the alum.


6.9 Phytoplankton P stage (s)
Why this stage. After p4 converged, the misfits that remain (surface FRP about 34% low, chlorophyll about 25% high, TP about 17% low) did not respond to the alum, sediment P or particulate parameters. The seasonal cycle in Figure 7 shows what was wrong: in p4 surface FRP is far too low from February to June (it is nearly zero in March and April against 0.003 to 0.006 g/m³ observed), and the summer chlorophyll peak is 5 to 6 µg/L too high (February to March), so the phytoplankton were taking up more P than the lake data allow. The phytoplankton P kinetics have not been touched since the early biology stages, which predate the alum module and the current inflows, so stage s frees them: the half-saturation constant for P uptake K_P, the minimum and maximum internal P quotas X_pmin and X_pmax, and the respiration rate R_resp, for each of the cyano, green and diatom groups (12 parameters).

In Figure 7 stage s lifts summer FRP back to the observed level (January) and lowers the summer chlorophyll peak, but it still leaves FRP near zero in March to April, over-predicts FRP from August to December (0.005 to 0.008 g/m³ against 0.0025 to 0.004), and under-predicts chlorophyll from June to December. The remaining seasonal errors are one reason for the joint stage (Section 6.12).
Figure 8 shows how far the stage moved: most s parameters moved by a modest fraction of their range, with the green group’s R_resp running to its lower bound. Most parameters end well inside their ranges, so the ranges were not what limited the fit.
Why the next stage. Stage s fixed the nutrient and chlorophyll fit, but more production delivers more organic matter to the bottom, and anoxic days rose from 242 to 287. The oxygen parameters had been fitted when production was lower, so they were refitted next (o3).


6.10 Oxygen refit (o3)
Because the stage o oxygen parameters were fitted under the earlier, less productive biology, they were refitted on top of the stage s member: the four zone fsed_oxy values, ksed_oxy, theta_sed_oxy, rdom_minerl, rpoc_hydrol and theta_minerl (9 parameters), with the calibration window ending 2017-06-30 as in the original stage o. The concern was equifinality, that the oxygen parameters would restore anoxia by shifting the nutrient fit back. They did not: the best member keeps FRP at -8.5%, chlorophyll at +4.9%, total TP at -6% (annual TP RMSE 0.0067 g/m³, year correlation 0.51) and total N at -34%. Anoxia improved only modestly, to 275 days against 239 observed. Calibration-period anoxia is on target, but the 2018 to 2022 validation period is over-predicted, and the strongest sediment oxygen demand moved to the deep zone 4 (-176 to -296 mg/m²/d). The o3 member is the best member of this stage.








Figure 9: Days per year with bottom DO (mean of the 17 m and deeper samples) below 2 g/m³, on the sampled days, for the observations and the p4, s and o3 members.





Figure 9 shows that the anoxia count hides a timing problem. The observations have most low-oxygen days in 2008 to 2010 (27, 34 and 42 days) and in 2015 (31); the model misses 2008 and 2009 (about 9 and 8 to 16 days) and overshoots 2017 (37 days against 18) and 2018 to 2019. Stage s also creates a spurious anoxic year in 2013 (29 days against 4), which o3 removes. Since the early years are under-predicted and the late years over-predicted, a single sediment oxygen demand per zone cannot fix it: the oxygen demand and the production supply have to be adjusted together.
Why a joint stage next. The oxygen and nutrient parameters are correlated (production supplies the organic matter that the oxygen parameters consume, and sediment P release depends on bottom oxygen), but they were fitted one after the other, so each stage was conditional on the last. The remaining misfits (summer FRP and chlorophyll timing, TN about 34% low, anoxia timing) cross those groups. The next stage therefore frees them together and adds targets that measure them directly (Section 6.12).
Two problems cost compute time and are worth recording. A first o3 run optimised nothing because the calibration end date (S2_CALEND, default 2003) left no data in the window, so every residual was zero. A second attempt was contaminated when a watchdog killed model runs that had stalled while the laptop went into standby; the truncated runs scored zero and looked like perfect members. The ensemble code now treats an all-zero residual vector as a failed run, and sleep was disabled for the long runs.

6.12 Joint stage (j)
Why. The sequence above fitted production, then particulate P, then alum and sediment P, then oxygen, each conditional on the last, and the remaining errors cross those groups: summer FRP and chlorophyll timing, total N (-34%), the timing of anoxia, and the stratification that controls when it starts (the model’s thermocline is about 4 m shallower than observed in the calibration period). An ensemble built by combining the s and o3 ensembles would be invalid, because the two are correlated through the productivity and oxygen-demand trade-off. The ensemble has to be estimated with both groups free.

Most parameters barely narrow: the 10 to 90% band of 33 of the 40 parameters is still more than 80% of the prior width after six updates (median 86%), so they are not identified by this set of targets. The parameters that converge are the ones the targets act on directly: cyano R_resp (81% reduction in spread, moving to the upper half of its range), diatom R_resp (52%, moving down), the zone 1 sediment oxygen demand (54%), rdom_minerl (40%), rdenit (32%) and diatom X_pmax (28%). Figure 13: How each target pulls each parameter. For every target, the change in its residual per unit of each parameter is estimated by regression over the first four iterations (about 400 members); the colour is the downhill direction for that target’s squared residual at the start member, scaled within each target (blue: asks for a higher parameter value; red: a lower value). Blank cells have no identified link.





How the targets pulled the parameters (Figure 13). The links that are identified are few and physically sensible:

Cyano R_resp is the dominant lever. It is linked to the chlorophyll, TP (including the wet-year terms), TN and oxygen residuals at once. The chlorophyll, TP, wet-year and year-to-year TP targets ask for a higher value, the two TN bias targets ask for a lower value, and FRP bias asks for a lower value while FRP RMSE asks for a higher one. This is the trade-off between the chlorophyll and phosphorus fit and the nitrogen fit.
Oxygen targets (bottom DO bias, anoxic days, annual minimum, drawdown slope) pull on the zone sediment oxygen demands, ksed_oxy, theta_sed_oxy and rdom_minerl. The zone 1 oxygen demand is pulled towards a weaker demand by the bias terms (the model’s bottom DO is too low), and ksed_oxy is pulled in the opposite direction on the same targets.
FRP targets pull on R_resp and X_pmax of the diatom group (in opposite directions) and, for the summer bottom FRP, on K_P of the cyano group and rdom_minerl.
Nitrogen is only weakly linked to the nitrogen parameters: rdenit is the only one with a clear effect on TN, and fsed_amm zone 2 on the year-to-year TN correlation.
Temperature and thermocline targets are linked weakly to a few parameters, mainly cyano R_resp (through the light climate), and not to the oxygen or nitrogen parameters.









Figure 14: Scaled residual of every target in the calibration window for the start (o3) member and the best joint member (0 is a perfect fit; each unit is the target’s tolerance). The nitrogen terms move from slightly low to above the observations, while FRP, chlorophyll and the oxygen bias terms improve.





What this means for the next step. The joint stage keeps the phosphorus and chlorophyll fit and improves oxygen a little, but it cannot be read as a tightly constrained posterior: most parameters remain close to the prior, and the nitrogen targets compete with the phosphorus and chlorophyll targets through cyano R_resp. The ensemble from the final iteration is a fair description of that uncertainty, so the historical and scenario ensembles use it directly.

Phosphorus. Alum lowers surface TP by 59% on average (members 46% to 69%) and surface FRP by 81% (69% to 88%). Without alum the model TP stays at 0.04 to 0.06 g/m³, near the observed 2005 and 2006 values (before dosing took effect) and well above the observed values from 2007, so the model needs the alum to reproduce the observed TP. The relative effect is 37% in 2005 to 2010, 70% in 2011 to 2016 and 65% in 2017 to 2022.
Chlorophyll. The annual mean falls by 29% on average (from 13.0 to 9.2 µg/L) and the summer (December to March) mean by 43%. The range across members is wide (0% to 52%), because the phytoplankton parameters are weakly constrained.
Total N falls by 38%, presumably through the lower phytoplankton biomass, but I have not checked the mechanism. This is a model result and was not compared with observations (the calibrated TN also overshoots in the best member, see above).
Anoxia hardly changes. Anoxic days fall by 0.5 per year on average (3%), with members ranging from 33% fewer to 23% more, and mean bottom DO is unchanged. Chlorophyll falls by almost a third, so the lower settled algal load does not translate into less bottom oxygen demand. In this model the bottom oxygen demand is evidently dominated by the sediment terms (fsed_oxy, rdom_minerl) and not by settling algae. I have not tested this by varying those terms. It matters for the scenarios: the model cannot say that alum reduces anoxia.

Before dosing the model is close, apart from FRP. TP is 11% low, chlorophyll 13% high and bottom DO 5% low, but there are only 30 TP, 101 chlorophyll and 11 FRP samples (about 17 months), and the surface FRP is 66% high on 11 samples, which is too few to say much. The member bias ranges are wide for FRP (-61% to +173%).
After dosing the alum run matches the level and the no-alum run does not. With alum the surface TP bias is -19% (members -36% to +6%), FRP -21% and chlorophyll -10%. With no alum the same members are +118% for TP (+65% to +166%), +391% for FRP and +27% for chlorophyll. Bottom DO is the same with and without alum (bias -3%, r 0.88).
The skill is in the level, not in the individual samples. After dosing, the correlation of the alum run with the observations is at most 0.09 for TP, FRP and chlorophyll, so the model gets the long-term level but not the sample-to-sample or season-to-season variation. With no alum the TP and FRP correlations are negative (-0.53 and -0.43), because the untreated model TP is highest in the years when the observed TP is lowest. Bottom DO is well simulated (r 0.88 to 0.91), but it does not depend on the alum.
A reading of the result. The data before 2006 support the model without alum (the TP is within the observed range) and the data after 2010 support it with alum, so the model needs the alum to explain the fall in the observed TP and FRP. This does not show that the alum parameters are right: the same level could be reached with a different split between alum and other processes.

Trophic level index. The NZ TLI (Burns et al.) was calculated from the annual means of chlorophyll-a (TLc), total N (TLn), total P (TLp) and Secchi depth (TLse), with TLI3 the mean of the first three and TLI4 the mean of all four (the AEME formulas). The year runs from July to June and is labelled by the year it ends in. For the model, the top 5 m stands in for the epilimnion; TP and TN include the refractory DOP and DON offsets used in the calibration; and the Secchi depth is 1.7 divided by the model’s extinction coefficient (the conversion used in calibration/light; AEME’s own LKE_tli4 uses the euphotic depth as the Secchi term, so it would give different values). The observations are the Site 2 and Site 5 samples from the top 5 m, with at least four dates per year (calibration/historical/tli_alum.R).

Alum lowers TLI4 by about 0.6 units after 2010. The mean difference is -0.22 in 2006 to 2010, -0.56 in 2011 to 2016 and -0.59 in 2017 to 2022 (members -1.03 to -0.36 in the last period). For TLI3 the difference is -0.77 in 2017 to 2022. Most of it comes from TLp (-1.4 to -1.5 units), then TLn (-0.4 to -0.5) and TLc (-0.3 to -0.4). TLse hardly moves (-0.02 to -0.03).

The observed TLse varies by about ±0.3 from year to year (3.75 to 4.35), which the model does not reproduce. Both are caveats for using TLI4 in the scenarios.
Against the observations. The observed TLI4 is 4.63 in 2006 to 2010 and 4.2 afterwards. The alum ensemble gives 4.25, 4.05 and 4.15, and the no-alum ensemble 4.47, 4.61 and 4.74. The mean TLI4 bias is -0.18 with alum (members -0.40 to +0.07) and +0.29 without (members -0.05 to +0.73). The correlation of the annual TLI4 with the observations is +0.31 with alum (members -0.02 to +0.60) and -0.48 without, so the model without alum has the wrong trend.
Where the alum run misses. TLp is too low in every period (about 0.4 in 2006 to 2010 and 0.3 afterwards, the TP low bias; the outlet data show it starts in the first dosing years, see the Ōhau Channel page), which makes TLI3 and TLI4 too low, and TLc is about 0.8 units too low in 2006 to 2010 (the chlorophyll peaks of those years are missed). Both are in the list of known misses above.
Management target. The strategy page quotes 4.2 as the BOPRC TLI target (to be verified). The observed TLI4 sits close to it in 2011 to 2022. With alum the ensemble is just below it (4.05 to 4.15), and without alum it would be 0.4 to 0.5 units above (4.6 to 4.7).

How much to trust the observed TLI. The observed annual values are means of a few snapshots, and the model value is a full-year mean, so we looked at two sources of uncertainty (calibration/historical/tli_uncertainty.R). Both use only the dates when each variable was sampled (11 to 13 per TLI year, 8 in 2020; the rule of at least four is never binding).

Sampling error in the model world. The model was sampled on the observation dates and compared with its own full-year mean (850 member-years per run). This is the effect of the sampling design alone, assuming the model’s temporal variability is right (Figure 23).
Bootstrap of the observations. The dates within each TLI year were resampled with replacement (1000 draws) and carried through the TLI formulas. The band in Figure 22 is the 5th to 95th percentile. It reflects the real scatter between sampling dates, so it also tells us how much the sampling pattern could move the annual mean in the real lake.

The sampling design is not the main problem in the model. The sampling error is 0.01 to 0.03 for TLI3 and TLI4 (0.03 for TLc with alum, 0.05 without), against observed bootstrap sds of 0.05 to 0.07 (TLc 0.14, TLp 0.12). The one clear exception is 2020 (only 8 dates), where the model sampled on those dates is 0.03 to 0.12 low for TLc and TLn (median of members, with alum and without). Comparing the model sampled on the observation dates with the full-year mean changes the bias and correlation by 0.01 to 0.03, so the earlier comparison was not distorted.
The observed annual values are uncertain by roughly the size of the smaller model misses. The bootstrap sd of the observed TLI4 is 0.05 (up to 0.09) and its 90% band is about ±0.1, which is smaller than the bias in TLp (-0.36) and about half the TLI4 bias (-0.19). Sampling is nearly monthly (11 to 13 dates in every year but 2020, which has 8), so the sparse-data worry applies mainly to 2020 and to a single date’s weight in any one year. TLc has the widest band (about ±0.2 to ±0.5), so a 0.2 miss in TLc in any one year cannot be called a miss.
The conclusions about bias are firm and the correlation is weak. With alum the TLI4 bias is -0.19 (-0.20 to -0.16 over the bootstrap), so the low bias is not an artefact of the sampling. The correlation of +0.36 (+0.25 to +0.44) looks narrow only because the bootstrap covers the observations alone. With 17 years the correlation itself has a 95% interval of about -0.15 to +0.72, so it does not distinguish the model from no skill. Without alum the correlation is -0.49 (about -0.79 to -0.01), so the wrong trend is borderline significant. These values are for the ensemble median, so they differ slightly from the member averages above.
Observed band against the ensemble range. With alum, the observed 90% band overlaps the range of the sampled ensemble in 82% of years for TLI3 and TLI4 (TLn 100%, TLc 94%, TLp 76%, TLse 71%), and without alum in 59% (TLp 41%). So alum is needed to explain TLp, and the no-alum ensemble rarely reaches the observations. The observed value itself lies inside the ensemble range in only 59% of years for TLI4, and for Secchi in 18%: the observed Secchi swings (3.75 to 4.35) are well outside what the model produces, even allowing for the sampling band.
A limit of this check. The model sampling error assumes the model’s variability in time is realistic. The observed bootstrap sds are several times larger than the model sampling errors (TLc 0.14 against 0.03, TLse 0.06 against 0.02), which suggests the real lake varies more between dates than the model does, so the model sampling error is probably an underestimate of the true one. The bootstrap needs no such assumption but is only as good as the 8 to 13 dates per year.

P retained because of alum. The two runs have the same P load, so the P kept in the lake by alum is the drop in P exported at the outlet plus the drop in the water-column TP store (Figure 24). The outlet export is taken as surface TP times the total inflow volume (evaporation and rain assumed to cancel), so this is an approximation, and P in the sediments is not tracked separately.








Figure 24: P retained in the lake because of alum (t P per year; median and range across members). Dashed line: the roughly 16 t P/yr of Hamilton et al. (2015) and ERI 128. 2022 is a part year.






Retention. The mean over 2006 to 2022 is 15 t P/yr (members 9 to 23), which agrees with the 16 t P/yr of the reports. Retention peaks in the wet years (28 t in 2011 and 29 t in 2017, medians), when the load is highest, and the median falls in 2019 to 2022 (to 2 t in the part year 2022), with a long upper tail of members. I have not examined why.
Where it goes. About 14 t P/yr of the effect is a lower export through the outlet, and the water-column TP store is 24 t lower by the end (about 12 t instead of 37 t). The model therefore says that alum reduces the P in the water, of which most would otherwise have left through the outlet, and that its main effect is the lower in-lake concentration. This is not an independent check, because the same module and parameters produce both the lake TP and the retention.
The late years. In 2019 to 2022 a few members have no-alum TP up to 0.12 g/m³ (Figure 16), so the upper end of the alum effect in those years comes from members whose untreated lake keeps accumulating P. The median is more representative.

Is 50 members enough? The running mean and the bootstrap interval of the mean effect against the number of members (Figure 25) show it is for TP and FRP: the mean effect on TP is -59.4% with 20 members and -59.2% with 50, the interval narrows from ±1.7 to ±1.2 percentage points, and FRP is -80.3% and -80.4%. Chlorophyll needs more members (the interval of the mean is -30% to -17% with 20 and -28% to -20% with 50), and the anoxic-day effect is within the noise at any size. (The convergence figure averages the member-level percentage effects, so its chlorophyll mean, -24%, differs slightly from the -29% of the ensemble means in the table.) For the TP and FRP effect, 20 members would have been enough; 50 is needed only to pin down the chlorophyll effect. The members are the best 50 of 100 by objective, so the spread reflects the posterior ensemble and not the alum parameters or the stream binding fractions, which are fixed.

This section sets the aluminium applied against the phosphorus it removes, for the streams and for the lake separately, and follows the alum and the bound P through the lake module. In mass, that is about 26 g Al per g P (29 for the Puarenga and 24 for the Utuhina; mol ratio × 26.98 / 30.974).
The ratio is far above the thesis values. The Sanila thesis gives 0.7:1 in the jar test and about 7:1 for field dosing in the streams (Section 4.4). The stream ratio is about four times the operational figure and 40 times the jar-test figure. Only the lowest dose days come near it (below).

For the Puarenga the rule ramps with R up to a 90% cap at R = 23, so the ratio is flat at 26 below 23 and rises to 35 and 72 above (observed: 6, 21, 22, 27, 36 and 73).
Most of the Al is applied at high dose ratios. 98% of the Puarenga Al and 74% of the Utuhina Al went out on days with R above 10, where the ratio is 27 or more. Only the Utuhina days at R of 2 to 5 come near the 7:1 field figure (8), and they carry 3% of its Al.

The module does not output its ageing, settling, burial and resuspension fluxes. The pelagic and benthic uptake are diagnostics. Ageing, burial and resuspension are the rate times the pool (k_age x pool and so on, from the module source), and settling is the closure of the benthic balance. Table 6 is that reconstruction.

Most of the capacity ages out before it does anything. In the water column about 57% of the capacity lost leaves by ageing (k_age_w = 0.39 d⁻¹, four times the default and not constrained by data), 28% settles to the bed and 14% is used to bind P. About 1% leaves through the outlet.
The bed is a sink, not a store. Settled capacity is lost at 0.063 d⁻¹ by ageing, 0.129 d⁻¹ by burial and 0.011 d⁻¹ by resuspension: of each unit, 63% is buried, 31% ages out and 6% is resuspended. The settled pools are small: at the end of the run 0.20 t Al of capacity and 0.49 t P of bound P (about 0.6 t Al in all), which turn over in days.
The fate fractions depend on parameters the data do not pin down. k_age_w, k_bur and w_ala are the three that set it (10 to 90% of the p4 ensemble: 0.06 to 0.73 d⁻¹, 0.005 to 0.14 d⁻¹ and 0.3 to 4.4 m/d; Section 7.3). The sensitivity screen found k_age_w the first driver of the alum in the water (Section 8.3). Read the split as the structure of the best member, not a measurement.



6.15.3 Fate of the P that alum binds
Figure 33 shows the whole-simulation fate of the alum and of the P it binds, in the style of the nutrient budgets above (Figure 26). The binding fluxes are model diagnostics; settling, resuspension, ageing and burial are the reconstruction described below, so the water column arrows do not balance (red note in each panel).

Nearly all the P that alum binds ends buried. Of 12.4 t P/yr bound, 0.2 t (2%) leaves through the outlet as bound P and under 0.1 t/yr is held in the pools, so about 12.2 t P/yr (97%) is buried. Burial is the only way the module removes P for good; the bound P is never released again.
Resuspension recycles a small share. Each time bound P settles, 92% is buried and 8% is resuspended (k_bur 0.129 against k_res 0.011 d⁻¹). The rate times the pool gives about 2 t P/yr resuspended, which settles again, so resuspension delays the burial and does not change where the P ends.
The lake does most of the binding. 82% of the bound P is bound in the water column, 16% in the streams and under 2% at the bed. Benthic uptake is small because k_s is 0.029 d⁻¹ (against 3.4 d⁻¹ in the water).
Where the P goes at the lake scale. In the GLM P budget (Section 6.14) the alum run takes 29.1 t P/yr in and exports 9.7 t P/yr, against 24.6 t P/yr without alum, so alum cuts the export by 14.9 t P/yr (61%). Total uptake by phytoplankton falls from 161 to 70 t P/yr. The unexplained P of the budget moves from +11.5 to -5.5 t P/yr, a difference of 17 t P/yr, which is the size expected if the alum-bound P buried by the module is not one of the budget’s pools. The P removed from the export (14.9 t) is therefore of the same size as the P buried in the alum pools (12 to 17 t/yr), within the precision of the budget (about 10 t P/yr); this was inferred from the two runs and not tested directly.

The reconstruction does not close, so the burial and settling values above are a range and not a measurement. If the uptake diagnostics are right, 12.4 t P/yr is bound, yet the pool sizes and the module rates give a burial of 22.9 t P/yr and a settling of 24.7 t P/yr, about twice the supply. The pelagic balance of bound P misses by 85% of its inputs and that of capacity by 22%. Three explanations are possible: the diagnostics are instantaneous values at the output time and undercount the daily uptake; the benthic zones return more bound P than the pelagic cells lose; or the day-to-day pulses of the inflow make a daily sum of the pools too crude. The GLM P budget points at 15 to 17 t P/yr, between the 12 t of the uptake diagnostics and the 23 t of the pools. The conclusions that hold in every case are that the bound P is buried, not released, that resuspension is a small recycling term, and that most of the Al capacity never binds P. The absolute rates need the module to write its fluxes.
To close it: add diagnostics for deposition, ageing, burial and resuspension (fluxes in mmol per m² per day) to aed_alum.F90 (libaed-dev), rebuild GLM and rerun the best member. That gives a closed alum and P budget for the lake and settles the three explanations above.



6.16 Housekeeping
The run and build folders of stages q to p4 were deleted after the best members and ensembles were saved (about 90 GB). Each stage keeps step2_best.rds (best member), step2_ies.rds (ensemble history and parameter table) and step2_table.rds. The evaluation runs keep result_*.rds and base_*.rds in calibration/alum/stream. The run folders are rebuilt by step2_build when a stage is rerun.

7 Parameter calibration summary
This section collects the calibrated parameters by group: what was freed, where the final values sit, and whether the ensemble converged. The final model has 149 parameters. Of these, 40 were free in the joint stage (j), the alum and sediment P parameters were set in the alum refits (p4), and the rest are held at the values from the earlier stages. The numbers come from the stage ensembles (step2_ies.rds), read by calibration/alum/40_param_summary.R.

7.1 How to read convergence here
Each stage is an ensemble smoother (ES-MDA): an ensemble of parameter sets is run, scored against the targets, and updated towards lower objective, several times. Two things can converge, and they do not have to go together:

The objective converges when the ensemble members all score about as well as the best one.
The parameters converge when the ensemble narrows towards one place in the allowed range, which means the targets identify them. If the objective converges but the parameters do not, many different parameter sets fit equally well (equifinality).

In the figures below, the band is the 10 to 90% range of the ensemble by iteration (iteration 0 is the prior), and the red point is the best member at the end. A parameter that is identified shows a band that narrows and a median that settles; a parameter that is not identified keeps a band as wide as the prior.

The objective converges, the parameters do not. The ensemble median objective fell from 8.8 to 1.0 and the interquartile range from 2.2 to 2700 down to 0.93 to 1.15 (Figure 34), so by the last iteration the middle half of the ensemble scores within about 10 to 15% of the median. The spread of the parameters fell only to 87% (phytoplankton), 88% (oxygen), 89% (nitrogen) and 91% (sediment P) of the prior. The 40 parameters are therefore largely not identified by the targets, and the ensemble is better read as an uncertainty description than as a set of estimates.
The best member is one draw, not the centre. Its objective (0.712) is not the lowest seen (0.634 in iteration 5), and for several parameters it sits away from the ensemble median (for example the oxygen demand of zone 4, at the weak-demand end of its range while the ensemble median is near the middle).
Three parameters are at a bound in the best member: the zone 2 sediment P release (upper), the zone 4 sediment oxygen demand (lower) and the diatom K_N (lower). A parameter at a bound means the range is limiting or the parameter is compensating for something else, and these are the ones to look at before widening ranges.

title: Alum calibration: next steps
section: 8 Sensitivity analysis on the latest setup
text:
8 Sensitivity analysis on the latest setup
The calibration shows which parameters the ensemble could narrow. It does not show which parameters the targets respond to. A Morris screen answers that, so it was rerun on the latest setup after the joint stage. This section reports the result and sets it against the calibration (Section 7). The scripts are calibration/sa/sa_latest.R (the runs), sa_latest_eval.R (the outputs of each run), sa_latest_analyse.R (the statistics and figures) and sa_compare.R (the comparison with the calibration).

8.1 Design

Base point. The joint-stage best member (step2j), with the V1 inflows, the flood x 0.5 base, the alum module on, and the same window as the calibration (2005-01 to 2022-06).
Parameters. 142 parameters varied over the ranges of the sensitivity specification (sa_spec): 54 phytoplankton, 25 physics, 25 sediment, 13 organic matter, 8 alum, 8 nitrogen, 7 light and 2 phosphorus. This covers every row of the parameter table that can be varied, plus nitrate release (fsed_nit), the settling and resuspension parameters of the suspended solids, the weir crest (crest_elev, crest_factor) and the sediment temperature. Wind speed is varied over 0.8 to 1.35 times the measured value as a diagnostic, although the calibration holds it at 1.
Trajectories. 30 Morris trajectories on 6 levels, 4,290 runs of about 3 minutes each. Two runs failed and are treated as missing. The earlier screens had 4 to 5 trajectories per parameter on an older base.
Outputs. For each run, about 190 outputs with variation: the 27 residuals of the joint-stage objective in the calibration window (2006-06 to 2018-06) and in the held-out window (2018-07 to 2022-06); the CSPS signatures and state errors; and about 40 summaries in physical units (mean and summer TP, FRP, TN, chlorophyll, light attenuation, bottom oxygen, anoxic days, stratification, production, alum pools, year-to-year TP).
Statistics. The elementary effect is the change in an output for a step in one parameter, with parameters on a 0 to 1 scale across their range. mu* is the mean absolute effect over the 30 trajectories, with a 95% bootstrap interval over trajectories. sigma is the standard deviation of the effects: when it exceeds mu*, the effect depends on where the other parameters are (interaction) or is non-linear.
The objective. The raw objective (mean square of the 27 scaled residuals) has a few blow-up runs where phytoplankton collapse gives residuals in the hundreds, and these swamp the ranking. The ranking therefore uses log10 of the objective, so mu* is in decades of the objective over the full range of a parameter. The share quoted below is the parameter’s mu* as a fraction of the sum over all 142 parameters. It is a relative measure and not a fraction of variance.
