Cyanobacteria control the objective. Seven of the top 14 parameters are cyanobacteria parameters: respiration (R_resp), settling (w_p), the phosphorus half-saturation (K_P), light attenuation by the phytoplankton (KePHY), the minimum internal P (X_pmin), P uptake (R_puptake) and growth (R_growth). The diatom and green groups matter far less (the diatom and green R_resp, w_p, R_puptake and KePHY are at 0.9 to 1.6% each). The blow-up runs of the raw objective were driven mainly by cyanobacteria settling and the P half-saturation, which is also why the mu* intervals of these parameters are wide.
Physics is second, and wind is the largest single physical term. Wind speed (fourth overall), the drag coefficient cd, long-wave radiation, the light extinction Kw, wind stirring, air temperature, hypolimnetic mixing and the bulk transfer coefficient ce all have shares above 1%. They act on temperature, stratification and oxygen (Table 14).
Oxygen sensitivity sits in one sediment parameter. Of the 25 sediment parameters, only zone 1 fsed_oxy is above 1% (3.0%). The other three zones’ fsed_oxy are at about 0.2% each, and the release of ammonium, nitrate and phosphorus are lower still.
Alum. K_P (rank 9), k_w (17) and k_age_w (30) are the alum parameters above 1%. w_ala, k_s, k_age_s, k_bur and k_res are not, but k_bur and k_res control the sediment alum pool (Table 14), which the objective does not include.
Little sensitivity in sediment P release. The four fsed_frp parameters each have a share of 0.08 to 0.17% (rank 90 to 137), and ksed_frp 0.2%. Over its sampled range, the release of phosphorus from the sediment barely moves the objective around this base point. The same holds for the sorption parameters w_po4ads (rank 129), which ranked high in the earlier screens on the older base; the likely reason is that the alum module now carries the P binding.
Agreement with the earlier screens. Cyanobacteria R_resp and K_P, MET_radlwd, cd and alum k_w were also at the top of the earlier screens (ranks 1, 3, 11, 6 and 17 here); w_po4ads is the one that dropped.









Figure 41: mu* against sigma for the calibration objective (log axes). Points above the dashed line have an effect that varies more than it averages.





For the 30 most influential parameters, sigma is a median of 2 times mu*; for the seven cyanobacteria parameters among them it is 2 to 4 times, and for the physics and alum parameters about 1.4 times. The responses are therefore strongly non-linear or interacting: the effect of changing cyanobacteria respiration depends on the other settings, especially where the change tips the cyanobacteria into collapse. The physics and alum parameters sit closer to the dashed line and respond more evenly. The ranking says which parameters to look at, and the sizes should be read as relative, not additive.


8.3 Which parameters drive which targets








Figure 42: Sensitivity of each calibration-window target to the 45 most influential parameters (mu* divided by the standard deviation of that output over all runs, capped at 1.5).









Table 14: Main drivers of the targets and physical summaries (scaled mu* in the figure above; the first three or four parameters are listed).

Temperature is set by the heat budget. Long-wave radiation, the bulk transfer coefficient ce and air temperature dominate, ahead of mixing.
Oxygen and stratification are set by wind and sediment oxygen demand together. Wind speed, zone 1 fsed_oxy and cd are the top three for bottom oxygen and anoxic days, and wind speed, cd and the stirring coefficient for the stratified fraction. The calibration holds wind at the measured value, so the anoxia targets are tied to the wind forcing and to the compensation placed in cd, the stirring coefficient and the mixing coefficients (Table 12).
Nutrients and chlorophyll respond to the cyanobacteria. Surface TP, TN and chlorophyll all respond most to cyanobacteria respiration, settling and the P half-saturation. Cyanobacteria R_resp is first for TN, chlorophyll and the cyanobacteria fraction. A change in how many cyanobacteria the lake supports shifts all three together.
FRP and the year-to-year TP pattern depend on alum. k_w is the first or second driver of FRP and of the year-to-year TP correlation, and k_age_w of the aluminium and of the year-to-year correlation. The alum parameters therefore matter for the targets that the alum stage is meant to fit, even though they carry only 6.5% of the objective.
Wet-year TP depends on particulate organic P. rpop_hydrol is the main driver of the difference between wet and dry years in TP, consistent with the wet-year misfit traced to storm particulate P in Section 6.5.

136 of the 142 parameters have at least one target they affect strongly. A parameter with a small share of the objective is not necessarily irrelevant: the objective averages 27 terms, and some parameters matter for a single one.
The parameter ranking is the same in the held-out window. The Spearman correlation between the sensitivities of the calibration and held-out objectives is 0.91.


8.4 Against what the calibration identified








Figure 43: Sensitivity of the objective against the narrowing of the joint-stage ensemble, for the 40 free parameters. A parameter can only be identified if the objective responds to it, but responding does not guarantee it.






Sensitivity is needed but is not enough to identify a parameter. Every parameter whose spread fell by more than 30% in the joint stage ranks in the top 32 for sensitivity (Figure 43); none of the insensitive parameters narrowed. Several highly sensitive parameters did not narrow: cyanobacteria K_P (rank 3, spread reduced by 12%) and X_pmin (rank 13, 13%). They respond strongly but with sign and size depending on the rest of the set (the large sigma above), which is the case where an ensemble smoother is least able to pin a single value.
The joint stage freed mostly parameters the objective barely responds to. 30 of its 40 parameters rank below 40, among them fsed_frp (all zones), ksed_frp, fsed_amm, K_N and most of the other sediment and nitrogen parameters. That is consistent with the weak narrowing in those groups (9 to 13% median). Only six of the 40 have a share above 1% and were free: cyanobacteria R_resp, K_P and X_pmin, zone 1 fsed_oxy, rdom_minerl and diatom R_resp (ranks 1, 3, 13, 7, 20 and 28).
Most of the sensitive parameters were not free. 24 parameters have a share above 1% and are not in the joint stage. Three of them, the alum K_P, k_w and k_age_w, were calibrated in the alum refit (p4), where none narrowed by more than 17% (Section 7.3). The other 21 were held at the values of the earlier stages: wind speed and seven physics parameters (cd, MET_radlwd, Kw, coef_wind_stir, MET_tmpair, coef_mix_hyp, ce), nine phytoplankton parameters (cyanobacteria w_p, KePHY, R_growth and R_puptake, and w_p, R_puptake and KePHY of the other groups), rpop_hydrol, w_pom, and the light parameters w_ss z2 and epsilon.
What this means for the fit. The objective has fallen to about 1 while the parameters remain largely unidentified, which is consistent with a large share of the response being carried by parameters that were not adjusted in the last stage. That is not a defect of the ensemble. It means that remaining misfit (FRP low, chlorophyll high, wet-year TP) may be reached more directly through the sensitive parameters than through the 30 insensitive ones that the joint stage spent its freedom on.



8.5 Suggested next calibration set
These are suggestions from the screen, not decisions.

Free these (16 parameters carrying 45% of the sensitivity): the cyanobacteria set R_resp, w_p, K_P, KePHY, X_pmin, R_growth and R_puptake; fsed_oxy zone 1, rdom_minerl, rpop_hydrol and w_pom; the alum K_P, k_w and k_age_w; and the light parameters w_ss zone 2 and epsilon. The cyanobacteria group needs a tighter prior on respiration and settling or a bound that rules out the collapse runs, because the wide intervals and large sigma come from collapse.
Physics and wind. Wind speed, cd, MET_radlwd, Kw, coef_wind_stir, MET_tmpair, coef_mix_hyp and ce have 17% of the sensitivity, and they are the compensation for holding wind at 1. They were fixed after the physics stage. Whether to reopen them is a decision about the wind policy, since freeing MET_wndspd itself is excluded by the standing choice to use the measured wind. The screen shows that oxygen and anoxia respond as strongly to wind and cd as to sediment oxygen demand.
Fix these: the 66 parameters with a share below 0.2% (18 of 25 sediment, 20 of 54 phytoplankton, 8 of 13 organic matter, 10 of 25 physics, 5 of 8 nitrogen, 2 of 2 phosphorus, 2 of 7 light, and one alum parameter). Holding them at their present values removes 46% of the 142 dimensions and about 8% of the summed sensitivity.
Keep for specific checks: k_bur, k_res and w_ala determine the sediment alum pool and the alum in the water, which the objective does not penalise. Keep them if the alum pools matter for the scenario results.
Sediment P release stays an open problem. If fsed_frp and ksed_frp do not move the objective, the targets cannot calibrate them, and the zone values need to come from the measured fluxes (Burger et al. 2007) with a tight prior.



8.6 Limits of the screen

One base point. The effects are measured around the joint-stage best member. With strong interactions, they would differ at another point in the parameter space, so the ranking holds for this region.
Interval widths. The cyanobacteria mu* intervals are wide. Their ranks within the top 5 are not reliable; the ranking of the group as a whole is. The rank agreement of 25 trajectories with the full 30 is 0.98 and 9 of the top 10 are shared, so the set of influential parameters is stable but the order within it is not (Table 15).
What is not varied. The stream-fractionation multiplier, the inflow and flood scaling and the structural switches are not in the design.
Wind range. Wind is varied between 0.8 and 1.35 times the measured value, which sets how large its mu* appears. Another range would give a different size, not a different sign.

title: Alum calibration: next steps
section: 9 Checks that decide the next step
text:
9 Checks that decide the next step

Step 2. If V1 or V2 fit total P, FRP and chlorophyll better than the old base and the efficiency scale moves towards 1, the in-stream step is doing its job. If V0 fits best, the lake kinetics are absorbing the stream reaction and the step needs a different form.
Step 3. Parameters at their prior bounds (for example w_ala well above the thesis range) mean the module is compensating for something missing, and the cause should be sought before the scenarios are rerun.
Step 5. Settled alum in the main basin should be small (ERI 178 found no accumulation there), and the in-lake P removal should be of the same order as the 16 t P/yr implied by the reports.

title: Alum calibration: next steps
text:
10 Open questions

Provenance of the files. How the Puarenga with-alum series (the 90% cap, the unassigned DRP) and the Utuhina untreated reconstruction were produced.
Utuhina dose dependence. Hamilton et al. show the downstream DRP:TP falling with dose; the files show a nearly flat removal. A dose-dependent Utuhina rule could be tested if the paired data exist.
Puarenga DRP. Part of its decline after 2009 may come from wastewater treatment changes, so the upstream series is not purely untreated stream P.
Late-record TP. The 2020 to 2022 TP rebound has not been reproduced; it may reflect event loads or alum ageing, not the inflow handling.

title: Alum stream step: calibration design from the thesis stoichiometry
text:
The alum calibration so far treated the reaction between alum and stream phosphorus (P) before the lake with two rules taken from field data: a ramp to a 90% cap at 23 mol Al per mol DRP for the Puarenga, and a flat 45% removal for the Utuhina (Section 2). Together they used about 30 mol of aluminium per mol of P removed in the streams, and 5.5 in the lake (see “Alum applied per P removed, and the fate of alum and P” on the next-steps page). The thesis (Sanila) gives a different picture, which this page turns into a calibration design.

The thesis finding. Alum reduced DRP in all waters, and the Al:P molar ratios ranged from 0.7:1 to 15.1:1. Where DRP stayed measurable after treatment, the ratio was near 1:1 (Lake Rotorua 0.7:1, Puarenga Stream 0.98:1). Where DRP fell below detection, the dose was in surplus and a minimum effective dose could not be determined.
What that means for the comparison. Only days where DRP stays measurable carry a ratio. Most of the Al in the model goes out on surplus days (98% of the Puarenga Al at a dose ratio above 10, see the next-steps page), so the earlier comparison with the thesis (ratio of 30 against about 1) mixed both kinds of day. The ramp also spends 26 mol Al per mol P on the days the thesis says 1:1, so the two disagree even on the days that can be compared.
The design. Three stream-step hypotheses on the same lake: the previous rule (H0), the thesis stoichiometry in both streams (H1), and the thesis in the Puarenga with the measured Utuhina removal kept (H1b). A calibrated efficiency (H2) follows if H1 does not settle it (Section 4).
First results. H1 and H1b have been run on the best member of the joint stage (Section 5). The stream rule was then fitted to the Utuhina data (Section 6): removal is a plateau near 43% and the efficiency ε is not identified, so the thesis value is neither confirmed nor excluded. The thesis lake stoichiometry is applied by scaling the input in R, not by a new module parameter (Section 7).

title: Alum stream step: calibration design from the thesis stoichiometry
text:
3 What the thesis gives
The thesis result, as stated by the author:

Alum reduced DRP across all waters, but the Al:P molar ratios, ranging from 0.7:1 to 15.1:1 and post-treatment pH values ranging from 6.9 to 7.9, indicate that alum dose requirements varied with differing water chemistry. Where post-treatment DRP remained measurable, Al:P molar ratios were near 1:1 (Lake Rotorua 0.7:1; Puarenga Stream 0.98:1). Where DRP fell below detection, results indicated surplus alum (aluminium) dosing, and a minimum effective dose could not be determined.

Three consequences for the model:

The stoichiometric rate is about 1 mol Al per mol P when P is limiting, for both the Puarenga and the lake water. The module’s capacity ratio of 1 matches this. The 26:1 of the stream ramp does not.
Surplus doses cannot give a ratio. If DRP is removed to below detection, the ratio is an upper bound on the dose needed, not a measurement. The model ratio should be compared on days when the model leaves measurable DRP (unsaturated days), and the share of Al applied on saturated days should be reported with it.
The data are from jar tests with hours of contact in mixed samples. The stream reaches are 680 to 1360 m, with minutes of contact, so the thesis gives the efficiency of the chemistry, which the reach can only equal or fall short of. This is the reason to keep an efficiency parameter (H2) and not fix it at the thesis value.

The thesis range also includes surplus-dose ratios up to 15.1:1. The thesis also cites an operational field ratio of about 7:1 for the Utuhina and Puarenga inflows (McDowell and Hawke, 2006), which it attributes to turbulence, short flocculation contact times and hydrodynamic losses in the stream. That is a dose-over-removal figure for real dosing, so it includes surplus days. Its jar-test value for Lake Rotorua (0.7:1, a 1.0 mg Al/L dose removing 1.60 of 1.62 mg DRP/L) is the best-case chemistry.

4.2 Lake side, the same for all runs

Stoichiometry, set in R. The module uses capacity one for one with P (aed_alum.F90), and no parameter is added. The thesis lake ratio of 0.7:1 means 1 mol of Al binds β = 1/0.7 = 1.43 mol P, so the input is scaled instead (Section 7): ALU_ala and ALU_alp become P-binding capacity, β times the Al dose, and aluminium is the capacity divided by β wherever it is reported. H1 and H1b keep β = 1.
Rates. Refit w_ala (thesis 0.3 to 1.5 m/d), K_P (about 0.3), k_w, k_s, k_age_w, k_age_s, k_bur, k_res as in stage p4, from the member of the joint stage. The sensitivity screen found the alum parameters carry 6.5% of the objective, and k_age_w is the first driver of the alum in the water.



4.3 Targets

Streams. The measured Utuhina downstream DRP, and the McIntosh Puarenga paired up- and downstream samples used directly. The Puarenga series in the inflow file cannot be used because it is built from the ramp.
Lake. The existing calibration and held-out targets of the joint stage (TP, FRP, chlorophyll, oxygen), and the ERI 178 aluminium survey once the values are in hand.



4.4 What to compare across runs

The objective on the calibration and held-out windows, and the surface TP, FRP and chlorophyll bias.
Al:P on unsaturated days for the streams, the lake and the whole system, against about 1.
The share of Al applied on saturated (surplus) days for each stream.
The reduction in P export with alum (14.9 t P/yr in the previous setup).
Whether the new parameters narrow under the ensemble, and whether ε and k_w trade off (both set how fast P is removed).



4.5 Stages

H1 and H1b on the best member (this page, Section 5): one run each, no refit. Shows what the thesis rule does before any calibration.
H2 ensemble: ε and f_max free together with the lake alum parameters, ES-MDA as in stage p4.
Compare H0, H1b and H2 on the criteria above, and decide the stream rule.

With the thesis rule the 90% cap is reached on 99.6% of the dosed days in both streams, and the dose is in surplus on virtually all of them. The ratio is 1.0 only on the 0.4% of days where the dose is below the FRP. This is the situation the thesis describes for the surplus case: the field doses cannot show what the minimum effective ratio is. Over all dosed days the ratio is 27 (Puarenga) and 13.5 (Utuhina) under H1, close to the previous Puarenga value (33) because the dose is large either way. In that sense the previous ramp and the thesis rule agree on the Puarenga: both remove most of the FRP when the dose is large, and the Al:P over all days is mainly the dose.
The rule changes the removal most at low doses. For the Puarenga the P bound rises from 16.0 to 19.7 t (+23%). For the Utuhina, H1 would double the removal (16.7 to 33.4 t, 90% of the FRP), which contradicts the measured downstream DRP: the observed removal there is 16.4 t, 44% of the FRP (Table 1). H1 is therefore rejected for the Utuhina, and H1b is the version to carry forward.

The fit does not distinguish the rules. H1b is within 0.2 percentage points of the previous bias for TP and chlorophyll. H1 is slightly worse (TP -8.9% against -7.5%, FRP -24% against -21%), because binding more P in the streams leaves less FRP in the lake, and surface FRP is already low in the best member.


5.3 What this shows

The thesis and the ramp agree where it matters. Both give near-complete removal at large doses. They differ only at low doses, which are a small part of the Al applied.
The thesis 1:1 cannot be tested against the field doses. On 99.6% of the dosed days the thesis rule saturates, so the data cannot show an efficiency. The thesis says this too (“a minimum effective dose could not be determined”).
H1 fails for the Utuhina because the measured downstream DRP shows only 44% removal at the same doses. The Utuhina reach therefore does not reach the jar-test efficiency, which supports a calibrated ε (H2) at least for that stream.
The lake data do not respond to the stream rule, so the choice should rest on the stream measurements and on physical grounds, not on the lake fit.

This is one member with its parameters unchanged, not a calibration. The lake alum parameters (k_w, K_P, w_ala, ageing and burial) were fitted under the previous rule and the lake already compensates for the difference, so a refit is the proper test of whether the thesis stoichiometry changes the lake parameters.

6 Step 1: the stream rule against the stream observations
This step fits the rule f = min(f_max, ε R) to the stream data alone, with no lake model (calibration/alum/62_stream_fit.R). R is the dose over the untreated DRP, in mol Al per mol P, and ε is the mol of P bound per mol of Al.
The data. The Utuhina inflow was sampled downstream of the dosing point, so on dosed days the removal is f_obs = 1 − DRP(measured) / DRP(untreated), taking the untreated DRP from the reconstructed no-alum series (Hamilton et al. 2015, p. 36). Both series are daily, interpolated from monthly samples, so the 4,980 dosed days of 2007 to 2022-06 are not independent. The intervals below come from a bootstrap over the 178 calendar months.
For the Puarenga there is nothing to fit. The McIntosh spot samples (Hamilton et al. 2015, Fig 20) are not in the repository, and the Puarenga treated DRP in the with-alum file is built from the ramp: its removal by dose-ratio bin follows 0.9·min(1, R/23) (Table 5), so fitting it would only return the ramp. The report text constrains the Puarenga only from below: more than 80% reduction at a mass ratio Al:PO₄-P of about 20 (R = 23 mol/mol) needs ε ≥ 0.8/23 = 0.035, and the ramp (0.9/23 = 0.039) sits at that bound. The thesis value of about 1 is 25 times higher, and the data in hand cannot choose between them.

Figure 2: Utuhina removal against dose ratio, with the fitted and previous rules.





What the Utuhina data say

The removal is a plateau near 43%, not a function of the dose. The fitted f_max is 0.42 (0.40 to 0.45), and the flat rule fits as well as the two-parameter rules (RMSE 0.200 for all three). The previous flat 0.45 is inside the interval and is as good (RMSE 0.202). The previous ramp is worse (0.266) and H1 much worse (0.514), because both over-remove at low and moderate doses.
ε is not identified. Its interval runs from 0.14 to 2.1, so the Utuhina data are consistent with the thesis value (1) and with values 5 times lower. The plateau is reached at the lowest doses (a mean of 25 to 45 kg Al/d at R between 1 and 5 already gives 43 to 49%), so the dose never limits the removal, and the data cannot show what limits it.
The removal rises only slightly at high doses: 55% at R of 23 to 50 and 65% above 50, from 480 days. This is the only sign of a dose response.
Something other than capacity limits the Utuhina removal. A dose-limited reaction at the thesis stoichiometry would remove 100% of the DRP at R above 1, and the Utuhina removes 43%. Either the 1360 m reach is too short for the reaction to finish (a contact time limit), or the reconstructed untreated DRP is biased, because it comes from the pre-dosing DRP:TP ratio and that ratio may have moved for other reasons. The data in hand cannot separate the two.

title: Alum stream step: calibration design from the thesis stoichiometry
text:
7 Lake stoichiometry set in R
The module binds one mol of P per mol of capacity, and nothing is added to it. The thesis lake ratio (0.7 mol Al per mol P) is applied in R by scaling the input (calibration/alum/63_stoich_base.R): the dose delivered to the module is β = 1/0.7 = 1.43 times the Al dose, so ALU_ala and ALU_alp are in mmol of P-binding capacity per m³, not mmol of Al. The stream step is applied to this capacity (B = min(f_max · FRP, capacity)), and the Al reported anywhere is the capacity divided by β. The run below uses the Puarenga with the thesis rule (cap 0.9) and the Utuhina with its measured 0.45 (H1b), on member 46.
This changes the model, as intended: each mol of capacity consumed now stands for 1/β mol of Al, so the same Al binds 1.43 times more P. It is not independent of the lake rates, though. Capacity is lost mostly by ageing and settling (57% and 28% of the water column losses in member 46), so a larger β raises P uptake by much less than β, and β trades off with k_w and k_age_w, which set how much capacity binds P before it ages out. In a refit β is therefore fixed (at 1 or 1.43) and the rates are fitted, not both.

text:
8 Next steps

Puarenga data. The Puarenga rule is the open question: the ramp (ε 0.04) and the thesis (ε about 1) both fit what is available. The McIntosh paired up- and downstream spot samples (2011 to 2013, Hamilton et al. 2015 Fig 20) or the BoPRC upstream and downstream monitoring would fit ε and f_max directly. They are not in the repository.
Utuhina. Use the plateau (0.43, interval 0.40 to 0.45) as the removal rule, which is the previous 0.45 within error. Decide whether the plateau is a contact-time limit or an artefact of the reconstructed untreated DRP (the pre-dosing DRP:TP ratio).
Refit the lake alum parameters with H1b and β fixed at 1 and then at 1.43, as in stage p4, and compare the objective, the rates and their spread. β = 1.43 with the previous rates fits worse (Table 7).
Report the surplus share with every ratio, so that the comparison with the thesis uses only the unsaturated days.

The code is in calibration/alum/60_h1_base.R (H1 and H1b inflows), 61_h1_compare.R (comparison), 62_stream_fit.R (step 1), 63_stoich_base.R (lake stoichiometry in R) and calibration/historical/run_hist.R (the member run, with HIST_BASE set to the new base).

title: Staged PEST++ Calibration of GLM-AED
text:
The Lake Rotorua GLM-AED model was calibrated in stages with aemetools and PEST++ (pestpp-ies): (1) water balance, (2) water temperature, (3) AED biogeochemistry, (4) alum with FRP and chlorophyll-a. This page reports the run that used the updated daily temperature and oxygen observations and the corrected calibration pipeline.

Water level and temperature are well calibrated (level KGE 0.81, RMSE 8 cm; temperature KGE 0.98, RMSE 0.54 °C on 38,000 daily observations).
Oxygen is now reasonably simulated (KGE 0.69, RMSE 1.25 mg/L, r = 0.84). Chlorophyll-a has some skill (KGE 0.20, r = 0.24), FRP is unbiased but weakly correlated (r = 0.19), and ammonium and nitrate are still poor.
Alum has a modest effect on modelled FRP in the calibrated model. With the stage 3 parameters, removing the dose raises mean FRP from 0.0034 to 0.0044 mg/L (about 30%) and leaves the FRP error unchanged, and the alum parameters barely change the fit within their ranges. FRP is low in the model with or without alum, and only 56 to 73 observations, mostly near the detection limit, constrain it.
An earlier version of this page was wrong for oxygen, FRP, ammonium and nitrate. A unit-conversion bug in the calibration (below) made PEST compare observations with values 30 to 70 times too small. The results here were rerun after fixing it.

Double unit conversion fixed. aemetools multiplied simulated oxygen, FRP, ammonium and nitrate by their conversion factor (0.032, 0.031, 0.014) after AEME::read_model_outputs() had already converted them. PEST therefore scored observations against values about 1/32 of the true model value.

Bottom-water anoxia added as a target (CHM_oxynal, number of anoxic layers)
Scored with weight 2


Surface oxygen down-weighted (weight 0.1)
Surface oxygen follows air–water exchange and temperature, which the calibrated parameters barely move


One FRP group over the whole column and all months
Split into surface and bottom summer groups the two held only 5 and 9 observations at the detection limit, and one of them carried a weight of 431


log1p scoring for chlorophyll-a
Reduces the pull of bloom peaks; needs the patched aemetools

The measured values could not draw bottom water down in the model (see Stage 3)


Simulation window set with set_time() only
Earlier runs simulated the full 2011 to 2022 record each time because suggest_sim_period() overrode the window; runs are now 3 to 4 times faster

text:
11 Ammonium and nitrate
Ammonium and nitrate are the weakest variables. What the data and a set of forward runs show (stage 3 best fit, 2017 to 2020, bottom water = 17 m and deeper, December to April):

Observed ammonium is high through the lower water column in summer, not only at the bed: the mean is 0.11 mg/L at 10 to 17 m, 0.12 at 17 to 21 m and 0.16 at 21 to 25 m (maximum 0.73), against about 0.003 mg/L everywhere in the model.
Total N is also short in the model (0.26 mg/L at the bottom against 0.44 observed, and about 0.25 against 0.30 at the surface).
Bottom nitrate is 2 to 3 times too high in the model (0.041 against 0.017 mg/L), consistent with ammonium being nitrified rather than accumulating.

More sediment ammonium release does not produce the observed ammonium. Scaling the flux 10, 30 and 70 times raises bottom ammonium only from 0.003 to 0.003, 0.004 and 0.007 mg/L (total N rises from 0.26 to 0.31, so the nitrogen enters the model but not as ammonium). Adding two or three times the oxygen demand (bottom oxygen then matches the observed 5.8 mg/L) gives at most 0.009 mg/L, and lowering the oxygen half-saturation for release changes nothing.
The released ammonium does not accumulate. In the 30 times run the bottom layer is anoxic (below 1 mg/L) on 11% of days and the flux (0.9 mmol m-2 d-1) adds about 0.7 mmol m-3 d-1 to the 1.2 m bottom layer, yet its ammonium on those days averages 0.004 mg/L. Anoxic spells in the model are short, so it is mixed away and lost (denitrification in the bottom layer averages about 0.7 mmol m-3 d-1); the observations imply weeks of isolation.
Faster breakdown of organic N does not help. Raising rpon_hydrol 10 to 20 times lowers total N (to 0.16 to 0.19 mg/L) and leaves ammonium at 0.006 mg/L; the extra nitrogen is lost.

A nitrogen-only calibration with wide ranges confirmed this. I ran a separate pestpp-ies step (80 model runs, everything else held at the joint stage 3 result) that opened the levers above: sediment ammonium flux by zone from 0.5 to 150 times the measured value (up to 2.7 to 5.9 mmol m-2 d-1 in the ensemble), ksed_amm, rnitrif, knitrif, rdenit, kdenit and f_an, scored on ammonium and nitrate in three depth bands over December to April. The error score did not improve (9.42 at the start, 9.44, 9.90 and 9.69 in later iterations; the best realisation was one of the starting ensemble). Across the starting ensemble, which spans those very wide ranges, the bottom and mid-depth ammonium groups changed by only 10 to 20%. So the ammonium shortfall is not a parameter problem: these parameters cannot make the model hold ammonium in the lower water column.
Likely causes, in the order I would check them:

Units of the measured sediment fluxes. The measured ammonium flux (0.011 to 0.039) is in the range expected for g N m-2 d-1 (0.8 to 2.8 mmol m-2 d-1), but AED takes mmol m-2 d-1. If the study reported grams, the ammonium flux is entered about 70 times too small (the FRP flux about 30 times). This is unconfirmed: the study’s units need checking against its source. The nitrogen step above covered fluxes of that size and still could not fit ammonium, so correcting the units may be right but would not fix ammonium on its own.
Structure and mixing (the most likely cause now). See the next section: the calibrated wind scaling is 1.64 and the model cannot combine moderate stratification with the observed anoxia and ammonium. The model also has no deep pit (hyps_no_hole, 21.5 m deep) while the observed ammonium is highest at 21 to 25 m, and the model hypolimnion is not isolated for long enough. Also check denitrification (rdenit is 15 of a range to 20) and the external N load, given the 0.05 to 0.18 mg/L total N deficit.

title: Staged PEST++ Calibration of GLM-AED
text:
12 Mixing and stratification
The checks above point to mixing. The question is whether the model’s lower water column is mixed too strongly to hold ammonium. The answer is more awkward than “too strong”.
The calibrated wind scaling is very high. Stage 2 settled on a wind scaling of 1.64 (limit 2.0) applied to an ERA5 series that is already bias-corrected. That series averages about 5.2 m/s (2017 to 2020), against 4.6 m/s measured at the buoy (2022 to 2026), so the model is driven by a mean wind of about 8.6 m/s. Mixing energy goes with the cube of wind speed, so this is about 4 times the stirring of the corrected forcing. The wind scaling was fitted to the heat and water budget, not to mixing, so it is acting as a compensating parameter.
The model needs that wind to avoid over-stratifying. The table re-runs the stage 3 best fit (with the sediment ammonium flux 30 times higher, so that release is not the limit) at lower wind scaling and with weaker hypolimnetic mixing (coef_mix_hyp). At the calibrated wind the model is already more stratified than the lake (53% of days against 39%, mean ΔT 1.4 against 1.0 °C), yet bottom oxygen drops below 2 mg/L on only 2% of days (10% observed) and bottom ammonium stays at 0.003 mg/L (0.18 observed).
Lowering the wind makes stratification far too strong long before ammonium gets close. At a scaling of 1.3, 70% of days are stratified (ΔT 2.4 °C) and 36% of days are anoxic; at 1.0 the model is stratified on 92% of days with a ΔT of 6.6 °C, a bottom temperature 1.6 °C too cold and anoxia on 87% of days, and bottom ammonium only reaches 0.075 mg/L.
Weaker hypolimnetic mixing alone (coef_mix_hyp 0.1) changes little (anoxia 14% of days, ammonium 0.007 mg/L).

So the model cannot reproduce what the lake does: moderate stratification, anoxia on about 10% of days, and ammonium of 0.18 mg/L together. Ammonium only accumulates in the model when most of the days are anoxic, which is far from the observed 10%. Two things follow:

Wind scaling cannot be used to fit the heat budget. It is hiding a heat or evaporation error and, through the cubed dependence of mixing on wind, it sets the stratification. The wind scaling should be fixed near the buoy-based value, and the heat and evaporation terms (ce, ch, cd, radiation and humidity factors) and the mixing coefficients (coef_mix_conv, coef_mix_shear, coef_mix_turb, coef_mix_KH) should carry that error instead.
Stratification should be a calibration target. The current temperature targets (surface, bottom, metalimnion bands) fit the temperatures well but leave the surface-to-bottom difference, Schmidt stability and thermocline depth unconstrained (KGE about −0.2 and −0.1 in the first cut).

title: Staged PEST++ Calibration of GLM-AED
text:
13 Issues and next steps

Ammonium and nitrate are poorly simulated for structural or unit reasons, not because of tuning (see the section above). First confirm the units of the measured sediment fluxes, then re-open the ammonium flux range and use total N as a target to constrain the budget.
Alum parameters are weakly identified. FRP is dominated by the dose and the efficiency; treat alum efficiency and settling as scenario dimensions, not fitted values, in any projection. Only 56 to 73 FRP observations fall in the windows, mostly near the detection limit.
TLI4 depends on total P, total N and Secchi, none of which are calibration targets yet. Add them before using LKE_tli4 (see the climate strategy).
Stage 3 was calibrated without alum. Consider running stage 3 with alum on from the start, using the dosing history.
Parameters at their bounds in stages 2 and 3 (wind scaling, crest elevation, sediment temperature amplitude, rpoc_hydrol, diatom R_growth) suggest compensating errors; test whether the projections are sensitive to them.
Fix the upstream bugs: the double unit conversion in aemetools and the rainfall units in the era5_corrected_hourly target.
Housekeeping. The large PEST working directories (pest/, pest_smoke/, pest_diag/), the test folders in calibration/ and aeme_base_prerainfix.rds can be deleted. Archived (invalid) results are in calibration/checkpoints/archive_prevdata/.

title: Lake Rotorua inflows and alum: what the reports say and how the model inflows are built
text:
The Lake Rotorua inflow files used by the model come from the University of Waikato catchment-load and lake-modelling work for Bay of Plenty Regional Council (BoPRC). This page summarises three of those reports, describes how the daily inflow series are constructed, and explains why the alum-dosed streams need special handling.
Key points

The inflows are reconstructed, not measured. Daily flow comes from a lake water balance plus gauged and synthetic stream flows. Daily concentrations come from linear interpolation of monthly baseflow samples, plus regressions on discharge for stormflow particulate nutrients (ERI 123).
The two dosed streams are sampled on opposite sides of the dosing point. Utuhina is monitored downstream of dosing, so its measured DRP is already treated. Puarenga is monitored upstream, so its measured DRP is untreated (ERI 123, Hamilton et al. 2015).
Hamilton et al. (2015, pp. 36 to 38) fixed this in opposite directions for the two streams. For Utuhina they rebuilt the untreated DRP from pre-alum monthly DRP:TP ratios. For Puarenga they estimated the treated DRP from a dose-response fitted to paired up- and downstream samples.
Whichever scenario is run, one stream must be adjusted. An alum-explicit lake model needs untreated inflows for both streams. A model with no alum module needs treated inflows for both. Mixing the two double counts alum in one stream.
Total P hardly changes in the stream; the form of P does. Alum converts dissolved P to particulate P in the stream while TP stays much the same. Hamilton et al. attribute this to turbulence keeping the adsorbed P in suspension.
Two new files hold both versions (rotorua_inflows_populated_noalum.csv and ..._withalum.csv). They differ only in DRP and the particulate or sorbed P of the Utuhina, the Puarenga and the ungauged quick-flow inflow. This page compares them (Section 4.4).

text:
2 The reports









Report

Purpose

Hamilton, McBride & Jones, Feb 2015
Effect of alum on lake water quality compared with external load reductions
DYRESM-CAEDYM

McBride, Abell & Hamilton, Feb 2019 (PC10 Module 5)
Daily water balance and nutrient loads by inflow; long-term lake water quality
Water balance and load calculation


ERI 128, Assessing the effects of nutrient load reductions to Lake Rotorua: model simulations for 2001-2015
McBride, Allan & Hamilton, Feb 2019 (PC10 Module 5)
36 N and P load scenarios and the in-lake effect of alum
DYRESM-CAEDYM




2.1 Hamilton et al. (2015), ERI 49
Question. Did alum dosing of the Utuhina and Puarenga streams improve the lake beyond what the external load reductions would explain?
Method. The previously calibrated and validated DYRESM-CAEDYM model (calibration July 2004 to June 2007, validation July 2001 to June 2004) was run for 2007 to 2012 with the observed inflows. The authors analysed stream and lake monitoring data, built a dose-response for stream DRP (pp. 36 to 38), and then ran scenarios with and without alum effects.
Key findings

Dosing history. Utuhina dosing began in 2006. The report gives 2009 for the Puarenga (the later reports and BoPRC records give 2010, see Section 6). Daily doses were very variable; the one-month combined mean reached about 400 kg Al/d, with doses consistently higher from 2011 to 2012.
Stream effect. Dosing was highly effective at locking up DRP above threshold doses of about 100 kg Al/d (Utuhina) and 75 kg Al/d (Puarenga), giving very low DRP and low DRP:TP below the dosing point. TP stayed largely unchanged, which the authors attribute to turbulence keeping the adsorbed P in suspension.
Puarenga paired data. John McIntosh (BoPRC) sampled above and below the dosing point from July 2011. A dose above 75 kg Al/d typically reduced dissolved P by more than 80%, and at an Al:DRP ratio above 20 most dissolved P became particulate. The observed ratio reached about 90, so free aluminium may have reached the lake.
In-lake effect. With the stream effect alone, the model stayed well above the observed trophic state in 2009 to 2012. Matching it needed higher sedimentation of particulate organic matter (flocculation) and a lowered sediment phosphate release (about 50%). The authors estimated that these effects might last 2 to 3 years after dosing.
Scenarios. Without any alum effect the simulated TLI was about 0.5 units higher. Meeting the TLI target at the current nitrogen load needed, in the modelling, a 25% cut to catchment P plus alum transferring about half the DRP load to particulate form.
Caveat. The alum effects were fixed model parameters, not simulated alum, so year-to-year variation was not captured.
Puarenga confound. The Puarenga DRP showed a clear decline from about 2009 with little change in TP. The authors attribute at least part of it to changes at the Rotorua wastewater treatment plant, so the raw upstream series is not free of other influences.



2.2 McBride, Abell & Hamilton (2019), ERI 123
Question. What were the daily water and nutrient loads to Lake Rotorua from 1965 to 2017, and how do they compare with the sustainable-load targets (435 t TN/yr and 37 t TP/yr)?
Method

Water balance. Daily balance for July 1964 to June 2017 from the Ōhau Channel outflow, lake level change, evaporation and rainfall (airport rainfall multiplied by 1.19 for the lake surface). The residual is split into ungauged slow flow (30%, groundwater) and quick flow (70%, minor streams).
Stream flow. Nine major inflows. Gaps in the gauged records are filled by synthetic models (symbolic regression or LOESS). Hamurana is interpolated from monthly spot gaugings. Geothermal inflow is a constant 0.5 m³/s.
Concentrations. Daily DIN and PO4-P are linear interpolations of monthly BoPRC baseflow samples (samples above 120% of baseflow are excluded). Earlier years use the Fish (1975) means for 1967 to 1969 and reference concentrations for about 1900. Total nutrients add a stormflow particulate term from log-log regressions on discharge.
Other sources. Geothermal concentrations are volume-weighted spring means (1992 to 1994). Slow and quick flow take average concentrations of the groundwater-fed and quick-response streams. Atmospheric deposition comes from Verburg et al. (2015). Wastewater to 1991 was interpolated from Hoare and council data; after 1991 the land treatment system is captured in the Puarenga data.

Key findings

Targets. Annual N loads have risen steadily from below the target in the 1960s, up to about 300 t N/yr above it in wet years. P loads met the target after the 1991 land treatment system but have exceeded it in medium and wet years recently.
Stream P. Concentrations were fairly stable from 1970 to 2010, with increases in several streams since 2010. Hamurana and Awahou (groundwater, high-phosphate ignimbrite) supply the largest share of dissolved P.
Alum. The estimated external loads do not explain the improvement in lake P since about 2010, so the authors infer the improvement comes mostly from alum dosing and its in-lake effects, possibly with some exhaustion of the legacy wastewater P in the sediments.
Sampling sites (p. 33). Utuhina PO4-P is measured downstream of the dosing site, so it reflects the alum. Puarenga is monitored upstream, so the post-dosing PO4-P was estimated by the Hamilton et al. (2015) method.



2.3 McBride, Allan & Hamilton (2019), ERI 128
Question. What N and P load reductions are needed to reach the TLI target of 4.2, and how much has alum changed the lake’s internal loading?
Method. DYRESM-CAEDYM with an hourly internal step, driven by the daily inflow loads of ERI 123. It was calibrated for July 2001 to June 2004 and validated for July 2005 to June 2007, before alum could confound the fit. The authors ran 36 catchment N and P load combinations over 2001 to 2007, then ran the model through 2001 to 2017 with no alum treatment as a baseline.
Key findings

Load reductions. Cutting both N and P in the catchment could take the TLI from about 4.8 (2001 to 2007) to about 4.3, close to the target, without alum. N or P reductions alone were not enough.
Alum. The no-alum baseline greatly overestimated nutrients and chlorophyll after 2006. Reducing modelled sediment release by about 50% (about 16 t P/yr) reproduced the post-2010 lake, so the in-lake effect of alum was similar in size to halving the internal load. Chlorophyll would not fall to post-2010 levels without a 50 to 75% reduction in internal N and P loading.
Mechanism. The authors propose that flocculation increases sedimentation of particulates, lowers organic matter in the sediment and reduces anoxia, with direct adsorption of DRP in the water column where the dose exceeds stream DRP.



2.4 Related: Tempero (2026), ERI 178, and Sanila (2026)
These are not inflow reports but constrain the alum fate. ERI 178 (sediment aluminium survey, 2024) found no accumulation of alum-derived aluminium in the main basin (about 5 g Al/kg, as before dosing) and attributes it to nearshore deposition (under 10 m), storm resuspension and export through the Ōhau Channel; 993 t Al had been dosed by the end of 2023. The Sanila thesis (jar tests) gives an Al:P of 0.7:1 in the lake water but about 7:1 operationally in the streams, fast binding (most within 20 minutes), floc settling mostly 20 to 60 m/d, and a pH window of 6 to 8 for efficient binding.

3 How the daily inflow series are created

3.1 Flow
Daily flow for each major stream is the gauged value where it exists and a synthetic model elsewhere (ERI 123). The ungauged residual of the lake water balance is split into slow and quick flow and smoothed with 15-day and 2-day rolling means. The geothermal inflow is constant. The model files hold flow in m³/d.


3.2 Concentrations
Monthly baseflow samples are linearly interpolated to daily. Stormflow samples (flow above 120% of baseflow) are excluded from the interpolation and instead handled with a particulate-nutrient regression on discharge. The resulting annual mean concentrations of the nine major streams are in Figure 1: P in most streams was fairly stable between 1970 and 2010, with increases after 2010 in several.






Figure 1: Annual mean DRP and TP of the nine major inflows (untreated, no-alum file).

Adding flow and concentration gives the external P load. Figure 2 shows the total TP load to the lake in the no-alum file by source group, with the 37 t TP/yr sustainable load, and Table 1 the period means. The DYRESM-format file is renamed to AEME variable names by format_dyresm_inflow() (DRP to PHS_frp, DOPL to PHS_dop, POPL to PHS_pop, PIP to PHS_pip, and so on). text:
4 Alum and the monitoring sites

4.1 What alum does to the stream P
Alum in the stream converts dissolved reactive P to particulate P. Figure 3 shows the annual DRP of the two dosed streams in the two files, with the aluminium dosed each year. The with-alum file drops at the start of dosing in the Utuhina (2006) and the Puarenga (2010), and the no-alum file does not.






Figure 3: Annual mean DRP of the dosed streams in the no-alum and with-alum files (top) and aluminium dosed (bottom).



Figure 4 is the equivalent of Hamilton et al. Fig 19 for July 2011 to July 2013, when the paired Puarenga data were collected.






Figure 4: Daily DRP in the two files with the Al dose (grey).





4.2 Utuhina: reconstructing the untreated DRP
Hamilton et al. (p. 36) calculated the mean monthly DRP:TP for 2001 to 2006 (pre-alum) and applied it to the TP measured after 2006 to estimate the DRP without alum. Figure 5 compares the monthly DRP:TP of the pre-alum record, the measured post-alum record and the reconstruction in the no-alum file. The mean pre-alum ratio is 0.70 (monthly medians 0.72 to 0.81); the measured post-alum ratio falls to 0.37; the no-alum file’s reconstruction is 0.64 (monthly medians 0.62 to 0.67), a little below the pre-alum ratio. A strict application of Hamilton’s method (pre-alum monthly ratio times the measured TP) gives a mean untreated DRP of 0.051 g/m³ for mid-2006 to 2012, against 0.044 in the file, so the file’s untreated DRP is about 14% lower. Using Hamilton’s value, the stream removal would be about 0.52 instead of 0.45 for that period.

4.3 Puarenga: estimating the treated DRP
For the upstream-sampled Puarenga, the treated DRP comes from a dose-response fitted to McIntosh’s paired samples (Hamilton et al., Fig 20). Figure 6 shows the removal fraction implied by the with-alum file against the Al dose and against the Al:DRP ratio. It matches the report: removal is about 65% at 75 to 100 kg Al/d, about 80% above 100 kg Al/d, and rises with Al:DRP towards a maximum. The Utuhina is much flatter, at about 40 to 50% whatever the dose.






Figure 6: DRP removal fraction in the dosed streams (1 minus with-alum DRP over no-alum DRP) against Al dose and Al:DRP. Red: smooth and exponential fit. Dashed: 75 kg Al/d and Al:DRP of 20.



The Puarenga with-alum series follows an almost straight ramp from zero removal up to a 90% cap at an Al:DRP of about 23 (the tight line in the lower left panel of Figure 6). It is therefore a dose-response rule applied to the daily dose, not a smoothed measurement, and the 90% cap is part of the rule. An exponential saturation, f = fmax (1 - exp(-R / R0)) with R the Al:DRP ratio, approximates both streams (Table 3). The Puarenga has a high maximum and a clear dose dependence; the Utuhina saturates at about 0.43 immediately (R0 hits its lower bound).

The last row is the inconsistent case: the Utuhina stream removal was in the inflow data and the alum module acted on the same P in the lake, while the Puarenga had only the module. The calibrated alum efficiency may therefore have absorbed part of the Utuhina stream effect (a first test found the effect on lake TP small, within about 3%; see the next-steps page), and the scenario runs labelled “no alum” still contained the Utuhina stream treatment (about 30% less DRP).


5.2 Recommended handling

Use the no-alum file for all streams with the alum module on, so the dose is the only driver and the with/without alum scenarios are clean.
Add an in-stream reaction step before the lake: the Puarenga (about 680 m) and Utuhina (about 1360 m) reaches react a fraction of the DRP with the dosed alum. Move that fraction of FRP into the suspended alum-bound pool (ALU_alp) and reduce ALU_ala by the same amount. Use fmax and R0 from Table 3, with the Utuhina range (about 0.4 to 0.52) reflecting the reconstruction uncertainty.
Treat the in-lake effects separately. Hamilton et al. and ERI 128 both needed an additional in-lake effect (about 50% less sediment P release, more flocculation). The module’s settled-alum uptake and the sediment P flux parameters should be checked against that, once the inflows are consistent.
Keep the free-aluminium point in view. At Al:DRP well above 20 most of the dosed Al is not used in the stream and reaches the lake; this excess is what the lake-side module acts on.

title: Lake Rotorua inflows and alum: what the reports say and how the model inflows are built
text:
6 Open questions

Dosing start dates differ between sources. Utuhina is 2006 in all of them. Puarenga is 2009 (Hamilton et al. 2015), 2010 (ERI 178, ERI 128 intro and the BoPRC dose record used in the model); two other passages swap the streams. The model uses the dose record.
Provenance of the two files. The method that made the with-alum Puarenga series (the cap of about 90% removal, the unassigned DRP), and the untreated Utuhina reconstruction (a DRP:TP about 14% below what Hamilton’s pre-alum monthly ratios give), should be confirmed with whoever produced them.
Puarenga DRP before alum. Hamilton et al. link part of the post-2009 DRP decline to wastewater treatment changes, so the upstream series is not purely untreated stream P.
Dose dependence in the Utuhina. Hamilton et al. show DRP:TP falling with dose below the Utuhina sampling site (their Fig 17); the file’s removal is nearly flat. Monthly spot samples against a variable daily dose make this hard to resolve.
Timing. Monthly samples are matched to a daily dose, so short high-dose events are not captured.

title: Sensitivity of the CSPS Metrics to Model Parameters
text:
4 Findings by target

4.1 Polymixis
Stratification is controlled by the wind and mixing parameters: wind scaling, coef_wind_stir, the drag coefficient cd, the hypolimnetic mixing coefficient and the radiation scalings (heat input). More wind, stirring and drag reduce stratification; more long-wave radiation and warmer air increase it. Biogeochemical parameters have no meaningful effect on any mixing metric. coef_mix_shear is inert.
The wind scaling has the largest single effect, which is the reason it must not be used as a free parameter (the wind is measured on the lake): the mixing coefficients (coef_wind_stir, cd) have comparable leverage over the same metrics and are the right place for the adjustment.


4.2 Anoxia
Bottom-water oxygen and anoxic days are driven by the same mixing parameters as stratification, because the length of a stratified spell sets how long the bottom water can be drawn down. The only biogeochemical lever of comparable size is the sediment oxygen demand in the deepest zone (fsed_oxy zone 1), which also controls whether the model has anoxic years at all. The rate of oxygen decline during stratified spells (a process-level measure of oxygen demand) responds to cyanobacteria respiration and to the zone-1 oxygen demand.


4.3 Internal loading
This is the least well-controlled target. No parameter moves any loading metric by more than about 3 tolerances. Bottom-water ammonium responds to nitrification (rnitrif) and, less, to wind and the cyanobacteria nitrogen uptake. Sediment ammonium flux has a smaller effect than expected. The bottom FRP and TP gradients respond to almost nothing, including the sediment FRP flux and the P adsorption parameters.


4.4 Phytoplankton
Chlorophyll-a is controlled by the cyanobacteria group (respiration R_resp, light I_K, phosphorus half-saturation K_P, KePHY, buoyancy w_p), and by the alum rates when alum is on. A large part of the sampled space produces runaway cyanobacteria blooms (the median chlorophyll-a spans 0 to over 1,000 mg/m3), so the effect sizes for chlorophyll are dominated by those regions and overstate the sensitivity in the realistic range.

Physics and oxygen are unchanged on average (means agree to 3 figures). Individual paired runs do scatter by up to about a tolerance for some mixing metrics; this is a noise floor of the experiment (small differences amplified near stratification thresholds), so effects under one tolerance on those metrics should not be interpreted.
Phosphorus responds as expected: the 90th percentile of bottom FRP falls by about 60% and bottom TP by about 25%, and the mean simulated TLI3 is lower by about 0.8 units.
Chlorophyll-a is lower with alum in the bloom-prone parameter sets and unchanged in typical runs.
Bottom to surface contrast is larger with alum (alum removes surface phosphorus more than bottom), so the internal-loading signatures read stronger in a dosed lake.




Parameter influence with and without alum.


Parameter rankings are broadly the same (Spearman 0.69), but with alum the alum rate k_w, K_P, k_age_w, k_s and w_ala become influential for chlorophyll and phosphorus and compete with the phytoplankton and sediment parameters. This is the case for calibrating phosphorus and phytoplankton parameters with the alum module off, on years without dosing, and the alum parameters afterwards.

Parameter influence under hourly and daily forcing on the same window.


The two forcings give the same picture of which parameters matter, but different absolute behaviour:

Rankings agree. The overall rank correlation of parameter influence is 0.86, no lower than the 0.85 between the two daily windows (2010 to 2013 and 2012 to 2015), so changing from hourly to daily forcing alters the rankings no more than changing the years. The same parameters lead each target in both: wind scaling, coef_wind_stir, cd and fsed_oxy zone 1 for anoxia and mixing, and the cyanobacteria respiration, light and phosphorus parameters (and the alum rates) for chlorophyll.
Response to the parameters agrees. For identical parameter sets the outputs correlate at 0.93 to 0.98 for the main stratification and anoxia metrics (the spell-length metrics are noisier, 0.25 to 0.84) and 0.99 for chlorophyll-a, so a parameter set that is better under one forcing is better under the other.
But daily forcing is systematically more stratified. For the same parameters the daily-forced model is stratified on 48% of days against 37% with hourly forcing (a difference of about 1.8 tolerances, almost all of it in winter), has a bottom temperature 1.7 °C lower in the stratified season, and has more anoxic days (14% against 9%). Averaging the wind over a day removes the short windy periods that break stratification, so the daily-forced model has less mixing energy for the same parameters.
The mixing parameters matter somewhat more under daily forcing (physics group mean effect 2.1 against 1.6; wind scaling 5.6 against 4.1): with less mixing energy built in, the model leans harder on them, which is also why daily forcing is more likely to produce a compensating wind scaling.
The observed stratification is easier to reach with hourly forcing: 19% of sampled parameter sets land within tolerance for the stratified fraction, against 8% with daily.
Internal loading and phosphorus targets are unreachable under both (bottom FRP and TP 90th percentiles within tolerance in 0% of runs).

What this means: the sensitivity conclusions are transferable between forcings, but fitted parameter values are not. Mixing coefficients calibrated to daily forcing would absorb the missing sub-daily wind and would be too strong when used with hourly forcing, such as the climate scenarios disaggregated to hourly. The physics should be calibrated with hourly forcing, and daily forcing is acceptable for ranking parameters and for screening.

title: Sensitivity of the CSPS Metrics to Model Parameters
text:
9 Implications for the calibration

Fix wind at 1 (it is measured). Calibrate stratification, mixing and anoxia with coef_wind_stir, cd, ce/ch, the hypolimnetic and other mixing coefficients, the radiation scalings (kept narrow), and the deep-zone oxygen demand.
Hold coef_mix_shear, ksed_nit and rcpom_bdown fixed: they do not affect any target.
Calibrate phosphorus and chlorophyll parameters with alum off, on years without dosing, because k_w, K_P and the other alum rates otherwise compete with the cyanobacteria and sediment parameters for the same data. Use narrow cyanobacteria ranges to avoid the runaway-bloom region.
Do not use bottom FRP and TP concentration as targets in the current structure; they cannot be reached.
Use the ensemble smoother with the CSPS residuals, not a single best parameter set, because the response is strongly interacting.

title: Sensitivity of the CSPS Metrics to Model Parameters
text:
10 Limitations

Morris screening with 12 trajectories ranks parameters but does not give variance shares; interactions are large, so a variance-based analysis (Sobol) on the 15 to 20 parameters chosen for calibration would be the next step.
Some phytoplankton temperature parameters (theta_growth, T_std, T_opt, T_max) were restricted to the region where AED’s temperature-function solver converges; outside it the model stops with “Cannot solve for fT”.
Three years are scored per run, so the signatures that depend on rare events (anoxic years, long spells) are noisy.
The daily-forced window before 2011 uses an extension of the raw daily ERA5 that correlates poorly with the hourly record (wind r = 0.45, rain r = 0.42), which affects the spin-up of the first setup only.
